title: Murder: the most serious offence
statement: Murder is the most serious offence: its deliberate taking of life is always a matter of the utmost seriousness, and anyone who contemplates an unlawful killing must anticipate that the penalty may be severe. (That passage is about murder; the other chapter-21 offences — notably infanticide, with its own regime and 5-year maximum — are assessed under their own items.) Chapter 21 covers murder (intentional and reckless), statutory murder, defensive homicide, infanticide, attempted murder and incitement to murder.

refs.q: Murder is the most serious of all criminal offences. It has always possessed a special significance as the law attributes enormous significance to the sanctity of human life, and its deliberate taking must never be regarded as anything other than a matter of the utmost seriousness. Anyone who contemplates the unlawful killing of another must anticipate that the penalty to be imposed on conviction may be severe.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder

refs.q: This includes the following offences: • Murder (intentional and reckless); • Unintentional killing in the furtherance of a crime of violence; • Defensive homicide; • Infanticide; • Attempted murder; and • Incitement to murder.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder

title: Murder: current sentencing practices
statement: Practices for murder have steadily increased. A guilty plea to murder is generally accepted to attract a non-parole period. Inciting the murder of a partner, former partner or family member is an extreme form of family violence whose gravity is not reflected in current practices, which should increase.

refs.q: Current sentencing practices for murder have steadily increased over time.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 21.1.2 – Current sentencing practices

refs.q: It is generally accepted that a plea of guilty to murder will attract the imposition of a non-parole period.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 21.1.2 – Current sentencing practices

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has also stated that inciting the murder of a partner, former partner or family member is an extreme form of family violence whose gravity is not reflected in current sentencing practices, which should be increased to adequately deter and denounce family violence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 21.1.2 – Current sentencing practices

title: Murder: purposes
statement: The court must denounce and condemn the conduct, impose just punishment, vindicate the rights of the deceased and acknowledge the grief and trauma of those left behind; general deterrence is important. A murder to punish or take revenge on someone who assisted law enforcement calls for punishment and denunciation of a very high order.

refs.q: When sentencing an offender for common law murder, the court has a duty to impose a sentence that denounces and condemns the offender’s conduct. It must impose a just punishment, vindicate the rights of the deceased, and acknowledge the grief and trauma for those left behind. The principle of general deterrence is also an important consideration, and a murder that is motivated by a desire to punish or take revenge against a person who has assisted law enforcement in the prosecution of a crime is very serious and ‘calls for punishment and denunciation of a very high order’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.1 – Murder

title: Statutory murder (unintentional killing in furtherance of a crime of violence)
statement: Statutory murder is not inherently less serious than common law murder and may be more serious than some instances of it. It covers a wide range (from accidental death to intended death); the issue is the nature of the violent act and the offender’s state of mind when committing it. The characterisation of a type of murder is not determinative of objective gravity (fn 3320). The Manual adds that “It ‘has no bearing on the sentencing outcome’” without making clear what “It” refers to (presumably the statutory rather than common-law classification). (See csp.uplift_statutory_murder.)

refs.q: Statutory murder (unintentional killing in the furtherance of a violent crime) is not an inherently less serious crime than common law murder. It might even be more serious and attract a higher sentence than some instances of common law murder.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.2 – Unintentional killing in the furtherance of a crime of violence

refs.q: These killings may encompass a wide variety of circumstances, ‘from the case where the death is an accidental result of the act of violence to the case where the death is the intended result of the act’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.2 – Unintentional killing in the furtherance of a crime of violence

refs.q: The relevant issue for sentencing is the nature of the violent act which caused the victim’s death, and the offender’s state of mind when committing that violent act.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.2 – Unintentional killing in the furtherance of a crime of violence

refs.q: the characterisation of a particular type of murder is not determinative of the objective gravity of a case
It ‘has no bearing on the sentencing outcome.’
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.2 – Unintentional killing in the furtherance of a crime of violence

title: Reckless murder
statement: Reckless murder may be regarded as seriously as intentional murder and is not necessarily of lesser seriousness or culpability.

refs.q: Similarly, depending on the circumstances, an offence of reckless murder might be regarded as seriously as a murder where specific intent has been proved. It is not necessarily a crime of lesser seriousness or moral culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.3 – Reckless murder

refs.q: A distinction cannot always be drawn between a premeditated murder, and one committed where the offender went armed with a loaded weapon, to a place they knew to be occupied, intending to use it and cause, at the least, property damage.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.3 – Reckless murder

title: Defensive homicide (abolished offence)
statement: Defensive homicide is serious (intentional taking of life; maximum 20 years). Seriousness is usually assessed by the disproportion between the perceived threat and the response. That is difficult in the family violence context, where the legislation allows reasonable grounds for believing the conduct necessary even if it involves excessive force or the victim is not the person posing the threat (and, e.g., a woman “invariably uses a weapon” and may strike multiple times); outside that context multiple strikes in response to a verbal or minor physical attack may make it a very serious example. The critical question is what inference to draw about state of mind. The authority for several of these propositions (fns 3329–3331) is uncertain (flag.ibid_chain_21_2_4).

refs.q: The crime of defensive homicide is a serious crime, involving the intentional taking of the life of another. The maximum sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment indicates its gravity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.4 – Defensive homicide

refs.q: In assessing the seriousness of defensive homicide, ‘courts have usually looked at the degree of disproportion between the perceived threat or violence and the offender’s response to it’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.4 – Defensive homicide

refs.q: Moreover, in the family violence context a man will often use his hands against a female partner where a woman ‘invariably uses a weapon’ against a male partner fearing that otherwise she will be overpowered and injured further. For that same reason it is not unusual for a woman to strike multiple times.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.4 – Defensive homicide

refs.q: Conversely, in cases not involving family violence, multiple strikes in response to a verbal or minor physical attack may be seen as so totally disproportionate that the killing becomes a very serious example of the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.4 – Defensive homicide

refs.q: The critical question is what inference should be drawn about the offender’s state of mind from the fact of their having inflicted such violence and from the surrounding circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.4 – Defensive homicide

refs.q: But this is difficult in the family violence context where the legislation provides that an offender might have reasonable grounds for believing their conduct is necessary to defend themselves or family, even if it involves the use of excessive force or where the victim of the crime is not the one who poses the threat to the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.4 – Defensive homicide

title: Infanticide
statement: Infanticide requires that the balance of the woman’s mind was disturbed by a disorder consequent on giving birth within the preceding two years; sentence is fixed by reference to the five-year maximum and the nature and gravity of the disturbance. Acceptance of an infanticide plea does not affect sentences for other offences committed at the same time, which follow their own maxima and Verdins: although the same evidence will likely be considered, sentencing for the other offences is not informed by the unique infanticide regime. Labels like “very serious example” should not be applied simplistically.

refs.q: The mental condition relevant to infanticide is that the balance of a woman’s mind was disturbed because of a disorder consequent on her having given birth within the preceding two years. The sentence to be imposed is then determined by reference to the maximum penalty of five years for that offence and having regard to the nature and gravity of the disturbance of the woman’s mind.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.5 – Infanticide

refs.q: However, the prosecution’s acceptance of a plea to a charge of infanticide is not relevant to the sentences imposed on any other offences committed at the same time. Those are to be imposed by reference to their maximum penalties and in accordance with Verdins.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.5 – Infanticide

refs.q: Use of phrases such as a ‘very serious example’ do not attach to this offence in a simplistic manner and the surrounding circumstances need to be considered.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.5 – Infanticide

refs.q: While this is likely to require consideration of the same evidence, sentencing for the other offences is not to be informed by the unique sentencing regime created for the offence of infanticide.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.5 – Infanticide

title: Attempted murder
statement: Attempted murder requires a specific intent to kill; there is no specific practical ceiling below the maximum — each case turns on its facts, given the seriousness of the offence and the maximum penalty; gravity is assessed by reference to the murderous intent. Family violence, an informer victim, or catastrophic injuries can aggravate; those who attempt to kill a former partner, or those close to one, must expect very substantial sentences (Malovski, fn 3313).

refs.q: Attempted murder is a very serious offence which, unlike murder, requires a specific intent to kill. There is no specific practical ceiling on the period of imprisonment that may be imposed, each case must be decided on its facts, given the serious nature of the offence and the maximum penalty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.6 – Attempted murder

refs.q: The gravity of an attempted murder is assessed by reference to the murderous intent.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.6 – Attempted murder

refs.q: Attempted murders committed in the context of family violence, of a police informer, or where the intended victims suffer catastrophic injuries can aggravate the seriousness of the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.6 – Attempted murder

refs.q: See also Malovski v The King [2025] VSCA 72, [67] finding that those who attempt to kill their former partners or those close to their former partners must expect very substantial sentences of imprisonment.

title: Incitement to murder
statement: Seriousness depends on the crime incited; incitement to murder is a special, serious category that may call for more punishment than some murders; the circumstances giving rise to it must be considered. Inciting the murder of a partner is an extreme form of family violence: sentences must increase and culpability will typically be high.

refs.q: The seriousness of the incitement depends on the gravity of the crime being incited.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.7 – Incitement to murder

refs.q: Where murder is incited, the case is in a special category in the sense of being a serious example of the crime of incitement and in some cases will call for more serious punishment than some instances of murder. In considering the appropriate sentence, the court must consider the circumstances that gave rise to the incitement to murder.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.7 – Incitement to murder

refs.q: Inciting the murder of a partner is an extreme form of family violence. The Court of Appeal has held that sentences for incitement to murder in the context of family violence must be increased to reflect the degree of criminality involved in inciting another person to kill a victim. The degree of moral culpability of the offender in such a case will typically be high, as they will have intended the death of the victim and taken active steps to bring it about.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.2 – Offence gravity > 21.2.7 – Incitement to murder

title: Murder: aggravating circumstances (location, manner of death, post-offence conduct, domestic killings)
statement: These are possible aggravating circumstances that may lead to a more severe sentence. The location is frequently important: a killing in the victim’s home may aggravate; a stranger killing in a family home with children present is particularly serious; killings in public places endangering ordinary members of the community, or in remote locations, can aggravate. A more severe sentence usually follows a particularly painful or degrading death: prolonged and excruciating death, torture, a particularly callous or cold-blooded killing, sexual defilement of the body, mutilation or dismemberment; failing to reveal or hiding the remains may significantly aggravate. Domestic or relationship killings are particularly grave; breach of an intervention order is a serious aggravating feature.

refs.q: Prolonged and excruciating death;

refs.q: Where a victim was tortured, degraded or made to suffer a particularly painful death;

refs.q: Murder attracts a number of possible aggravating circumstances that may lead to a more severe sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence

refs.q: A murder committed in the victim’s home may be an aggravating feature. A murder committed by a stranger in a family home where children are present is also considered particularly serious.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.1 – Location of murder

refs.q: Murders committed in public places where ordinary members of the community are endangered can constitute aggravating circumstances, as can murders committed in remote locations.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.1 – Location of murder

refs.q: A more severe sentence will usually be imposed where victims are made to suffer a particularly painful death or are degraded by the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.2 – Manner of death and post offence conduct

refs.q: Cases involving domestic or relationship killings are particularly grave.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.3 – Cases involving domestic or relationship killings

refs.q: Breach of an intervention order is a serious aggravating feature for murder, as the purpose of the order is to protect the individual who was entitled to the protection of such an order.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.3 – Cases involving domestic or relationship killings

refs.q: The location of the killing is frequently important.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.1 – Location of murder

refs.q: This includes circumstances such as: • Prolonged and excruciating death; • Where a victim was tortured, degraded or made to suffer a particularly painful death; • Particularly callous or cold-blooded killing; • Defilement of the body through sexual intercourse; • Mutilation or dismemberment of the victim’s body. • Failing to reveal the victim’s remains or hiding the victim’s body may be a significant aggravating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 21.3.2 – Manner of death and post offence conduct

title: Murder: life imprisonment without parole; fixing a non-parole period
statement: Life without parole is an exceptional step and a dreadful punishment, imposed in a handful of Victorian cases, typically for the most dreadful crimes given the offence and history; only three cases involved a guilty plea. Youth is not a bar, but life for a young offender is a grave step. Additional imprisonment for a person already sentenced to, or serving, life can only be concurrent (hard-checked: cum.life_parole). No type of murder automatically warrants life; the case usually must be in the worst category for that type of killing; those who kill a number of victims in horrendous circumstances, with no substantial factor of clemency, must in general expect to be seriously considered for the possible imposition of life without parole. Non-parole periods have generally been fixed on life sentences for murder (even with prior murder convictions); declining one removes a major incentive to rehabilitation.

refs.q: The imposition of a life sentence with no parole is an ‘exceptional step and is a dreadful punishment.’ It has only been imposed in a handful of cases in Victoria.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: The refusal to impose a non-parole period is typically reserved for the most ‘dreadful crimes,’ taking into account the nature of the offence and the offender’s history.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: There have only been three cases where an offender has pleaded guilty to a murder and has received a life sentence with no parole.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: The fact that an offender is youthful will not be a bar to the imposition of a life sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: However, it is a grave step to pass a sentence of life imprisonment on a young offender for the obvious reason that the younger the offender, the more severe that sentence will generally be.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: Additional sentences of imprisonment cannot be imposed on persons already sentenced to, or serving a life sentence, other than concurrently with the life sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: There is no particular type of murder for which a life sentence is appropriate, but the case will usually need to fall into the worst category for that type of killing.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: The fixing of a non-parole period will depend in any case on all its circumstances; and ‘those who kill a number of victims in horrendous circumstances, where no substantial factor of clemency is present, must in general expect to be seriously considered for the possible imposition of life sentences unmitigated by the hope of parole.’
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

refs.q: Generally, non-parole periods have been fixed on life sentences for murder, even where the offender had previous convictions for murder. Declining to fix a non-parole period removes one of the most significant incentives to rehabilitation and the hope of ultimate release.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.2 – Fixing a non-parole period

refs.q: For example, the abduction and subsequent murder of a 6-year-old child while she rode her bicycle in broad daylight was considered to belong in this category.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 21 – Murder > 21.4 – Formulation of sentence > 21.4.1 – Life sentence with no parole period

title: Manslaughter, child homicide and homicide by firearm: scope
statement: Manslaughter comprises unlawful and dangerous act, criminal negligence and suicide pact manslaughter — three disparate offences involving a killing in circumstances not treated as murder. Child homicide (victim under six) and homicide by firearm (death caused by discharge of a firearm) are analogous statutory offences. Culpable and dangerous driving causing death are in ch 23; workplace manslaughter in ch 31. Schemes: common-law manslaughter (unlawful and dangerous act or criminal negligence) is not a “serious violent offence”, but it is a “serious offence” and may attract an indefinite sentence (22.1.1). Where the offender was 18 or older (Category 2), manslaughter and child homicide committed on or after 20 March 2017, and homicide by firearm committed on or after 1 July 2020, require a custodial sentence (other than imprisonment combined with a CCO) unless specified circumstances exist (offence register; cat2.custodial_unless; flag.suicide_pact_category2).

refs.q: • Manslaughter by unlawful and dangerous act; • Manslaughter by criminal negligence; and • Suicide pact manslaughter.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm

refs.q: This chapter also considers the statutory offences of child homicide and homicide by firearm, which are analogous to manslaughter, with the added respective elements that the victim was under six years of age and the discharge of a firearm caused the death of the victim.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm

refs.q: Additional homicide offences of culpable driving causing death and dangerous driving causing death are addressed in 23 – Indictable driving offences. The additional homicide offence of workplace manslaughter is addressed in 31- Occupation health and safety offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm

refs.q: Manslaughter is not a ‘serious violent offence’ for the purposes of the Act.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.1 – Penalties

refs.q: However, it is a ‘serious offence’ and may attract an indefinite sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.1 – Penalties

refs.q: The modern manslaughter offence encompasses three disparate offences that involve the killing of another person in circumstances that are not treated as murder.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm

refs.q: If either the first two offences was committed on or after 20 March 2017, or if homicide by firearm was committed after or on after 1 July 2020, the court must impose a custodial sentence (other than a sentence of imprisonment imposed in addition to making a community correction order) unless specified circumstances exist.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.1 – Penalties

refs.q: Manslaughter (whether by unlawful and dangerous act or by criminal negligence) is a common law offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.1 – Penalties

refs.q: The offences of manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm are Category 2 offences if the offender was 18 or older at the time of offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.1 – Penalties

title: Manslaughter: current practices (increased maximum; limited use of comparisons and statistics)
statement: Generally, sentences for all forms of manslaughter have significantly increased since 2011, and on 1 July 2020 the maximum rose from 20 to 25 years, suggesting past sentences were inadequate. Current practice is hard to use given the vastly different circumstances and wide ranges; statistics are of little utility, especially where they do not distinguish intentional from negligent manslaughter or identify the bases of sentences.

refs.q: Generally, sentences for all forms of manslaughter have significantly increased since 2011, and specifically, on 1 July 2020, Parliament increased the maximum penalty for manslaughter offences from 20 years to 25 years’ imprisonment, thereby suggesting that past sentences for this type of offending have been inadequate.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.1 – Manslaughter - Generally

refs.q: However, consideration of current sentencing practices for manslaughter is difficult because of the vastly different circumstances that may give rise to the charge. It can be difficult to infer that a particular sentence for manslaughter is severe when compared to other cases because the ranges of culpability and possible sentences are so wide.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.1 – Manslaughter - Generally

refs.q: For this same reason sentencing statistics are also of little utility, particularly where they do not differentiate between intentional and negligent manslaughter, and do not identify the circumstances and bases for the sentences imposed.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.1 – Manslaughter - Generally

title: Child homicide: current practices
statement: Circumstances and sentences vary, though probably less so because every victim is under six. When introducing it, the Attorney-General explained the offence responds to concerns about the perceived inadequacy of sentences for the manslaughter of young children, highlighting the victim’s age and vulnerability and freeing courts from past practices while generally being guided by them. The Court of Appeal (Woodford) held it does not require punishment closer to the maximum than past young-child manslaughter cases, but it uncoupled child homicide sentences from constraint by current manslaughter practices. Caveat (fn 3396): after Dalgliesh the limiting effect of past manslaughter practice is further reduced, and since Woodford Parliament has increased the child-homicide maximum, indicating a perceived insufficiency in existing sentences.

refs.q: The circumstances in which child homicide might arise and the sentences imposed for it can vary widely. The variations will probably be narrower, however, because every victim will be a child under six.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.2 – Child homicide

refs.q: Despite this intention, the Court of Appeal has held that creation of the new offence did not manifest an intention by Parliament that people found guilty of child homicide must receive a punishment closer to the maximum term than the sentences imposed in past cases involving the manslaughter of a young child.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.2 – Child homicide

refs.q: But it also noted that creation of the offence had one clear legislative purpose: it uncoupled sentences for child homicide from any constraint in current sentencing practices for manslaughter.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.2 – Child homicide

refs.q: When introducing the new offence, the Attorney-General explained that the offence of child homicide was being created in response to concerns regarding the perceived inadequacy of sentences for the manslaughter of young children. The new offence was intended to highlight the aggravating factors of the victim’s age and vulnerability and give the courts scope to develop new practices freed from the constraints of past practices, while generally being guided by those same practices.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.2 – Child homicide

refs.q: Following DPP (Vic) v Dalgliesh (2017) 262 CLR 428, the limiting effect of past sentencing practices for manslaughter has been further reduced. Moreover, since Woodford, Parliament has increased the maximum penalty for child homicide, which indicates a perceived insufficiency in existing sentences for the offence.

This is because the text of the relevant legislation says nothing about how a court should approach sentencing for child homicide; it merely retains all the elements of manslaughter and adds the requirement that the victim be under six years old.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.2 – Child homicide

refs.q: The Court concluded that if Parliament had intended heavier sentences to be imposed for child homicide it would have used directive language.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.2 – Child homicide

title: Homicide by firearm: current practices
statement: Circumstances vary widely (including where intent for murder is hard to prove, or dangerous use of a firearm). Like child homicide, it was created to let courts develop new practices freed from past constraints while generally guided by them.

refs.q: The circumstances in which homicide by firearm might arise are likely to vary widely and include situations where it may be difficult to prove the intent necessary to support a murder charge beyond a reasonable doubt, or where a person has used a firearm dangerously, regardless of whether that use was reckless or intentional.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 22.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 22.1.2.3 – Homicide by firearm

title: Manslaughter: gravity and culpability factors
statement: Manslaughter is extremely serious (unlawful taking of life, the key element), and sentencing is highly fact-specific along a spectrum. Unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter is generally more serious than negligent manslaughter, but not as a fixed rule. Historically (before 23 November 2005), provocation manslaughter was regarded as generally more serious than unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (fn 3403).

title: Unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (including single-punch killings)
statement: Gravity also depends on the gravity of the underlying unlawful act, its dangerousness and the offender’s subjective awareness of the danger; the more dangerous the act, the more serious. A single-punch killing may be a serious example (knowledge that punching toward the head is inherently dangerous; see also the single-punch minimum, mmnpp.manslaughter_10y). Comparisons with the abolished defensive homicide offence require care: defensive homicide required an intent to kill or cause really serious injury (or recklessness), whereas this form of manslaughter requires neither intent.

refs.q: In addition to the factors outlined above, the gravity of this form of manslaughter is influenced by the gravity of the underlying unlawful act, the degree of dangerousness and the accused’s subjective awareness of that dangerousness.

refs.q: For example: a killing which is the result of a single punch, may be a serious example of unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter. An objectively serious feature being the offender’s knowledge that throwing a punch towards the head of another person, regardless of their intent to strike, is inherently dangerous. The general rule is the more dangerous the act, the more objectively serious is the offence.

refs.q: The offences also involve significantly different states of mind. Defensive homicide required proof of an intent to kill or cause really serious injury (or recklessness with regard to those consequences), whereas unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter does not require either intent.

refs.q: Manslaughter by unlawful and dangerous act occurs where an offender causes the death of another person by an act that is both unlawful and dangerous, and which a reasonable person in the circumstances would have realised was exposing others to a risk of serious injury.

title: Manslaughter by criminal negligence
statement: Relatively unusual; occurs where conduct falls so far short of the standard of care, with such high risk of death or serious injury, that criminal punishment is merited; failing to summon medical assistance may reach this standard where a duty of care is owed (e.g. parent to child; a person who caused the injury). Culpability rises with the degree of negligence and the length of inaction. Usually less culpable than unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter (the negligent offender will not have intended to kill or harm, whereas the other usually, but not always, intends at least harm), but not inflexibly. Child homicide and homicide by firearm committed by criminal negligence are linked here (link_conditions). The Manual notes contrary authority on when a duty is owed to an adult (fn 3432) and on the lower culpability of negligent killers (fn 3436): flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6.

refs.q: Manslaughter by negligence is relatively unusual. It occurs where death is caused by actions that fall so short of the standard of care that a reasonable person would have exercised in the circumstances, and that involved such a high risk of death or serious injury, that criminal punishment is merited. Failing to summon medical assistance may reach this standard if the offender owes the victim a duty of care, such as the duty owed by a parent to their child, or the duty owed by a person who causes injury to another.

title: Child homicide: gravity, purposes and burden of custody
statement: Child homicide has the elements of manslaughter with a victim under six; the age is central (a young and vulnerable victim has always been a significant aggravating factor in violent manslaughter). It is serious, more so where committed by someone entrusted with the child’s care. Where death results from excessive corporal punishment, the offender’s right to use such punishment may mitigate; excessive punishment by a person who knows they have no right is a more serious example. Anger and frustration may explain the context but do not mitigate (but see Vinaccia, fn 3445). Courts must send a strong message that significant deprivation of liberty will follow. Imprisonment may be more burdensome (likely protective custody); the weight depends on the actual conditions (hardship.protection_prisoner).

refs.q: As a result, the offence has the same elements as manslaughter except that the victim is a child under six. The age of the victim is central to the criminality involved.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.3 – Child homicide

refs.q: By definition, child homicide is a serious offence and it is more so when it is the result of criminal behaviour by someone entrusted with care of the child.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.3 – Child homicide

refs.q: Where the death is caused in circumstances of excessive corporal punishment, the offender’s right to use such punishment may be a mitigating factor. This is because an offence involving excessive corporal punishment, by a person who knows they have no right to do so, would be a more serious example of the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.3 – Child homicide

refs.q: Child homicide is a serious offence and ‘the courts have a responsibility to impose sentences which send a strong and unequivocal message to the community that any person who unlawfully caused the death of a young and vulnerable child by either criminal negligence or by an unlawful and dangerous act will…suffer a deprivation of [their] liberty for a significant period of time’.

title: Homicide by firearm: gravity (standard sentence 13 years)
statement: A statutory offence created on 1 July 2020 with a standard sentence of 13 years; it has the elements of manslaughter except that death must be caused by the discharge of a firearm. The dangerousness of the use of the firearm is likely to be central. When introducing it, the Attorney-General indicated it is more serious where it would amount to murder but for the inability to prove intent due to lack of witnesses, or where death resulted from the dangerous handling of a firearm (extrinsic material, not a settled gravity rule).

refs.q: Homicide by firearm is a statutory offence with a standard sentence of 13 years that was created on 1 July 2020.

refs.q: The dangerousness of the manner in which a firearm is used is likely to be central to the criminality involved. By definition, homicide by firearm is a serious offence. When introducing the offence, the Attorney-General indicated that it is more so when committed in circumstances that would amount to murder but for the inability of the prosecution to prove intent due to lack of witnesses and in circumstances where the death resulted from the dangerous handling of a firearm by an individual.

title: Provocation and excessive self-defence in homicide sentencing
statement: Provocation can no longer reduce murder to manslaughter but remains a sentencing consideration (a person who forms an intention to kill or cause really serious injury after being provoked is sentenced for murder: fn 3453). Its relevance depends on its degree (low provocation increases gravity toward the confines of murder; great provocation reduces it; the court may look at an entire course of conduct, not just a “triggering event”: fn 3456) and the time to loss of control (if short, this may reduce gravity and culpability). As a sentencing factor it is not limited by the old common law test, though it appears that meeting that test gives it more weight. It is likely to be of limited relevance where the offender previously used domestic violence against the victim (deterrence, denunciation and just punishment remain primary), but likely relevant where the provocation was a further instance of domestic violence by the victim (but see Edwards, fn 3463: culpability is not lessened where the offender was equally or more abusive). Excessive self-defence remains relevant (in its own right or under cover of provocation); where there is a history of family violence it must be approached with caution, especially where the offender acted from anger rather than fear. Historically (before 23 November 2005) “provocation manslaughter” was usually seen as the most serious form of manslaughter. In causing-injury cases the Manual states provocation more narrowly (flag.provocation_injury_vs_homicide).

refs.q: Following the abolition of the partial defence, provocation by itself cannot reduce murder to manslaughter. Despite this, provocation remains relevant as a sentencing consideration because a court may temper its sentencing discretion by understanding the reasons that led to the criminal behaviour.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: The relevance of provocation as a sentencing consideration will depend on: • The degree of provocation. If provocation is low, then the gravity of the manslaughter increases and may even reach ‘the very confines of murder’. Conversely, where provocation is great, gravity and culpability are reduced. • The time between the provocation (whether isolated or cumulative in its effect) and the loss of self-control. If the period is short this may reduce gravity and culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: As a sentencing factor, provocation is not limited in this way and may be relevant even where the offender’s conduct was excessive. However, it appears that where provocation would meet the common law requirements, it will have greater weight as a mitigating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: Alleged provocation is likely to be of limited relevance where the offender has previously engaged in domestic violence against the victim. In such circumstances, sentencing principles of general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment will remain primary considerations. Conversely, where the provocation consists of a further instance of domestic violence by the victim against the offender, then provocation is likely to be a relevant mitigating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: Now, with the abolition of both excessive self-defence and provocation as factors giving rise to discrete offences, excessive self-defence may be relevant either in its own right ‘or under cover of provocation’. However, as with provocation, excessive self-defence where there is a history of family violence must be approached with caution, especially where the offender’s actions spring from anger rather than fear.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: But see Edwards [70] (culpability is not lessened where the offender was equally or more abusive in the domestic relationship).
In considering this, the court may look at an entire course of conduct and not just a ‘triggering event’.

A person who forms an intention to kill or cause really serious injury after being provoked will be sentenced for murder, whereas a person who kills following provocation without forming that intention may be sentenced for manslaughter (usually by an unlawful and dangerous act).
This ‘provocation manslaughter’ was usually seen as the most serious form of the offence because the fatal act was intended even if the result was not.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: Historically, provocation manslaughter (where murder was reduced to manslaughter by the partial defence of provocation) was regarded as generally more serious than unlawful and dangerous act manslaughter. With the abolition of the partial defence of provocation on 23 November 2005, this is likely to be of historical relevance only.

At common law, provocation could only reduce murder to manslaughter where the provocation caused the accused to lose control and the provocation was capable of causing an ordinary person to lose control and act in the way the accused did. As a sentencing factor, provocation is not limited in this way and may be relevant even where the offender’s conduct was excessive.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: Before the defence was abolished in 2005 a person who intended to kill could be convicted of manslaughter, instead of murder, because they had only acted after being provoked to such a degree that they lost control of themselves.

refs.q: Excessive self-defence is also a factor that, while no longer capable of excusing criminal liability, remains relevant to sentencing.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: Historically, excessive self-defence was capable of giving rise to provocation manslaughter.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.2 – Gravity and culpability > 22.2.5 – Provocation and excessive self-defence

refs.q: This recognised that while provocation is often associated with anger, and self-defence often associated with fear, there was an overlap for the purposes of sentencing.

title: Manslaughter: purposes (and the suicide pact exception)
statement: Deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are the principal purposes, particularly for domestic or family violence, alcohol or drug fuelled public violence, one-punch attacks, weapon use (or use without proper safety), and child homicide; in those circumstances there is a particular need for the sentence to make clear that violence is intolerable (the strongest denunciation and stern punishment). Moral culpability is reduced where the offender was provoked against a history of domestic violence, but that does not remove the importance of general deterrence, just punishment and denunciation; even then a killing must be denounced and usually result in imprisonment (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 3473, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Suicide pact manslaughter is an exception: specific deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are lessened; general deterrence remains significant; mercy may permit a non-custodial sentence (Rolfe, 2008). Caution: for an adult offender and offending on or after 20 March 2017, whether suicide pact manslaughter is within Category 2 is unresolved in the Manual (flag.suicide_pact_category2).

refs.q: The principle sentencing purposes in cases of manslaughter are deterrence, denunciation and just punishment. This is particularly so in cases: • involving domestic or family violence; • of alcohol or drug fuelled violence in public places; • involving ‘one punch/strike’ attacks; • where a weapon is used or is used without proper regard for safety procedures; and • of child homicide.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.3 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Despite provocation and family violence, unlawful behaviour that results in the death of another must still be denounced and (usually) result in a term of imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.3 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: There is an exception in cases of manslaughter involving a suicide pact. In these cases, the principles of specific deterrence, denunciation, and just punishment are lessened.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.3 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: General deterrence remains significant because the law protects the sanctity of human life and its unlawful taking, even where an offender’s motives are pure. However, mercy has a part to play when sentencing in such circumstances, and a sentence may be imposed that releases the offender and does not carry a custodial component.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.3 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: In these circumstances, there is a particular need for the sentence to make clear that the use of violence is intolerable and calls for the strongest denunciation and stern punishment. Although an offender’s moral culpability is reduced where they were provoked in circumstances where there is a history of domestic violence, this does not remove the importance of general deterrence, just punishment, and denunciation when sentencing.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 22 – Manslaughter, child homicide, and homicide by firearm > 22.3 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: But see R v Gadzovic [2002] VSC 588, [9]–[10]; Stavreski 49 [20]–[27].

title: Indictable driving offences: current practice
statement: Driving offences causing death or serious injury are very serious; absent exceptional circumstances a substantial custodial sentence is required for general and specific deterrence, community protection and just punishment. A non-custodial sentence may be available where moral culpability is exceptionally low; ten years for single-fatality culpable driving invites scrutiny though may be within range for very grave offending. Practices for dangerous driving causing death were held inadequate (2016) and the increase is not to be gradual.

refs.q: A driving offence that results in the death or serious injury of another person is very serious. Absent exceptional circumstances, a substantial custodial sentence will be required to satisfy the need for general and specific deterrence, community protection, and just punishment.

title: Driving offences: aggravating features (Whyte and Victorian additions) — not a checklist
statement: Victorian courts apply R v Whyte (NSW guideline) to gravity of driving offences causing death or serious injury. The non-exhaustive features below may aggravate, but they are not a checklist: absence of some does not mean a case cannot be serious. Intoxication: alcohol or drug use may not be treated as aggravating culpable driving established under s 318(2)(c) or (d) (it is the basis of culpability), but may aggravate where culpability is under s 318(2)(b); the absence of alcohol or drugs may sometimes worsen the conduct (wilful disregard of road laws) (fn 3494). Comparables: NSW guidance on principles is useful, but NSW guidance on the length of custodial sentences is unhelpful in Victoria (different maximum penalties; some Victorian culpable driving may be charged as manslaughter in NSW) (fn 3492).

refs.q: Alcohol or drug use may not be treated as an aggravating factor for an offender who is to be sentenced with culpable driving established by culpability under s 318(2)(c) or 318(2)(d) of the Act. However, where culpability is established under s 318(2)(b), evidence of alcohol or drug use may be treated as an aggravating factor.

In some circumstances, the absence of alcohol or drugs may worsen an offender’s conduct if it indicates that they demonstrated a willful disregard for the road laws and the safety of other road users.

While NSW guidelines relating to principles are useful, guidelines about the appropriate length of a custodial sentence are unhelpful in the Victorian context, given the different structure of maximum penalties that apply in NSW. Additionally, some conduct that is charged as culpable driving in Victoria may be charged as manslaughter in NSW.

Whyte provides a non-exhaustive list of features that may aggravate the gravity of driving offences that cause death or serious injury, including: • extent and nature of injuries inflicted; • number of people put at risk; • speed; • degree of intoxication or of substance abuse; • erratic driving; • competitive driving or showing off; • length of the journey during which others were exposed to risk; • ignoring warnings; • escaping police pursuit; • sleep deprivation; • failing to stop.

title: Culpable driving causing death: forms of culpability; responsibility and causation
statement: Four forms: recklessness; gross negligence; alcohol, or a drug, to the extent of being incapable of proper control. There is no inherent distinction between negligence from intoxication and other negligence (mobile phone, fatigue), and no statutory hierarchy: gravity depends on the facts, and some gross negligence may be more serious than recklessness. For gross negligence, start with whether the offender was solely responsible for the manner of driving and whether it was the sole cause of death, and whether another’s conduct qualified either. The offender may qualify moral culpability by establishing that another person or an external circumstance was partly responsible for the decision to drive or the manner of driving, and causation by showing something else, outside their control, that was also a material cause of death. A passenger’s willingness to travel with an intoxicated or fatigued driver does not by itself make this showing; distraction by a passenger has limited mitigating effect. A victim not wearing a seatbelt will usually not, on its own, qualify causation (it must be shown on the balance of probabilities it would have prevented death, and even then weight is relatively modest; drivers are responsible for passengers’ seatbelts; compare the NCSI-by-driving treatment, guide.injury.ncsi_driving_gravity). Alcohol or drug use may not aggravate culpable driving under s 318(2)(c)–(d), but may under s 318(2)(b) (fn 3494).

refs.q: There is no inherent distinction between the gravity of negligent behaviour constituted by lack of good judgment due to excessive drug or alcohol consumption and other negligent behaviour, such as using a mobile phone while driving or driving while fatigued.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: In Pasznyk v The Queen, the Court of Appeal confirmed that the Crimes Act does not contain a hierarchy of culpability. The Court said that the objective gravity of each case is determined with reference to the relevant facts, including the offender’s state of mind. On their facts, however, some cases of grossly negligent culpable driving may be objectively more serious than reckless culpable driving.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: But a victim’s willingness to be a passenger despite knowing the driver is intoxicated or fatigued does not by itself make this showing, as the victim did not contribute to the offender’s conduct. Further, if evidence demonstrates that the victim’s conduct as a passenger was distracting, this has only limited mitigating impact as it is a driver’s responsibility to prevent passengers from causing distractions.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: The fact that a victim was not wearing a seatbelt at the time of collision will usually not be enough, on its own, to make this showing. Evidence would need to demonstrate on the balance of probabilities that the failure to wear a seatbelt would have prevented the victim’s death, and even then the weight to be given to the failure will be ‘relatively modest.’ Additionally, where the victim was the offender’s passenger, the offender as driver would have been responsible for ensuring they were wearing their seatbelt.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: Four forms of culpability can constitute culpable driving: • Recklessness: the offender consciously and unjustifiably disregarded a substantial risk that the death of another person, or the infliction of grievous bodily harm upon another person, might result from their driving. • Negligence: the offender failed unjustifiably and to a gross degree to observe the standard of care which a reasonable person would have observed in all the circumstances. • The offender drove while under the influence of alcohol to such an extent as to be incapable of having proper control of the motor vehicle. • The offender drove while under the influence of a drug to such an extent as to be incapable of having proper control of the motor vehicle.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: The first proposition goes to the offender’s moral culpability, which may be qualified if they establish that another person or external circumstance was partly responsible for their decision to drive or the manner of their driving.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: The second proposition concerns causation, which similarly may be qualified if the offender shows there was something else, outside of their control, which was also a material cause of the victim’s death.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.1 – Culpable driving causing death

refs.q: Alcohol or drug use may not be treated as an aggravating factor for an offender who is to be sentenced with culpable driving established by culpability under s 318(2)(c) or 318(2)(d) of the Act. However, where culpability is established under s 318(2)(b), evidence of alcohol or drug use may be treated as an aggravating factor.

In sentencing an offender for culpable driving by gross negligence, the starting points for assessing gravity and moral culpability are whether: • the offender was solely responsible for the manner of their driving; • the manner of the offender’s driving was the sole cause of the victim’s death; and • whether another person’s conduct qualified either of the first two propositions.

title: Dangerous driving causing death or serious injury; negligently causing serious injury by driving
statement: Dangerous driving causing death or serious injury is inherently serious, ordinarily attracting significant imprisonment. Dangerous driving causing death and negligently causing serious injury share a maximum (10 years; dangerous driving causing serious injury is 5 years); because negligent conduct is often more serious than dangerous driving conduct, the two may be regarded as similarly serious. Gravity turns on moral culpability and objective dangerousness (and, for serious injury, the extent of injuries); the extent to which the offender should have foreseen the consequences informs moral culpability. Culpability is higher where risks were known, lower for momentary inattention or misjudgment or external contributing circumstances (e.g. poor intersection design). Ask what degree of care and alertness was reasonably expected; dangerousness reflects the likelihood of something going wrong and the extent of resulting harm.

refs.q: ‘Dangerous driving causing death (or serious injury) is an inherently serious offence ordinarily resulting in a significant term of imprisonment being imposed’.

title: Failing to stop or render assistance after an accident causing death or serious injury
statement: For the s 61 offences (driver of the motor vehicle, s 61(3)) the maximum rose from 80 penalty units or two years to 10 years, a fivefold increase signalling markedly greater gravity (the s 61A(3) offence — driver of the other vehicle — has a Level 6, 5-year maximum in the register). Offences under s 61(3) are intended to deter fleeing the scene; excuses usually carry no weight, and failing to stop because of the quality of driving or capacity to drive aggravates. Rarely, the reason may mitigate (e.g. PTSD-driven panic; leaving to get help for an injured passenger; fear for physical safety). Promptly reporting to police (e.g. 15 minutes later) may mitigate as the main benefit (avoiding detection) is lost. It is error to consider grief and loss from a death where the offender is not convicted of an offence about the manner of driving. For s 61(3) the licence must be cancelled with a minimum disqualification (first offence: at least 4 years if a conviction is recorded, 2 years otherwise; subsequent offence: at least 8 years, or 4 years) — enforced by audit.mandatory_ancillary_orders.

limbs.text: Maximum history (s 61(3) only): 80 penalty units or two years, increased to 10 years.

refs.q: An offender’s excuse for fleeing an accident or failing to assist will usually carry no weight at sentence. Evidence that an offender failed to stop because of the quality of their driving or their capacity to drive will aggravate their offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 23 – Indictable driving offences > 23.2 – Gravity and culpability > 23.2.3 – Failing to stop or assist after an accident causing death or serious injury

refs.q: In rare circumstances, however, an offender’s reason for fleeing an accident or not rendering assistance may carry some weight in mitigation. For example, in R v Mohamed, the Court of Appeal accepted that evidence might support an offender’s claim that his post-traumatic stress disorder, caused him to panic and flee, thus reducing the gravity of the offence. The Court has also found a failure to stop was slightly mitigated when the offender, after stopping to determine that the victim who he had struck with his vehicle had no pulse, left to seek medical assistance for his injured passenger. The Court of Appeal has also suggested that fleeing out of fear for physical safety may be a mitigating factor.

refs.q: A court may mitigate a sentence for an offence under the RSA if an offender reports an accident to police very soon after fleeing the accident. For example, in DPP (Vic) v Fairley the offender reported the accident only 15 minutes after fleeing. By voluntarily giving up his identity, the offender lost the main perceived benefit of committing the offence, which is to avoid detection.

title: Driving offences: purposes; reduced weight of youth, good character and remorse; driving record
statement: General deterrence is often the principal consideration; the seriousness and need for deterrence mean youth, good character and remorse carry less mitigating weight. In culpable and dangerous driving cases a poor driving record (especially serious driving offences, drug/alcohol driving, disqualified driving) is important, affecting moral culpability, rehabilitation, specific deterrence, community protection and denunciation — but prior convictions cannot be used in aggravation to increase the sentence (factor.prior_and_subsequent_convictions). Community protection is usually significant, but less so where fatigue rather than speed, drugs, alcohol or deliberate wrong-side (“hooning”) driving triggered the offence.

title: Driving offences: multiple victims, cumulation and double punishment
statement: Avoid double punishment while recognising each victim: consider whether deaths or injuries arose from one course of driving; whether an act or omission forms part of more than one offence; order cumulation for different incidents, offences and victims; ensure each victim is recognised in the total and non-parole period (not a “meaningless statistic” — 50% cumulation for a second culpable driving victim is not uncommon); keep within totality. A single failure to stop affecting two victims is one act; separate failures to assist are separate acts (in Vasilevski the Court said it may have been more appropriate to cumulate on the failure to assist charges and little or none on the failure to stop charges, but refused leave because the total was appropriate and recognised both victims). Significant cumulation is required where offences from one accident are very different (e.g. dangerous driving and failing to stop).

title: Culpable driving by alcohol/drugs plus a related summary offence: wholly concurrent
statement: Where culpable driving is by intoxication (s 318(2)(c)–(d)), additionally punishing a related summary offence such as exceeding the prescribed blood alcohol concentration is double punishment; sentences should be wholly concurrent. This does not arise for other forms of culpable driving or for dangerous driving.

refs.q: double punishment will arise if an offender is additionally punished for a related summary offence such as exceeding the prescribed blood alcohol concentration. Taking that example, since excess alcohol in the blood is an element of both offences, if they are to be charged together, then sentences should be wholly concurrent.

title: Sexual offences: the maximum is fixed by the offence date (not a later increase; a later reduction applies)
statement: Sexual offences are often prosecuted years later; the Manual says the relevant maximum is the one in force at the time of offending, not at sentence, and that this is a common area of mistake. Read with 5.1.3, a later increase is disregarded but a later reduction must be applied (unless the maximum was reduced and then increased again before sentence to the same magnitude or higher, when the court may apply the original maximum: 5.1.3; audit.maximum_applicable (2)) (historic sexual-offence tables include reductions, e.g. Level 6 from 7½ to 5 years on 1 September 1997). The Manual does not reconcile the two statements (flag.maximum_at_offence_vs_later_reduction); audit.maximum_applicable applies 5.1.3.

refs.q: More than most offences, sexual offences are often prosecuted many years after they were committed. But the relevant maximum penalty in sentencing is the one that was in force at the time of the offending, not the time of sentencing. For this reason, careful attention is required to identify the maximum penalty that applied at the time of the offending. This is a common area of mistake which is discussed further in 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice

refs.q: For offences occurring before the date of a change of penalty, the court must sentence in accordance with any reduction in maximum penalty but must not consider any increase in maximum penalty.
