title: Sexual offences: current practices have increased (rape and incest; Dalgliesh)
statement: Sentences for serious sexual offences have increased, most significantly for rape and incest, following Dalgliesh (practices for incest inadequate; current practices not controlling).

refs.q: Sentences for serious sexual offences have increased in recent years; most significantly for rape and incest, following the decisions in Dalgliesh which established both that current sentencing practices for incest were inadequate, and that current sentencing practices are not a controlling consideration in the sentencing process.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices

title: Historic sexual offences: practices at sentence, equal justice and the old maximum
statement: Many sex offences are prosecuted years after they occurred. “Current sentencing practices” are those at sentence, and contemporary understanding of the impact on victims may be applied. Equal justice also requires regard to practices at the time of offending if it can be shown they would have required a materially lesser sentence; but if the offender’s own conduct made contemporaneous sentencing impossible, they may not be able to contend they should be treated as if responsibility had been established then. Practices are only one factor; past cases are not precedents and may not show a material difference. (The historical-practice inquiry is not an inflexible rule and applies only if reasonably practicable: csp.historic_offences.) The Manual notes a tension between these requirements and the need to consider them in light of the maximum in force at the time of offending — an area where care is required (guide.sexual.maximum_at_offence_date).

refs.q: It is well-established that for the purpose of s 5(2)(b) of the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’), “current sentencing practices” means the practices which apply at the time of sentencing, rather than at the time of offending. Contemporary practice reflects a greater understanding of the impact sex offending has on the victim, and so a court may bring its present understanding of that impact to bear even though it may not have been a feature of sentences imposed at the time of the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences

refs.q: But this is a complex exercise because in addition to considering sentencing practices at the time of sentencing, equal justice also requires a court to consider sentencing practices at the time of offending if it can be shown they would ‘have required the imposition of a materially lesser sentence for like offences’. However, if it was the offender’s conduct which made it impossible for them to have been sentenced contemporaneously with the offending, they may not be able to contend they should be treated as if their criminal responsibility had been established at that time.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences

refs.q: The key point is that current sentencing practices are only one of the many factors that a sentencing court has to consider. Previous cases are not precedents and while they may provide a broad sense of the appropriate parameters they do not necessarily demonstrate there is a material difference between practices at the time of offending and the time of sentencing.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences

refs.q: Many sex offences are not prosecuted until years after their occurrence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences

refs.q: Lastly, since there is a tension between these requirements and the need to consider this in light of the maximum penalty in force at the time of the offending, it is an area where care is required.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences

refs.q: They may be sufficiently harmonious to comply with the requirements of equal justice.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.1 – Historic sex offences

title: Sexual offences against adults: rape ordinarily attracts immediate custody
statement: Absent exceptional circumstances, rape usually attracts immediate custody with a substantial part actually served. Rape covers a wide spectrum; factors (usually in combination) such as an early plea, diminished culpability, genuine remorse and victim support or forgiveness may be exceptional and justify a suspended, non-custodial or substantially reduced term. Caution: the Manual states this without date limits, but rape is a Category 1 offence for an adult offender (custodial sentence required for offences on or after 20 March 2017) and suspended sentences have been progressively abolished since 1 May 2011 — a suspended or non-custodial term is open only outside those schemes; the hard checks govern (flag.rape_noncustodial_vs_category1). Other adult sexual offences have a wider range and little guidance; sentences imposed alongside more serious offences may be of little guidance.

refs.q: Absent exceptional circumstances, rape offences usually attract an immediate custodial term and the court should ensure that a substantial part of the sentence will actually be served.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.2 – Sexual offences against adults

refs.q: But since rape covers a wide spectrum of criminal liability and each case must be considered in light of its particular circumstances, some factors (usually in combination) such as an early plea of guilty, diminished culpability, genuine remorse, and instances where the victim supports or forgives the offender may be ‘exceptional’ and justify the imposition of a suspended, non–custodial, or substantially reduced term.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.2 – Sexual offences against adults

refs.q: For sexual offences against adults other than rape, a greater range of sentences may be imposed. There is little guidance on sentencing practice for these other offences, and instances of sentences imposed in conjunction with more serious sexual offences may be of little guidance because the more serious offending may aggravate the overall offending or raise the significance of principles such as deterrence, denunciation and incapacitation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.2 – Sexual offences against adults

title: Sexual offences against children: imprisonment is justified; non-custodial terms rare
statement: Sexual offending against children, particularly in the offender’s care, is a gross breach of trust justifying imprisonment; there is no tariff, but non-custodial terms are likely rare and particularly inappropriate for many victims over a long period. The same physical acts do not make cases relevantly comparable. For the Category 1 child offences (those marked “#” in 24.1.2) a non-custodial term is not available for an adult offender at all (cat1.custodial_required).

refs.q: Sexual offending against children, particularly those under the offender’s care and protection, is a gross breach of trust justifying a term of imprisonment. While there is no sentencing tariff for such offending because the circumstances may vary considerably, non-custodial terms are likely to be rare and particularly inappropriate where the offender has abused many victims over a significant period of time.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.3 – Offending against children

refs.q: The fact that the offending against children involves the same physical acts does not make cases relevantly comparable.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.3 – Offending against children

title: Incest: “dramatic change in sentencing parameters”
statement: In 2016 the Court of Appeal and the High Court found mid-range incest sentences disproportionately low (three years six months for incest resulting in pregnancy was given as inadequate); for incest in the mid-range of seriousness, sentencing must now take into account the dramatic change in sentencing parameters. Longer sentences involve long periods, younger children or multiple victims, threats or violence, or multifaceted, perverse or depraved offending; planned offending to capture child abuse material calls equally for a stern penalty.

refs.q: In 2016, the Court of Appeal and then the High Court found that sentences for incest in the mid-range of seriousness were disproportionately low. The Court of Appeal called for sentences in such cases to be adjusted upwards and gave, as an example of inadequate sentencing, the case before it where three years and six months’ imprisonment was imposed for incest resulting in pregnancy.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.3 – Offending against children > 24.1.8.3.1 – Incest

refs.q: Consideration of an appropriate sentence for incest offences in this range must now take into account ‘the dramatic change in sentencing parameters.’
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.3 – Offending against children > 24.1.8.3.1 – Incest

refs.q: Incest offences which attract longer sentences have involved offending that occurred over a long period, against younger children or multiple victims, accompanied by threats or violence, or which was multifaceted, perverse or depraved. Further, offending that was planned and motivated to capture (and perhaps distribute) child abuse material, calls equally for a stern penalty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.3 – Offending against children > 24.1.8.3.1 – Incest

title: Child abuse material: immediate imprisonment normally warranted
statement: Absent exceptional circumstances, possession, creation or transmission of child abuse material normally warrants immediate imprisonment, though each case depends on its circumstances and mitigating factors.

cautions.text: Commonwealth CAM offences require regard to national sentencing practices (outside this app’s Victorian scope).

refs.q: Moreover, Commonwealth offences, such as using carriage service to access child abuse material, require a court to consider sentencing practices across Australia, not merely Victorian practice.

refs.q: Absent exceptional circumstances, the possession, creation, or transmission of child abuse material will normally warrant an immediate term of imprisonment. However, each case depends on its own circumstances and a term of imprisonment is not necessarily appropriate, depending on the presence of mitigating factors.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practice > 24.1.8 – Current sentencing practices > 24.1.8.3 – Offending against children > 24.1.8.3.2 – Child abuse material

title: Harm of sexual offending
statement: Sexual offences are crimes of violence causing appalling, often irreparable harm. Rape’s impact (physical invasion and the loss of rights and freedoms) must be given proper weight. Harm from child sexual abuse is severe and long lasting; severe psychological repercussions are presumed from incest and may be a primary consideration.

refs.q: The law recognises that sexual offences are crimes of violence that cause appalling, and often irreparable, psychological and physical harm to the victims.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm

refs.q: Rape is an intensely personal crime. The effects on the victim are not just those that flow from the physical invasion of their person and security, but also from the more intangible loss of their rights and freedoms. This significant impact of rape on the victim needs to be given proper weight in sentencing; it cannot be overlooked or undervalued.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm

refs.q: It is also well established that the harm caused by sexual abuse of children and young people is severe and long lasting. And, more particularly, that ‘severe psychological repercussions’ are presumed to be the result of incest. In fact, in incest cases, harm of this sort, rather than physical harm, may be a primary consideration.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm

title: Presumption of harm to children (Clarkson): apparent consent is not mitigating
statement: A child under 16 cannot consent to sexual penetration; the prohibition protects children from harm and deters adults, and rests on a presumption of long-term harm unaffected by apparent consent, which is not mitigating. The presumption is rebuttable, and the offender bears the onus of rebutting it (fn 3602); rebuttal will be likely to succeed only in very limited circumstances (freely given consent reflecting genuine affection; focus on the circumstances, ages, exploitation or breach of trust); a child’s statement is not sufficient; independent expert evidence will normally be required; only in a very clear case might a material reduction be warranted. It applies to cybersex and in person offending with children under 16, preparatory offending (procuring, grooming) and child abuse material (including material depicting 16–17 year olds). The victim’s attitude, conduct or “attractiveness” is irrelevant. The degree of harm varies with the objective gravity and explicitness. It does not apply where there is no child victim (e.g. a police officer posing as a child) — but culpability and gravity are not thereby lessened (flag.police_child_presumption). The Manual does not say whether it applies to the care/supervision offences against 16- or 17-year-olds or to the non-contact offences (see link_conditions). The presumption rests on protecting children from “premature sexual experience of all kinds”; in person and cybersex offending share the same objectives, so there is no basis for distinguishing them; that the child may be exploring their sexuality online or enjoy the offender’s attention is irrelevant.

link_conditions.applies_if: not established: the Manual ties the presumption to children under 16 (child abuse material excepted) and does not say whether it applies to these offences against children aged 16 or 17
link_conditions.otherwise: caution; do not treat harm as presumed without saying the point is unresolved in the Manual

refs.q: Harm continues to be presumed by the interaction, with the responsibility on adults to avoid premature sexual activity with children under 16.

refs.q: Harm continues to be presumed by the interaction, with the responsibility on adults to avoid premature sexual activity with children under 16.

refs.q: Harm continues to be presumed by the interaction, with the responsibility on adults to avoid premature sexual activity with children under 16.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: In Clarkson v The Queen the Court of Appeal held that under the legislative scheme, a child under 16 cannot consent to sexual penetration. This prohibition has two purposes: protecting the child from harm that can come from premature sexual activity; and deterring adults who would contemplate having sex with someone under the age of 16.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: The prohibition is founded on a presumption that premature sexual activity will cause long term physical and psychological harm and is unaffected by the presence of apparent consent. To conclude otherwise, and to treat apparent consent as mitigating would run counter to the legislative purpose.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: The Clarkson presumption of harm is rebuttable. In circumstances where the apparent consent is freely given and reflects genuine affection, the offender may be able to demonstrate that the circumstances of offending are not likely to cause the kinds of harm the law presumes flow from premature sexual activity. This will require the court to focus on the circumstances in which consent was given, rather than on the mere fact of consent. In particular, the court will look at the ages of the offender and the victim, and whether consent was given in circumstances of exploitation or abuse of trust.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: Rebutting the presumption will be likely to succeed only in very limited circumstances. A statement from the child victim will not be sufficient to establish that no harm was caused or is likely to occur. Independent expert evidence will normally be required, and it will only be in a very clear case that a material reduction might be warranted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: Specifically, the presumption of harm applies to both “cybersex” offences and those committed “in person”.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: Similarly, the attitude, demeanour, conduct, “attractiveness” of the victim, and their effect on the respondent is irrelevant.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: This also includes “preparatory”’ offending, such as procuring or grooming, or offending with respect to child abuse material, which includes material where the victims include children who are 16 or 17 years old.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: The degree of harm will vary according to the objective gravity of the conduct; the character of the offending affects the severity of the harm that is inferred, and it may be lessened where the offending is less serious. Where the content of the activity is less sexually explicit the gravity of the offending may be reduced, in some instances to the point where it is almost negligible. Where there is no child victim (such as where a communication-based offence is committed with a police officer who is posing as a child) the presumption does not apply.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: The onus of disproving it rests on the offender.
Harm continues to be presumed by the interaction, with the responsibility on adults to avoid premature sexual activity with children under 16.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: The Clarkson presumption of harm is founded on the rationale that children will be harmed by and must be protected from ‘premature sexual experience of all kinds’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: Legislation prohibiting in person offending and cybersex offences both have the same objectives of deterring offenders and protecting children, so there is no basis for distinguishing between them.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: It is also irrelevant that the child may be exploring their sexuality online or may even enjoy the attention of the offender; this does not relax the protections for children online.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

refs.q: The fact that cybersex offences may occur without physical proximity is irrelevant because the internet permits intimidation and coercion to be employed to ensure the child’s participation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.1 – Harm > 24.2.1.1 – Presumption of harm to children

title: Sexual offences: gravity generally (no hierarchy of penetration; trust; the victim’s home)
statement: Sexual intrusion is serious (maxima up to 25 years) — but see Traeger (fn 3613): indecent assault is serious, but given the two maxima significantly less so than rape. Gravity depends on the facts; there is no hierarchy of penetration (digital rape is not necessarily less serious). Breach of trust, or offending in the victim’s home, is particularly egregious.

refs.q: Offences that violate the bodily integrity and personal dignity of another person by means of sexual intrusion are serious. This is reflected in the maximum penalties for sexual offences, which stretch to 25 years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: For penetration offences, there is no hierarchy of penetration making one offence inherently more or less severe than another. For example: although digital rape does not involve some of the risks of penile rape, namely disease and pregnancy, that does not mean a particular instance of it is less serious. An assessment of gravity, as always, depends on the facts of the case.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: However, sexual offences that involve a breach of trust, or which occur in the victim’s home, where they have a right to feel safe, are particularly egregious.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: But see, eg, Traeger (a pseudonym) v The Queen [2019] VSA 231, [2] (indecent assault is a serious offence, but given the maximum penalties of the two, it is significantly less so than rape).
The gravity of a sexual offence depends on the circumstances of the case.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability

title: Rape: gravity and culpability factors (maximum 25 years; standard sentence 10 years for ss 38(2)–(3))
statement: Rape is always very serious (maximum 25 years; for rape under ss 38(2)–(3) the standard sentence is 10 years — the 24.1.1 table prints no standard sentence against s 39(2) rape by compelling sexual penetration, which the register treats as outside the scheme, with a caution: flag.sso_rape_by_compelling): an act of violence even without other violence; all non-consensual penetration is objectively serious. There are no inflexible principles; the range is wide; there is no rule that partner rape is more or less serious than stranger rape; consider all circumstances, not just the elements. The relevant factors (below) are descriptive, not exhaustive, and explain seriousness even without violence or physical harm. For multiple rapes, care is needed not to doubly punish and to respect totality (fn 3638). Consent obtained by deceit bears on gravity (e.g. “stealthing”: consent to penetration does not extend to further penetration after a condom is removed without the victim’s permission or knowledge).

limbs.text: Standard sentence 10 years — rape under ss 38(2)–(3) only (not printed for s 39(2)).

refs.q: Rape ss 38(2)-(3) Level 2 imprisonment (25 years)# Standard sentence (10 years) 1 September 1997

refs.q: A rape that is opportunistic may tend to make the offending less culpable than one that has been premeditated or planned. refs.q: Rape must always be regarded as a very serious offence as indicated by the maximum penalty of 25 years and the standard sentence of 10 years. It is an act of violence, regardless of whether it is accompanied by other violent conduct.

title: Sexual offences against children: gravity and culpability factors
statement: Sexual crimes against children are abhorrent and without question serious, particularly with breach of care or trust. Dalgliesh’s observations on seriousness apply to all such offending. Common factors are listed below. The absence of a listed factor is not necessarily mitigating; it may simply be the absence of an aggravating factor. Passage of time since the offending is irrelevant to gravity and culpability. Where the “child” is a covert police operative, culpability and gravity are not lessened, although the presumption of harm does not apply (the Manual does not reconcile this with gravity “resting upon” that presumption: flag.police_child_presumption — caution: no presumed-harm component, but the absence of a real child is not mitigating). Sexual offences against cognitively impaired people are equally serious and their gravity may be compared with these offences (fn 3669; guide.cognitive_impairment.gravity). (The Manual’s passage on online grooming to procure children for overseas abuse concerns the Commonwealth provisions: guide.grooming.cth_online.)

factors.text: betrayal of trust (religious leader, teacher, family friend); protestations of love do not mitigate

refs.q: Was there a betrayal of trust, either of the child victim or their parents, such as where the offender uses their position as a religious leader, teacher, or family friend to abuse the child? Protestations of love for the child cannot mitigate the breach of trust involved in such offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: • The duration of the offending. Abuse over a protracted period is more serious and goes to the offender’s culpability as it shows a level of insight into the seriousness of their conduct.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

factors.text: premeditation, planning and grooming (higher and lower range grooming)

refs.q: • Was there premeditation or planning, including “grooming”? Grooming offences are not at the low end of seriousness if they are committed over a period of time, involve sexualised messaging or images, and the offender encourages the child to meet for sex, to send explicit photos, or delete messages.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: Conversely, grooming offences may fall at the lower end of the range where the offender does not seek to procure sex for themselves or another, offers no inducement, does not suggest or arrange a meeting, and does not disguise their identity or age.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: The vulnerability of the child, which may be exacerbated if they are impaired by alcohol.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: • Was there a significant age difference between the offender and the child, or an imbalance in power or authority between the two? The greater any age difference the more serious the offence and the offender’s culpability. If the age difference is not great and the sexual activity was truly consensual, with the result that the presumption of harm is rebutted, gravity and culpability may be lessened.

refs.q: Sexual offences against cognitively impaired people are equally serious and their gravity may be compared with sexual offences against children.

Courts have denounced these offences as ‘inherently evil and depraved’, violating the basic norms of civilised behaviour and striking at the value the community places on the lives and wellbeing of the young.

title: Sexual offences against people with a cognitive impairment or mental illness: equally serious as child sexual offences
statement: The Manual gives no separate gravity factors for these offences (24.1.4), but notes that sexual offences against cognitively impaired people are equally serious and that their gravity may be compared with sexual offences against children (fn 3669). (app policy) Use guide.child_sexual.gravity by analogy, as comparison rather than a rule, without its child-specific rules (the Clarkson presumption of harm and its onus; the child’s age); the general sexual-offence items (harm, gravity generally, purposes, orders) also apply.

refs.q: Sexual offences against cognitively impaired people are equally serious and their gravity may be compared with sexual offences against children.

Offences that violate the bodily integrity and personal dignity of another person by means of sexual intrusion are serious. This is reflected in the maximum penalties for sexual offences, which stretch to 25 years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability

title: Incest: gravity, culpability and the value of a plea
statement: Incest (commonly penetration of one’s children, step-children or a partner’s children) is mostly an aggravated form of child sexual offending, condemned in the strongest terms, especially where it breaches parental care. A guilty plea is entitled to more than the usual utilitarian benefit (sparing the victim and family a trial). Maximum 25 years for a parent against a child (ss 50C, 50D). Consider nature, extent, frequency, duration and circumstances. Particular considerations: violence or threats (inherent violence; penetration at the very high end; any sexual touching by a parent is very serious); breach of trust (very high culpability); degradation (filming, posting online, offending before family or involving others); concealment or continuation by bribes, coercion or secrecy. A representative charge may be significantly more serious than a single act. The two other incest offences (s 50E: the junior adult party in parent-child incest; s 50F: siblings; both 5 years) are generally not the target of the strongest comments, but share some of the same condemnation; a s 50F offence by a much older sibling may bear all the characteristics of the most serious incest offences (fn 3703).

limbs.text: Maximum 25 years (parent or step-parent against a child: ss 50C, 50D only).

refs.q: Incest by a parent against a child carries a 25-year maximum penalty,
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

limbs.text: Sections 50E and 50F (5 years): some of the same condemnation; an older sibling’s s 50F offence may bear all the characteristics of the most serious incest offences.

refs.q: There are two other incest offences. The Crimes Act s 50E criminalises the conduct of the junior party in parent-child incest if they are over the age of 18, and s 50F addresses the incest of siblings regardless of age. Both carry a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment. While the strongest comments in respect of incest offences that will be discussed in this section are generally not directed to these two offences, they still share some of the same condemnation, and in some instances of s 50F offences, where the offender is a much older sibling, the offence may bear all the characteristics of the most serious incest offences.

The most common forms of incest involve acts of sexual penetration by an offender against their minor children, step-children, or the children of their de facto partners. In practice, most of these offences may be viewed as an aggravated form of the broader category of child sex offences just discussed.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: A plea of guilty to a charge of incest is ‘entitled to more than just the usual utilitarian benefits’. This is because it means the victim and their family do not have to undergo the extreme stress of a trial.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: Incest by a parent against a child carries a 25-year maximum penalty, and the gravity of incest offences will usually be affected by the same considerations as those affecting the gravity of serious child sexual offences. In assessing the gravity of incest, a court must consider the nature and extent of the offending, its frequency, duration, and the circumstances of its occurrence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: Acts of incest that involve penetration are at the very high end of seriousness. However, ‘any sexual touching of a child by a parent or guardian is to be viewed as very serious.’
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: Incest involving a child is ‘an offence of very high culpability’ because it is contrary to the basic tenet of parental care for a child; ‘every parent is taken to understand that sexual activity is absolutely prohibited’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.2 – Offences against children

refs.q: Similarly, offending in the presence of other family members, or involving other people in the offending, whether for financial gain or to share the child as a ‘play-thing’ are deplorable acts that substantially aggravate the offender’s culpability by adding to the humiliation and degradation of the child.

title: Online grooming to procure children for overseas abuse (Commonwealth provisions)
statement: The Commonwealth suite of online child sexual abuse provisions (outside this app’s Victorian scope) responds to the growing use of the internet to groom adults to procure children for overseas abuse: where the grooming occurs is immaterial if the intent is to procure a child for abuse outside Australia, and it does not matter that the child is fictitious, that the abuse is impossible, or that no sexual activity “in real life” is involved. The essence of the offence is the intention to use the internet to gain access to children; a fictitious child does not lessen culpability; actual harm aggravates but the absence of a “real victim” does not mitigate; it is predatory, manipulative and corrosive behaviour that can never be anything but serious.

refs.q: The essence of the offence is the offender’s intention in using the internet to gain access to children for sexual offending. Their moral culpability is not lessened because the child is or might be fictitious.

refs.q: There is a ‘growing prevalence of offenders using the internet to groom adults with the aim of procuring a child for overseas sexual abuse’. For this reason, the Commonwealth has established a suite of provisions concerned with the online sexual abuse of children.

refs.q: It is immaterial where the grooming occurs if the intent is to procure a child for sexual abuse outside of Australia, nor does it matter if the child is fictious or if it is impossible for the abuse to take place, neither are the offences limited to sexual activity “in real life”.

title: Child abuse material: gravity (Minehan factors; ANVIL/CETS levels; numbers; possession is not victimless)
statement: CAM offences are especially grave and increasingly prevalent; the internet’s anonymity hampers detection. Minehan’s thirteen factors guide gravity (the twelve listed below; the thirteenth, any other matter in s 16A of the Crimes Act 1914 bearing on objective seriousness, concerns Commonwealth offences and is outside the app’s scope). The six-level ANVIL/CETS scale helps, but the actual content matters, not just the level (Level 1 images are not benign; absence of higher levels does not minimise lower-level possession); the number of children depicted matters. Numbers of images are not determinative and gravity is not a mathematical comparison with other cases. Prose describing child sexual abuse can itself be abhorrent. Possession is not victimless (it creates a market); possession for sale or distribution aggravates; active distribution increases culpability whether or not profit was made or payment given (but see Schulz, fn 3746: possession falls at the lower end of seriousness if the images are few and unsolicited). Also relevant: how long material was kept, whether stored or sorted, and the duration of offending. The authority for “the absence of material in higher categories cannot … minimise” (fn 3739, “Ibid 820–21 [71]”) appears to be Garside, not Hutchinson (flag.ibid_fn3739). The expanded breadth of internet offending and the increased maxima indicate gravity; possessing only a “moderate” number of images does not mean the offending cannot be serious; using the internet to exploit children is grave even if the offender is not procuring the exploitation.

refs.q: • Whether actual children were used in the creation of the material. • The nature and content of the material, including the age of the children and the gravity of the sexual activity portrayed. • The extent of any cruelty or physical harm occasioned to the children that may be discernible from the material. • The number of images or items of material — in a case of possession, the significance lying more in the number of different children depicted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.3 – Child abuse material

refs.q: • In a case of possession, the offender’s purpose, whether for his/her own use or for sale or dissemination. In this regard, care is needed to avoid any infringement of the principle in R v De Simoni (1981) 147 CLR 383. • In a case of dissemination/transmission, the number of persons to whom the material was disseminated/transmitted.

refs.q: • Whether any payment or other material benefit (including the exchange of child pornographic material) was made, provided or received for the acquisition or dissemination/transmission. • The proximity of the offender’s activities to those responsible for bringing the material into existence. • The degree of planning, organisation or sophistication employed by the offender in acquiring, storing, disseminating or transmitting the material. • Whether the offender acted alone or in a collaborative network of like-minded persons. • Any risk of the material being seen or acquired by vulnerable persons, particularly children. • Any risk of the material being seen or acquired by persons susceptible to act in the manner described or depicted.

refs.q: Nor is the possession of any image necessarily required. The distribution of prose describing child sex abuse, especially where for the purpose of self-gratification, is itself abhorrent given its tendency to normalise or encourage such abuse, to ignore the harm it entails and to undermine society’s unequivocal condemnation of it.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.3 – Child abuse material

refs.q: In other words, being charged only with accessing or possessing child abuse material does not mitigate the gravity of the offending or the offender’s culpability. This is because possession of child abuse material is not a victimless crime; it encourages and creates a market for the corruption and exploitation of children who are sexually abused in order to meet demand. The offending will be further aggravated where there is evidence the offender possessed the material for the purpose of sale or further distribution, rather than personal use.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.2 – Circumstances of the offence > 24.2.2 – Gravity and culpability > 24.2.2.3 – Child abuse material

refs.q: However, active involvement that goes beyond being a passive recipient, such as by the distribution or propagation of images, links an offender more closely to the market, increases the number of people viewing the material, and implicitly means they are more culpable given their affirmative acts of exploitation. Failing to earn a monetary profit from this offending does not detract from the offender’s status as an active participant. Not paying to access child abuse material is similarly irrelevant.

title: Child sexual offences: good character excluded only if it assisted the offending
statement: The court must not have regard to prior good character or lack of prior convictions if satisfied it assisted the commission of a child sexual offence. This requires an affirmative finding of a connection (with submissions; the Crown appears to bear the burden); taking advantage of that status is one way but not the only one; it requires a material contribution, not a high causal threshold.

refs.q: A court must not have regard to an offender’s prior good character or lack of previous convictions when sentencing for a child sexual offence if it is satisfied that the prior good character or lack of convictions assisted them in committing the offence. This limitation only applies where the sentencing court is able to make a finding of fact that good character (or more often, the absence of prior convictions) was “of assistance” in the commission of the offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: ‘[T]his requires the court to be affirmatively satisfied of the connection’ between character and offending and also requires that the parties be allowed to make submissions on the point (upon which it further appears the Crown bears the burden of proof).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: The requirement of “assistance” does not set a high causal threshold, but it does at least require that good character made a material contribution to the offender committing the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: One way in which good character might assist the offender in committing the offence ‘is if the offender “takes advantage” of that status in some discernible way to commit the offending.’ But this is not the only way in which an offender can be so assisted, and the term is sufficiently broad and flexible to allow the court some scope to apply it depending on the circumstances.

title: Sexual offences: purposes
statement: Courts emphasise general and specific deterrence, just punishment, community protection and denunciation. General deterrence has primacy for child pornography offending. Rehabilitation, especially for historic offending, may mitigate depending on the case.

refs.q: For this reason, ‘general deterrence is accorded primacy in sentencing offending involving child pornography.’ It is necessary that the courts, by the sentences they impose, ensure that those tempted to engage in such crimes understand they will lose their liberty if detected.

title: Sexual offences: cumulation reflects separate harms
statement: Although cumulation is less likely for a single incident with one victim and no fresh harm, for sexual offending acts closely associated in time represent separate and substantial harms appropriately recognised by cumulation; total gravity informs it. Counting penetrative acts is crude; punishing successive degradation is not double punishment. Sending an explicit image to a child is separate criminality from attempts to procure. Cumulation is not a mathematical exercise, but an effective 4 months for each of three penetrations of a child under 10 was “simply too low”, despite very significant mitigation. But see Flynn (fn 3768): in a single-transaction case, cumulating one third of a second rape sentence on the first was “significantly out of kilter”.

refs.q: For most offences, a court is less likely to order the cumulation of sentences where they arise out of a single incident involving a single victim, and where the individual offences do not involve fresh harm. However, in relation to sexual offending it is appropriate to acknowledge by orders for cumulation that acts closely associated in time do represent separate and substantial harms. The objective gravity of the total offending is relevant to assessing the need to cumulate sentences for individual offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.5 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Differentiating between rape offences by simple reference to the number of penetrative acts is a crude mechanism for determining punishment, particularly within the context of a complex progression of separate assaults, degradations, threats and rapes. Punishing an offender for successively degrading, harming, traumatising, and assaulting the victim is not double punishment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.5 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Similarly, transmitting an explicit photo of sexual arousal to a child involves separate criminality from those parts of an online conversation where the offender sought to procure the child to take part in sexual activity, and some cumulation is appropriate.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 24 – Sexual Offences > 24.5 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Although exercise of the discretion to impose cumulated terms is not a mathematical exercise, the Court of Appeal has found that orders for cumulation which result in the effective imposition of 4 months imprisonment for each of three incidents of sexual penetration of a child under 10 is ‘simply too low’, despite the existence of very significant factors in mitigation.

As a result, courts must often make orders regarding concurrency and cumulation.

title: Causing injury: mandatory minimums for gross violence and protected workers; the four special-reason exceptions
statement: The Act specifies minimum sentences for most causing injury offences in circumstances of gross violence or against a protected worker. 25.1.3.1 describes “four exceptions” — the four special-reason categories: assistance or an undertaking to assist; proven (balance of probabilities) mental impairment causally related to the offending that substantially and materially reduces culpability or would make imprisonment substantially and materially more burdensome (not where the impairment was caused substantially by self-induced intoxication: fn 2007); a proposed Court Secure Treatment Order or Residential Treatment Order; or substantial and compelling reasons that are exceptional and rare. The last requires powerful circumstances wholly outside run of the mill factors; the offender bears a heavy burden to show a special reason. The list is not exhaustive of the exceptions: 9.1.2.2–9.1.2.3 add an offender under 18; liability by complicity (for the protected-official minimums only where the offender proves on the balance of probabilities that their involvement was minor); and, for protected-official offences other than gross violence, a youth justice centre order for offenders under 21 on the 9.1.2.3 conditions (flag.mm_exceptions_25_1_3_1). The gating is done by the mmnpp.* hard rules with the full 9.1.2.x lists; this item is guidance only.

title: Intentionally causing serious injury: current practice
statement: ICSI sentences have increased; immediate imprisonment is generally called for (more so than RCSI). Intent to cause serious injury makes it graver in that respect than unintentional homicide; some cases warrant sentences like or exceeding manslaughter. The Court of Appeal has said Nash and Cedic are yardsticks where serious injury is intended and severe injury results, and that ICSI with life-threatening or catastrophic injuries or ongoing serious impairment “should usually attract” more than 10 years (a Court of Appeal statement about that category, not a floor).
note: params usually_exceeds_years is descriptive (a Court of Appeal statement about a category of ICSI): never a hard floor or range check. The Manual does not say whether this practice informs s 15A (ICSI with gross violence).

refs.q: Intentionally causing serious injury Sentences for intentionally causing serious injury (‘ICSI’) have increased recently. The offence generally calls for a term of immediate imprisonment, even more so than in cases of recklessly causing serious injury (‘RCSI’). An intention to cause serious injury is the essence of the offence and so in that respect it is graver than an unintentional homicide. Therefore, some cases of ICSI may be so grave and result in such serious consequences that they will warrant a penalty like (or even exceeding) one imposed for manslaughter.

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has said that in cases where there is an intention to cause serious injury and severe injury results, Nash v The Queen and Cedic v The Queen are the yardsticks for measuring a proposed ICSI sentence in that category of seriousness.

title: Recklessly causing serious injury: current practice
statement: RCSI is triable summarily; as the principal offence in the higher courts it generally attracts custody, which is usually required. In 2010 the Court of Appeal said glassing sentences (as RCSI) did not reflect the inherent dangerousness of the conduct and should be increased (csp.uplift_glassing). Where facts closely resemble ICSI (glassing; “king hit”) no meaningful difference is warranted. Caution in comparing older cases after Kilic and Dalgliesh.

refs.q: Recklessly causing serious injury RCSI is triable summarily and is commonly prosecuted in the Magistrates’ Court and the higher courts. Where RCSI is the principal proven offence in the higher courts it will generally attract a custodial sentence.

title: Negligently causing serious injury by driving: current practice (uplift)
statement: In 2015 practice for upper-end NCSI–Driving was held inadequate and to be uplifted, with flow-on to mid and low range; the maximum had been increased to 10 years without corresponding sentence increases. The most serious cases involve negligence of the very highest order; do not draw detailed distinctions between precise injuries in upper-end cases. A court may have regard to car NCSI sentences when sentencing the driver of a motor boat for the same offence (neither should be treated more leniently). NCSI–Driving and culpable driving share features (speed, inattention, intoxication, priors) allowing comparisons. Some cases may suit a CCO or combination sentence, less likely as negligence and injury increase.

refs.q: The Court of Appeal held in 2015 that current sentencing practice for negligently causing serious injury by driving (‘NCSI–Driving’) at the upper end of seriousness was inadequate and needed to be uplifted, and that this would have a flow-on effect for sentencing in mid and low-range instances of the offence.

title: Causing injury: injury is “serious” for serious-injury offences; no sentencing for a greater offence than pleaded
statement: For a serious-injury offence the injury must be regarded as serious, but on a plea to a lesser offence (RCI or ICI) the offender cannot be sentenced for a more serious offence, even if intent might be inferred or the injury might meet the definition of serious injury. The seriousness of the injury and the degree of recklessness remain major considerations.

refs.q: Where an offender is found guilty of a causing serious injury offence, a court cannot regard the injury sustained by a victim as anything other than “serious”. But this does not mean that when an offender pleads guilty to a lesser offence such as RCI or ICI that a court can sentence them for a more serious offence. This would be contrary to principle even if the evidence might permit an implication of intent to be drawn or if the injury caused might meet the statutory definition of a “serious injury”.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: However, a sentencing court is fully entitled to generally consider the seriousness of an injury or the degree of recklessness in a case. These are major considerations in determining the gravity of the offence and the offender’s culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability

title: Causing injury: shared gravity and culpability factors
statement: Shared factors (below): proven intent; seriousness of injury (present and future; physical and psychological; impact; how inflicted; obstruction of medical help; assessed when sustained); vulnerability; weapons (blades significantly aggravating — see also Ranger, fn 3822: slight injuries and the offender’s disabilities); persistence (an attack “of a relatively short duration” is not mitigating: fn 3823); company; violence (kicking, punching by trained fighters, choking); family violence (serious breach of trust, especially in the home; controlling conduct such as monitoring the victim; “I snapped” does not mitigate) and duties to children (exposure to domestic violence when young may explain but cannot excuse or reduce culpability for harming a child); post-offence conduct such as shifting fault illuminates moral culpability; public, alcohol-fuelled unprovoked violence (youth and rehabilitation take a back seat); premeditation; part of the body attacked. Provocation may significantly lessen culpability, but not for revenge or punishment; here it is limited to words or deeds causing near-immediate loss of control; cooling off lessens it; cultural sensitivity to language (swearing) may not suffice. In homicide the Manual states provocation more broadly (as a sentencing factor not limited by the common-law test for reducing murder to manslaughter; may be cumulative; may count even where the conduct was excessive): apply each statement to its own offence class and caution where both arise (flag.provocation_injury_vs_homicide).

refs.q: Although it is not a legal defence to charges of causing injury, the degree to which the offender was provoked to violence is also relevant to sentence and may be a significant extenuating circumstance that lessens the offender’s moral culpability. This does not apply when the offender acts from revenge or to “punish” the victim. Moreover, conduct recognised as being sufficiently provocative is limited to words or deeds by the victim that incite or induce the offender to lose control and offend almost immediately while agitated or angry. The passage of time or existence of a “cooling off” period after the allegedly provocative behaviour lessens the mitigation of “provocation” by the victim.

refs.q: These include: • the offender’s proven intent to cause injury, serious injury, really serious injury, or the maximum possible injury; • the seriousness of the injury caused: including, present and future harm, physical and psychological harms, the impact of the injuries on the victim, how the injuries were inflicted, and whether the accused delayed, refused or obstructed the victim from receiving medical assistance for the injury or to identify its cause. This assessment is made at the time the injury is sustained; • the vulnerability of the victim; • the use of a weapon, particularly one with a blade, is a significantly aggravating factor, as it is extremely dangerous and capable of causing both serious injury and death; • persistence: a prolonged or lengthy attack or failing to stop despite having an opportunity to do so, until after the victim has been rendered helpless, others intervene, or the victim escapes, are strong indications of serious and highly culpable offending; • whether the offender acted alone or in company; • the violence of the attack, which does not necessarily require the use of a weapon. An offender who repeatedly and forcefully kicks or strikes the victim may be just as culpable as someone who was armed. Similarly, a clenched fist may not be a weapon, but it can be extremely dangerous when punching someone hard, particularly if the offender is a trained and experienced fighter. And choking someone is a ‘pernicious and dangerous form of violence’ whose risk ‘cannot be ignored when assessing its gravity’; • family violence; brutal treatment of a domestic partner or family member involves a serious breach of trust, especially in the home where the victim is entitled to feel safe illustrates the gravity of the crime and the offender’s moral culpability. As do controlling actions such as monitoring the victim’s movements, habits, reactions, fears, and responses. Any sort of violence in the domestic realm is never permissible and self-justifying statements such as, “I snapped”, do not mitigate either the offender’s culpability or the seriousness of the offending; • similarly, inaction in the domestic context may be reflective of gravity and culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.1 – Generally

title: ICSI (maximum 20 years) and RCSI (maximum 15 years): key indicators
statement: ICSI: the Court of Appeal endorsed the first six shared factors as a useful, non-prescriptive framework; key indicators are proven intent, seriousness of injury and manner of infliction (persistence and repeated head blows may show intent; a finding of higher intent than the basis of the plea requires an opportunity to be heard: fn 3851). Not foreseeing the precise injuries does not reduce culpability (but see Marino, fn 3855, RCSI king-hit: a substantial disparity between the injury foreseen and the catastrophic injuries sustained); worse injuries being possible does not prevent a serious characterisation. Glassing is serious ICSI (worse if offender sober and victim intoxicated) and, all things being equal, intentional glassing should receive more than reckless. RCSI: consider the probability of serious injury and the seriousness of the probable injury foreseen — acting in the face of both shows high culpability — and the impact on the victim (a key consideration, albeit only one). An offender may be highly culpable for gross violence RCSI without inflicting the injuries or being present. RCSI glassing is not in a lower category than RCSI with conventional weapons.

refs.q: The 20-year maximum penalty demonstrates the seriousness of ICSI.

title: Negligently causing serious injury by driving: gravity and responsibility
statement: NCSI–Driving sits above dangerous driving causing serious injury and below dangerous driving causing death; gravity is assessed by the degree of negligence and seriousness of injury. Aggravating features listed below; their absence does not necessarily put the offence at the lower end; remaining and assisting at the scene is not mitigating. Start from the presumption that the offender was solely responsible for the driving and its consequences (qualifiable by evidence). A passenger’s knowledge of intoxication or fatigue does not, by itself, reduce responsibility, and the passenger’s failure to wear a seatbelt does not demonstrate it was a contributing cause — and even if it did, the driver remains responsible, given the legal obligation to ensure passengers are wearing seatbelts (compare culpable driving, where a seatbelt failure proved on the balance of probabilities to have caused the death gets relatively modest weight: guide.driving.culpable_driving). Victim conduct matters only if it bears on the driving or choice to drive (e.g. urging faster driving); the offender may establish factors outside their control that were a material cause of the injuries, which should reduce the penalty. Loss or injury of one’s own child may be relevant in both mitigation and aggravation.

refs.q: • drives while intoxicated (by alcohol or drugs) or fatigued; • drives knowing their licence is suspended or that they don’t have one; • has been previously apprehended for driving on a suspended licence; • drives significantly over the speed limit; • drives through red lights/intersections; • was warned against driving; • drives on the wrong side of the road, into oncoming traffic, on the verge of the road, or fails to take evasive action; • is an experienced driver with knowledge of the legal requirements for rest breaks and disregards them or drives without adequate sleep; • drives a long distance, gravity and culpability increase the further the offender proceeds; • drives a large vehicle; • drives knowing the victim is near the vehicle.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: NCSI–Driving sits above dangerous driving causing serious injury but below dangerous driving causing death.

refs.q: The objective gravity of the offence and the offender’s culpability are to be assessed by both the degree of negligence and the seriousness of the injury caused.

refs.q: Moreover, the absence of one or more of these factors does not necessarily put the offence into the lower end of the scale of seriousness. Similarly, complying with obligations under the Road Safety Act 1986 (Vic) to remain at the scene of an accident and render assistance are not mitigating factors.

refs.q: The court should start from the presumption that the offender was solely responsible for the manner of their driving and that it was the sole cause of the victim’s injury. However, evidence may qualify either of those presumptions.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: A passenger’s knowledge of the driver’s intoxication or fatigue does not, by itself, reduce the driver’s responsibility for negligent driving. Similarly, the passenger’s failure to wear a seatbelt does not demonstrate this was a contributing cause of the passenger’s injury. And even if it did so, the driver remains responsible given their legal obligation to ensure passengers are wearing seatbelts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: The conduct of the victim is relevant to the offender’s responsibility and moral culpability only if it bears on how bad their driving was or on their choice to drive.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: If there is evidence that another, either the passenger or another person in the vehicle, persuaded the offender to drive faster or more dangerously and that because of this their driving was worse than it otherwise would have been, the offender’s moral culpability for the negligent driving is reduced. The presumption that an offender was solely responsible for the manner of their driving may thus be qualified if evidence shows they were not solely responsible for their conduct in choosing to drive, or in their manner of doing so. An offender may also be able to establish that there were factors outside their control that were a material cause of the injuries, which should also result in a reduced penalty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: An offender’s loss or injury of their own child as a result of their criminally irresponsible driving and gross breach of duty is a relevant sentencing consideration as a factor both in mitigation, and aggravation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: Negligence, and culpability, may be increased where if the offender: • drives while intoxicated (by alcohol or drugs) or fatigued; • drives knowing their licence is suspended or that they don’t have one; • has been previously apprehended for driving on a suspended licence; • drives significantly over the speed limit; • drives through red lights/intersections; • was warned against driving; • drives on the wrong side of the road, into oncoming traffic, on the verge of the road, or fails to take evasive action; • is an experienced driver with knowledge of the legal requirements for rest breaks and disregards them or drives without adequate sleep; • drives a long distance, gravity and culpability increase the further the offender proceeds; • drives a large vehicle; • drives knowing the victim is near the vehicle.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 25 – Causing injury > 25.2 – Gravity and culpability > 25.2.3 – Negligently cause serious injury by driving

refs.q: These factors are relevant not only to whether the offender’s conduct has met the threshold of negligence for NCSI-Driving but also demonstrate the extent of the negligence and the gravity of the offending.

title: Administering substances, stalking and assault
statement: Administering substances (rarely charged): given the statutory language, its gravity would appear to turn significantly on the dangerousness of the substance and the motive. Stalking (usually Magistrates’ Court; in the higher courts it is usually not the principal offence but does result in immediate custody — a practice observation): serious because it intends physical or mental harm or fear; psychological harm can be devastating. Statutory assaults’ seriousness is often limited by overlapping offences with higher maxima; common law assault is limited by the availability of causing injury and threat offences.

refs.q: Given the statutory language, its gravity would appear to turn significantly on the dangerousness of the substance administered and the motivation behind the administration.

refs.q: When it is in the higher courts it is usually not the principal offence but does result in an immediate custodial sentence. It is a serious offence because it intends to cause physical or mental harm to the victim or to arouse fear or apprehension in them for their safety or the safety of another. This psychological harm can be devastating.

refs.q: Statutory assault There are four assault offences under the Crimes Act: • Assault with the intent to commit an indictable offence; • Assault of a protected worker; • Assault of a person who is lawfully assisting a protected worker; • Assault with the intent to prevent their lawful apprehension or detention. The seriousness of these offences is often limited by overlapping offences attracting higher maximum penalties.

refs.q: Common law assault This common law offence is constituted by an “assault”, which incorporates either or both an “assault” and “battery”. At common law it is defined as any act which intentionally causes another to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence. A “battery” is the actual application of unlawful force however slight to another person. Significant limitations on the range of the offence are the availability of the causing injury offences where an “assault” results in actual injury and of the statutory threatening offences where a threat fits the elements of those offences.

statement: Emphasise general and specific deterrence, just punishment/denunciation and community protection; general deterrence and denunciation are particularly important for family violence even if the victim supports the offender. Not CCE, automatic forfeiture or sex offender registrable offences. ICSI/RCSI in gross violence and ICSI are “serious offences” and “serious violent offences” (serious offender regime; indefinite sentence possible). Most gross violence or protected worker offences attract a mandatory minimum non-parole period.

refs.q: Causing injury offences call for emphasis of the following sentencing factors: • general deterrence; • specific deterrence; • just punishment/denunciation; • community protection.

refs.q: General deterrence and denunciation are particularly important for offending occurring in the context of family violence, even where the victim supports the offender and seeks leniency on the plea.

title: Kidnapping and false imprisonment: current practice
statement: Kidnapping is uncommon but extremely serious, generally warranting a substantial custodial sentence (as do related offences such as false imprisonment). For kidnapping only (not child stealing or taking away a child, whose maximum is 5 years): kidnapping for ransom or leading to sexual offending often attracts sentences in “double figures”; total effective sentences of eight to nine years for “payback” kidnappings are not unusual; over seven to just under ten years is not uncommon for kidnapping generally and associated offences (whole-case total effective sentences).
note: The figures describe practice (total effective sentences of whole cases, often with associated offences): they are never a default, tariff or range check.

limbs.text: Practice figures (kidnapping: s 63A and common law): descriptive only.

refs.q: Where the kidnapping is for ransom, or leads to rape or sexual offending, it often attracts sentences in ‘double figures’. Total effective sentences of eight to nine years for ‘payback’ kidnappings are not unusual, and sentences exceeding seven years to just under ten years are not uncommon for kidnapping generally and associated offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 26.1.4 – Current sentencing practices

refs.q: While kidnapping is not common, it is as an extremely serious offence against the person and generally warrants the imposition of a substantial custodial sentence; as do the offences with which it is often related such as false imprisonment. Where the kidnapping is for ransom, or leads to rape or sexual offending, it often attracts sentences in ‘double figures’. Total effective sentences of eight to nine years for ‘payback’ kidnappings are not unusual, and sentences exceeding seven years to just under ten years are not uncommon for kidnapping generally and associated offences.

title: Hybrid personal/financial offences: amounts demanded; meagre proceeds; revenge
statement: The amount demanded may indicate scale, but is assessed with all the circumstances. Brutality or callousness is not lessened by meagre proceeds (especially by fortune), receiving no benefit is irrelevant, and revenge is itself relevant.

refs.q: The amount of money demanded may be an indicator of the scale and seriousness of the offending, but this should be assessed with all of the circumstances and not in isolation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: An offence aggravated by brutality or callousness does not become less serious because the amount realised is meagre, especially if this was by fortune rather than design. Moreover, the fact the offender receives no benefit is irrelevant; being motivated out of a desire for revenge is itself a relevant consideration in determining gravity and culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Many of these ‘other offences against the person’ are hybrid offences involving a substantial personal component and a quantifiable financial component.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: For example: kidnapping for ransom involves personal harms in the deprivation of liberty and physical assault as well as a property element in the amount of money demanded.

refs.q: Similarly, extortion can combine the emotional consequences of a threat to kill or injure with the quantifiable element of the amount demanded or paid.

title: Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing: gravity
statement: Gravity is indicated by the maxima (kidnapping 25 years). Kidnapping has been described as a form of terrorism; for ransom, extortion, advantage or subjugation it is particularly grave; trickery is not less serious than force. Child stealing is very serious. For false imprisonment, knowing a further serious assault would follow, leaving the bound victim to further assault, and whether steps were taken to end the imprisonment are relevant. Gravity and culpability may be increased by: premeditation; length of detention; violence, threats, fear or harm (victim or family); breach of trust; motives such as perverting justice or intimidating a witness; isolation; vigilantism; exposure to serious health and safety risks.

refs.q: Kidnapping has also been described as a form of terrorism, and kidnappings for ransom, to extort money, gain an advantage, or out of a desire to subjugate the victim to the offender’s will are considered particularly grave. Kidnapping is not less serious because trickery or deceit is used rather than physical violence or coercion.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing

refs.q: The violent kidnapping of a child followed by threats to their life will cause a parent anguish, and it is because kidnapping can have this effect that Parliament set a maximum penalty of 25 years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing

refs.q: With respect to false imprisonment, the gravity of the offending may be increased where the offender knew a further serious assault would follow and that restraining the victim facilitated that subsequent attack. The victim being bound and left in the company of co-offenders to face further assault would have added significantly to the terror they would have experienced. It is also relevant in these circumstances whether the offender took any steps to end the false imprisonment before leaving the premises.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing

refs.q: • premeditation or planning; • the length of the period of detention; • violence, threats, fear or harm to the victim or their family; • any breach of trust; • motives such as intending to pervert the course of justice or intimidate a witness; • isolating the victim; • vigilantism; or • exposing the victim to serious risks to health and safety.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing

refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing

refs.q: The gravity of kidnapping, false imprisonment, and child stealing is indicated by their maximum penalties.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing
