refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.1 – Kidnapping, false imprisonment and child stealing

title: Blackmail, extortion and threats: gravity
statement: Blackmail (threat to expose/accuse, or threat of violence — the Manual says it is debatable which is worse) is inherently serious: a direct attack whose fear, stress and anxiety may resemble violence. Threat gravity turns on the nature of the threat; bomb threats call for heavy sentences, their gravity does not depend entirely on proof of the means then and there to carry out the threat, and they are serious where multiple, menacing and distressing; an imitation device reinforces the threat but its incapacity to harm is also relevant. Also relevant: impact and fear; planning; stand-over tactics; persistence and duration; weapons; breach of trust; number of victims and family relationships; purpose of deterring enforcement of a legal right.

refs.q: Blackmail as a whole, however, is an inherently serious offence because while it is not necessarily a crime of physical violence, its nature as a direct attack upon a specific victim means that its impact may be similar in the fear, stress and anxiety it engenders.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.2 – Blackmail, extortion, and threats

refs.q: The gravity of threatening offences often turns upon the nature of the threat, and those reinforced by threatening the use of a bomb are a serious variant of offending and call for a heavy sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.2 – Blackmail, extortion, and threats

refs.q: The gravity of the use of a bomb threat does not depend entirely upon evidence that the offender had the means then and there to carry out the threat.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.2 – Blackmail, extortion, and threats

refs.q: The offending is serious where there are multiple calls/threats, that are menacing, are designed to be taken seriously and which cause alarm, inconvenience and distress, to a number of people. Making a threat of being in possession of a specific explosive device and showing an imitation device to reinforce the threat is relevant to its gravity. But, when considered within a range of conduct, it is also relevant that the imitation was not actually a bomb or device capable of harming others.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.2 – Blackmail, extortion, and threats

refs.q: Blackmail cases commonly fall within one of two categories: • demanding money by means of a threat to expose or accuse the victim; or • demanding money under a threat of violence. It is debatable whether one is more serious than the other.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.2 – Blackmail, extortion, and threats

refs.q: The following are also particularly relevant when assessing the gravity of blackmail, extortion and threat offences: • the impact on the victim impact/fear created; • planning and premeditation; • the use of stand-over tactics; • persistence and duration in threats; • the use of weapons; • a breach of trust; • the number of victims or individuals threatened and any familial relationship between them; or • where the purpose of the offence is to deter the enforcement of a legal right.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.2 – Blackmail, extortion, and threats

title: Endangerment offences: gravity
statement: Key factors: the nature and degree of risk and whether a weapon was used; deliberately firing a firearm at close quarters toward a person (especially police on duty) is among the most serious. Disregarding risks to others to serve one’s own ends (even self-harm) must expect a substantial price. Injury or death is not aggravating but shows the risk was real. Genuine (even mistaken) fear may mitigate, but does not extinguish criminality — particularly for a prohibited person in possession of a weapon who fires after the danger has passed (fn 3953); taking the law into one’s own hands or acting to intimidate or retaliate may place it at the upper end.

refs.q: In considering the gravity of an endangerment offence, the key factors are the nature and degree of risk created, and whether a weapon was used.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.3 – Endangerment offences

refs.q: It is difficult to imagine a more serious instance of such an offence than where a firearm is deliberately fired at close quarters in the direction of another person, especially a police officer performing their duties.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.3 – Endangerment offences

refs.q: Those who disregard the risks they impose on others to satisfy their own ends, even if they do not intend to harm or kill others but only themselves, must expect to pay a substantial price.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.3 – Endangerment offences

refs.q: The injury or death of the victim is not an aggravating feature, but it is relevant to an understanding of the offence and an appreciation of the seriousness of the danger to which the offender exposed the victim. It demonstrates that the risk created by the offender’s actions was not artificial or hypothetical, but real.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.3 – Endangerment offences

refs.q: If the offender acted out of genuine fear, the seriousness of the offending may be mitigated even if the fear was erroneous. But an offender taking the law into their own hands, or acting to intimidate, threaten, or retaliate, is ‘patently dangerous, frightening, and unacceptable’ and may bring the offending into the upper end of the spectrum of seriousness.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 26 – Other offences against the person > 26.2 – Gravity and culpability > 26.2.3 – Endangerment offences

refs.q: It does not however extinguish the offender’s criminality, particularly if they are a prohibited person in the possession of a weapon and fire it after the danger to them has passed.

title: Other offences against the person: focus on actual harms; purposes; schemes
statement: These offences are broad and hard to categorise (person v property); focus on the actual harms in the case. Purposes: deterrence, just punishment/denunciation, community protection. Not CCE or sex offender registrable; blackmail, extortion with threat to kill and extortion with threat to destroy property are automatic forfeiture offences (26.5 does not name the threat-to-injure limb of s 27). Kidnapping and threats to kill are “serious offences” (so an indefinite sentence may be available: 8.7, indefinite.requirements) and “violent offences”; threats to kill is also a “serious violent offence”; threats to inflict serious injury (s 21) is a “violent offence” only. The serious offenders regime may apply (serious_offender.regime) — the Manual says “may apply” / “might be imposed”; an indefinite sentence requires a “serious offence”.

refs.q: The principal points to note with respect to the circumstances of these offences is, firstly, their breadth. For example, endangerment offences can take many forms from driving dangerously to avoiding arrest, discharging a firearm during a confrontation, to failing to provide adequate care or medical attention. And, secondly, the difficulty in definitively categorising them. Blackmail may involve a threat of personal harm in order to achieve a non-financial goal, thus constituting an obvious offence against the person. At the other end of the spectrum, it is commonly constituted by non-violent threats of negative personal revelations combined with demands for money, making it more naturally a property offence. The same is true of the extortion offences. The Crimes Act 1958 (Vic) s 27 clearly creates an offence against the person (making a demand with a threat to kill or injure), where s 28 creates an offence much closer to the standard property offence (making a demand with a threat to destroy or endanger specified forms of property). title: Theft and burglary: gravity
statement: Theft cannot be put in a hierarchy; gravity turns on what was taken, its value, from whom, and all circumstances including purpose. Value is commonly key but not decisive (generally, the greater the value the greater the culpability), and may be completely subordinate where another harm to the victim is involved. Key elements are planning, role and value. Particularly serious: brazen offending; breach of trust by a burglar who is or was employed by the victim; prolific and persistent offending. Distinguish poorly planned, haphazard thefts from highly organised commercial offending, though incompetence is not mitigating and a high degree of persistence may elevate seriousness. There is little distinction between burglary of commercial and residential premises: both are serious for different reasons (dwellings: breach of privacy, fear and terror, loss of sentimental items; commercial: often greater planning and professionalism). Vehicle theft is not categorically less serious. Going equipped has no noticeably different gradations of seriousness.

refs.q: It is impossible to categorise thefts in such a way that types of theft can be put into a hierarchy of seriousness. It is the presence or absence of particular factors which will indicate the gravity of the instant offence. The objective gravity of any theft must be considered by reference to what was taken, its value, from whom it was taken, and all other relevant surrounding circumstances, including the purpose for which it was taken.

title: Handling stolen goods
statement: Handling is generally more serious than theft (greater maximum), as it encourages and ensures the success of thefts; no general sentencing practice exists. Most serious where planned, of significant scale and sophistication, where the offender leads or organises (not a passive recipient), abuses power or trust (e.g. disguising goods as stock-in-trade), or handles specialised or unique property (sentimental items from domestic burglaries).

refs.q: Offences of handling stolen goods are most serious where: • the dealing in stolen goods is planned, as opposed to a ‘casual purchase in a bar’; • the scale of the operation is significant in its sophistication or professionalism and the volume and value of goods handled; • the offender’s role is that of a leader or organiser, or is, at least, not that of a mere passive recipient; • the offender abuses a position of power or trust or responsibility, especially where the offender can disguise the stolen goods as stock-in-trade of a legitimate business; or • the stolen property handled is specialised or unique – such as items of sentimental value procured through domestic burglaries.

title: Violent property offences: common features of gravity
statement: Violent property offences are serious: terrifying for victims and threatening the community’s sense of security. Sentencing decisions on home invasion as a form of aggravated burglary remain directly relevant to the new offence. By introducing mandatory sentencing requirements for a class of home invasion offences, the legislature signalled that those offences are, other things being equal, more serious than aggravated burglary (which class the Manual means is unclear: fn 4044 says the mandatory imprisonment scheme applies to aggravated home invasion but not home invasion, yet home invasion is a Category 2 offence — flag.home_invasion_mandatory_scheme_fn4044; the register’s Category 2 status governs). Value matters less (and may be irrelevant) than violence, threats and fear. Common features are listed below. As with burglary, there is little distinction between commercial and residential premises.

factors.text: planning and professionalism (selection; targeting a home; care before entry; restraints; disguise)

refs.q: planning and professionalism such as: • selection of the place to be robbed in advance; • the victim’s home is targeted for theft; • particular care is taken before entry; • carrying items for the purpose of restraining victims, which may also be important to an assessment of criminality because carrying such items will inevitably be terrifying to the victims; • use of a disguise, even if this is unsuccessful;

title: Aggravated burglary and home invasion: gravity; post-entry and uncharged conduct; no subtraction reasoning
statement: Hogarth’s six categories (intimate partner, sexual assault intent and confrontational most serious; intent to steal, rob and spontaneous encounter less so) are not to be applied rigidly. Other instances of the offence must be considered, but the absence of an aggravating factor seen in another case does not make the instant case necessarily less serious; reasoning by subtracting absent features is impermissible two-stage sentencing. Ordinarily relevant: intent at entry; mode of entry; weapon; company; time; what the offender knew about occupants; whether the victim was particularly frightened of the offender. Family violence context does not make the offending less serious, and the law now recognises the fundamental importance of general deterrence in domestic violence. The extent to which post-entry conduct is relevant is “not entirely straightforward”: conduct that could have been charged as a more serious offence (e.g. false imprisonment, assault) should not be treated as aggravating, and if not charged that criminality cannot be taken into account adversely — the principle that the judge considers all circumstances of the charged offence gives way to the principle that no one is punished for an uncharged offence. But carrying a loaded firearm during a home invasion has been held a “very significant aggravating feature” even where no firearm offence is charged, because it revealed premeditation, illuminated the intention at entry and greatly increased the danger of the entry (the boundary is not stated: flag.uncharged_firearm_clark). Separately charged conduct must not be double counted. Post-entry conduct may prove the intent at entry (sexual assault intent generally more serious).

refs.q: The following considerations will ordinarily be relevant to an assessment of the gravity of a particular instance of aggravated burglary: • the offender’s intent at the point of entry; • the mode of entry; • whether the offender was carrying a weapon; • whether the offender was alone or in company; • the time of day at which the burglary took place; • what the offender knew or believed about who would be inside, and where the person(s) would be; and • whether the offender was someone of whom the victim was particularly frightened.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.2 – Violent property offences > 27.2.2.2 – Aggravated burglary, home invasion and aggravated home invasion

refs.q: In Hogarth, the Court of Appeal adopted the terminology suggested by the Sentencing Advisory Council in dividing aggravated burglaries into six categories. The most serious included intimate partner, intent to commit a sexual assault, and confrontational, while intent to steal, intent to rob, and spontaneous encounter were considered to be, comparatively, less serious. The Court of Appeal has, however, subsequently discouraged a rigid application of the categories described in Hogarth.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.2 – Violent property offences > 27.2.2.2 – Aggravated burglary, home invasion and aggravated home invasion

refs.q: While it will be necessary to consider other instances of the offence, by reference to both the offender and the offending, and identify what made them more or less serious examples of the offence, that does not mean that the absence of an aggravating factor seen in another case means that the instant offence is necessarily less serious. Rather, it may simply mean that the cases are different. Any process of reasoning by way of subtraction of the absent potentially aggravating features is impermissible two-stage sentencing.

title: Weapons in violent property offences
statement: All weapons are serious (risk of serious injury or death; terror); a weapon of “great lethality” bears directly on gravity, and how a weapon is used is relevant to criminality. Unloaded firearms, imitation weapons and innocuous items plainly carry less risk and so are less dangerous than the genuine article, but can still instil terror, cause serious emotional damage and are dangerous given potential police responses (on the competing general authorities see flag.imitation_weapon_competing_authority). Where carrying a weapon is an element it is not an aggravating circumstance, but its nature, potential for harm and manner of use may be considered; the use of a weapon in aid of a carjacking will almost always heighten the gravity of aggravated carjacking, even though it is the qualifying circumstance. Do not double count separately charged firearm possession or discharge, though carrying a loaded firearm is generally a significantly aggravating feature (an uncharged firearm in an aggravated burglary or home invasion: flag.uncharged_firearm_clark). The absence of a weapon commonly places casual, opportunistic aggravated burglary at the lower end, but not necessarily otherwise grave offending. Examples: pointing a firearm while threatening to shoot has been characterised (in one case) as a “mid-range” armed robbery; pulling the trigger (a misfire) was particularly egregious; firing shots aggravates; lacerating a victim with a chainsaw or box cutter greatly elevated the criminality. Serious offending stays serious even with relatively minor injuries.

refs.q: All weapons are serious because the mere presence of a weapon carries with it the risk of serious injury or death, and may induce terror in victims.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.2 – Violent property offences > 27.2.2.3 – Weapons

refs.q: While unloaded firearms, imitation weapons, and innocuous items brandished as weapons plainly do not carry that same risk of injury or death and so are less dangerous than the genuine article, these are still capable of instilling terror in victims and possible serious emotional damage, and are dangerous in terms of potential police response.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.2 – Violent property offences > 27.2.2.3 – Weapons

refs.q: For several violent theft offences, carrying a weapon is an element of the offence and should not be treated as an aggravating circumstance. title: Deception and corruption offences: gravity; motive; absence of loss
statement: Deception offences are serious (calculated courses of conduct, repeated dishonesty, significant losses; hard to detect, expensive to prosecute, most often devoid of excuse). Particularly egregious: dishonesty by a solicitor or accountant in professional practice, or other abuse of a position of power, trust or responsibility to facilitate or camouflage the offending; an appalling breach of trust; a very large amount; systematic, deliberate dishonesty over a period, particularly where the offender persists despite opportunities to desist (voluntary cessation before exposure by a third party earns a real discount); a significant or “tragic” impact on small or vulnerable investors, on victims including both individuals and institutions, or where no funds are recovered. Value gained is generally an important indicator, but the extent, breadth and sophistication may make offending involving smaller sums more serious. Absence of loss significantly reduces gravity but must not unduly erode general deterrence. Greed versus need is a slight and usually illusory difference; the absence of greed is not uncommon, and motive may bear on the genuineness of remorse, specific deterrence or rehabilitation; extreme financial pressure only extremely rarely mitigates a significant breach of trust, and people in desperate financial straits cannot expect special leniency. Secret commissions threaten institutional and commercial integrity; profit, duration and scale matter.

refs.q: Deception offences are considered serious offending and often involve a carefully calculated course of conduct over a long period, repeated deliberate acts of dishonesty and the loss of significant funds. These offences are difficult to detect and investigate, expensive to prosecute and ‘most often devoid of excuse’.

title: Criminal damage and arson: gravity
statement: Criminal damage varies greatly; offences charged as arson are generally of substantial gravity and arson causing death is the most serious; computer and contamination offences are commonly at the lesser end — but the maximum still governs (e.g. sabotage, Level 2 – 25 years). Bushfire damage is always serious. Particularly serious arson or damage: multiple arsons; a leading role; substantial loss; revenge or reward motive; knowledge the building was occupied; risk to others (neighbours); fire danger periods, total fire bans or hot windy days; fires hard to detect. The offender’s intention characterises the seriousness; men directing violence (arson or damage) at former partners should expect condign punishment. At common law reasonably foreseeable unintended consequences could be considered; ss 5(2)(daa) and (db) have displaced that requirement: the court considers victim impact and the extent of loss or damage. Planned offending is generally more serious, but unplanned “add-on” arson may still be very serious; method dictates seriousness; landscape and spread risk matter. Arsonists are not uncommonly injured: whether such injuries mitigate is unsettled and depends on the circumstances (the cases go both ways: flag.extra_curial_test_scope).

refs.q: Offences of arson and criminal damage are considered particularly serious where: • one offender has committed multiple offences of arson; • the offender had a leading role (if the offending occurred in company); • the resulting damage or loss is substantial; • the offender is motivated by revenge or reward; • the arsonist knew or believed that the building they set fire to was occupied; • there is risk of harm to others in general and neighbours in particular; • the fire is lit during a ‘fire danger period’ declaration, during a total fire ban or on a hot windy day; or • the fire is difficult to detect.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences

refs.q: Criminal damage offences vary greatly in their gravity – the property damaged may vary from a book to a mansion - however offences charged as arson are generally regarded as being of substantial gravity, and arson causing death is the most serious offence in this section. Offending involving computers and contamination of goods are commonly at the lesser end of the scale of seriousness.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences

refs.q: In Australia, criminal damage caused by bushfire is always regarded as a serious offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences

refs.q: While the extent of the damage is relevant in arson cases, it is the intention of the offender which characterises the seriousness of the offence. In particular, men who direct violence (whether arson or criminal damage of property) towards former partners should expect ‘condign punishment’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences > 27.2.4.1 – Intent and unintended consequences

refs.q: Sections 5(2)(daa) and 5(2)(db) of the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) have entirely displaced the common law requirement of reasonable foreseeability. Under these provisions, the court must now have regard to the victim impact of the offending, and the extent of loss or damage resulting.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences > 27.2.4.1 – Intent and unintended consequences

refs.q: In general, criminal damage offences which are planned and premeditated are considered more serious than those which are impulsive. However, in arson cases, offending that is “completely unplanned”, and characterised as a mere “add-on” to other offending, has nevertheless been found to be very serious offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences > 27.2.4.2 – Planning, premeditation, and method

refs.q: The method by which the arson is accomplished also dictates its objective seriousness.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences > 27.2.4.2 – Planning, premeditation, and method

refs.q: The court may consider the nature of the landscape or physical environment, and the impact it has on the risk of fire spreading in assessing the objective seriousness of offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 27 – Property Offences > 27.2 – Gravity and culpability > 27.2.4 – Damaging property offences > 27.2.4.3 – Risk

In arson and other criminal damage cases, an offender who had no idea that by causing minor damage, a vast amount of damage would ultimately result, would not have such consequences 'used against him'.

title: Money laundering / dealing with proceeds of crime: gravity (Victorian Division 2A v Commonwealth s 400)
statement: The Manual’s principles “have so far emerged from the authorities on Commonwealth offending” (the first, the seriousness of the offence within the s 400 scheme, is Commonwealth-only), and it marks the Victorian differences: Division 2A grades seriousness by the fault element, not by value, and for Victorian offending value is relevant but not dominant (for Commonwealth offending value is highly significant and the primary identifier of the maximum). The court considers the precise circumstances of the conduct, including the nature of the dealing, its duration, and the number of transactions (in general, prolific offending involving small amounts will be more serious than a single larger transaction), the offender’s role, authority and initiative, and the extent of their belief or knowledge that the money is proceeds of crime. Do not consider what sentence might have followed for the predicate offence.
note: jurisdiction mixed: the Commonwealth principles (the s 400 Criminal Code scheme; value as highly significant and the primary identifier of the maximum; the fault element and value as the measure of seriousness) are outside the app’s Victorian scope; the Victorian points are the Division 2A fault-element grading and value as relevant but not dominant.

refs.q: Division 2A of the Crimes Act 1958 contains an offence scheme with gradations of severity based on the fault element involved but – unlike the Commonwealth offence scheme – not the value of the money dealt with.

title: Deception offences: reduced weight for good character; reputational loss
statement: Personal circumstances including good character ordinarily get less weight in deception offending, as white collar offenders typically have good character, references and prospects — often what gave them positions of trust and helped them avoid detection. Mitigating weight may be given to reputational damage and loss of capacity to practise their profession.

refs.q: An offender’s personal circumstances, including good character, will ordinarily be given less weight in offending involving deception. It is a feature of “white collar” crime that offenders are likely be of prior good character, have no prior convictions, have good character references, and good prospects of rehabilitation. Indeed that is often what enables them to attain a position of trust in the first place and facilitates offenders in avoiding detection for long periods. However, a sentencing court may give mitigating weight to the reputational damage involved in a conviction for dishonesty, and the offender’s loss of capacity to engage in their chosen profession.

title: Property offences: purposes
statement: Theft: the scale of the offence and the offender’s personal circumstances will generally be the strongest determiners of the dominant purpose; general deterrence is key for theft, burglary and handling (especially prevalent offences such as shoplifting and vehicle theft, and burglaries of vulnerable “soft targets” such as rural properties); just punishment and general deterrence are the key purposes for handling; specific deterrence matters for serial offending; going equipped is a deterrent or “preventative” offence in itself. Violent thefts: just punishment, denunciation, general deterrence and community protection, especially for vulnerable victims (a special protective obligation); aggravated home invasion forfeits liberty for a very long time; youth and rehabilitation are secondary in serious cases (rehabilitation may rarely displace deterrence where reform is a real prospect; it may be emphasised for less serious cases or young offenders without significant priors). Deception: white collar thefts are said to deserve utmost condemnation; general deterrence and strong denunciation of breach of trust; personal mitigation such as good character generally gets less weight than general deterrence; specific deterrence often minor. Arson: said to be hard to detect and to call for deterrence (easy to commit, destructive); both general and specific deterrence matter for violence towards former partners, “misguided vigilantism”, total fire bans and significant risk to others; community protection is key. Secret commissions (hard to detect, often committed by people of good character) and money laundering: general deterrence.

refs.q: For theft offences, the scale of the offence and the personal circumstances of the offender will generally be the strongest determiners of the dominant purpose. General deterrence is a key sentencing purpose in cases of theft, burglary and handling stolen goods, and especially for prevalent offences such as shoplifting and vehicle theft, and burglaries where those offences have been committed against vulnerable “soft targets” such as rural properties.

title: Property offences: serious offender scheme (arson), Category 1 and 2, forensic samples, forfeiture and CCE offences
statement: Each scheme applies only to the offences of its limb (below). Serious offender scheme: only arson offences (arson, arson causing death, causing a bushfire, and the listed Forests Act and CFA Act offences, conspiracy and interstate equivalents). Category 2 (offender 18 or older; offence on or after 20 March 2017): armed robbery only where the offender had a firearm, a victim was injured as a direct result, or it was committed in company; home invasion; carjacking; arson causing death (the register carries each condition). Aggravated home invasion and aggravated carjacking are Category 1 offences (offender 18 or older) with a three-year minimum non-parole period unless the offender was under 18 at the offence or special reasons are found (mmnpp.aggravated_home_invasion_carjacking_3y; 9.1.2.5 gives s 10AC for aggravated home invasion and s 10AD for aggravated carjacking; the 27.1.1.2 table footnotes cite s 10AD for both: flag.ahi_minimum_provision_10ac_10ad). All Victorian offences in the chapter are forensic sample offences except going equipped, dealing with property suspected of being proceeds and ss 247G–247H; civil forfeiture applies except to suspected proceeds and ss 247G–247H. Automatic forfeiture applies to the listed offences where the property is $50 000 or more (or $75 000 or more across multiple charges on the same facts or a series). The listed offences are continuing criminal enterprise offences where the property is $50,000 or more (dealing with proceeds of crime only under s 194(1)–(3); destroying or damaging property under s 197(1)–(3), (6)–(7)); a rolled-up count with one transaction of $50,000 or more is treated as a CCE offence (9.4 says the transaction must exceed $50,000; at exactly $50,000 the app does not rely on the doubled ceiling, and a sentence above the ordinary maximum but within it is a caution, not an error: flag.cce_value_threshold, cce.regime). Whether the property values are met must come from the user.

title: Cumulation: burglary/aggravated burglary and the ulterior offence
statement: Where a burglar is sentenced for the trespass with intent and the ulterior offence, cumulation reflects separate criminality but totality limits the total; factors common to several offences must be reflected in cumulation. Do not cumulate the whole aggravated burglary sentence on an ICSI sentence from the same occasion.

refs.q: Double punishment issues may arise where a burglar is to be sentenced for trespassing with intent to either steal, commit assault or damage property, and also for the subsequent theft, assault or property damage. Orders for cumulation are designed to ensure that the sentence reflects the separate criminality involved in the individual offences. But the principle of totality requires that the total effective sentence not be disproportionate to the aggregate criminality involved in all of the offences. Where a number of factors going to offence seriousness are common to multiple offences, this will impact the overall criminality and must be reflected in the orders for cumulation. A sentencing court should not order cumulation of the whole of a sentence imposed for aggravated burglary upon a sentence imposed for the offence of intentionally causing serious injury which was committed on the same occasion.

title: Commercial trafficking and cultivation: current practice (Gregory uplift; Fernando relativities)
statement: Generally, an immediate custodial sentence will be imposed for commercial trafficking or cultivation offences. Gregory held that practice for commercial-quantity (CQ) trafficking was inadequate and compressed at the upper end; because practice did not reflect the gravity, community impact and high maximum, courts are no longer constrained by existing practice, and relativities between the quantity-based offences must be maintained. The Court expected sentences to be spread across the statistical range, but said double figures might be expected where one or more listed features are present (a not guilty plea and relevant priors appear in the list, but neither can increase a sentence: see the caution). Pre-Gregory sentences and statistics need caution. Gregory said LCQ sentences will similarly need to increase substantially — obiter, but consistently followed since. Fernando: the uplift affects the upper range most, with a diminishing effect toward the middle and lower categories. The uplift is not controlling (Dalgliesh) but cannot be ignored. Each limb applies only to its own offences (plain trafficking, s 71AC, is not a CQ offence).
note: Practice statements in this item (e.g. “double figures might be expected”) are descriptive: never a default, tariff or range check (audit.statistics_and_medians; audit.comparable_cases_use).

title: Cultivation: current practice (hierarchy and relativities; trafficking comparators and the Nguyen uplift for CQ cultivation)
statement: Cultivation offences form a deliberate hierarchy, so what was said in Gregory about relativities applies equally to cultivation. For commercial-quantity cultivation, trafficking cases may be considered in assessing current practice (given the overlap), and Nguyen found mid-category CQ cultivation sentences inconsistent and compressed at a low level, capped by the overlap with LCQ cultivation, and required the range to be uplifted and substantially expanded (its “by increments” requirement has since been overruled; the uplift does not reach sentences previously reserved for less culpable offenders such as crop sitters: csp.uplift_cultivation). Each limb applies only to its own offences.

title: Quantity as a comparator: use a common denominator
statement: Trafficking (and importation) is quantity-based, so quantity is a key indicator of seriousness and of comparison, and must be presented simply and clearly. Where different drugs are compared, raw quantities, multiples of a minimum quantity or estimated wholesale or retail values are not a sensible common denominator (28.1.4.2); convert to a common denominator — preferably the commercial quantity or large commercial quantity (multiples or percentages). Value may still indicate scale and the offender’s benefit (28.3.2.2, 28.3.2.5); the Manual states the role of value in both ways (flag.drug_value_comparator). Tables of comparable cases help only with sufficient case features, not mere numbers. Quantity is only one factor; comparing by weight alone departs from principle. (Commonwealth: the Commonwealth scheme does not distinguish a CQ from an LCQ — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

refs.q: The sentencing scheme for trafficking and importation is quantity-based, which means that quantity is generally a key indicator of both offence seriousness and a key point of comparison between cases. Therefore it is important that information about quantity be presented simply and clearly to the court to enable it making meaningful judgments and comparisons about relative offence seriousness.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.4 – Current sentencing practice > 28.1.4.2 – Quantity as a comparator

refs.q: In cases where quantity is a guide to offence seriousness, comparisons to other cases ‘by reference to the quantity of drug trafficked or imported will usually be illuminating’. This is straightforward where the drug in both cases is the same, but where different drugs are involved simply identifying the raw quantities will not allow for a sensible comparison to be drawn.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.4 – Current sentencing practice > 28.1.4.2 – Quantity as a comparator

refs.q: If a past sentence is to provide a meaningful basis for comparison, the quantities involved must be given a common denominator, and courts have identified that the preferred common denominators are a commercial quantity (for a commercial or marketable quantity) or a large commercial quantity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.4 – Current sentencing practice > 28.1.4.2 – Quantity as a comparator

refs.q: Towards that end the provision of tables of comparable cases may be helpful, provided they give sufficient information about the features of each case that will allow useful comparisons to be drawn and are not merely numerical tables, charts, or graphs.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.4 – Current sentencing practice > 28.1.4.2 – Quantity as a comparator

refs.q: Lastly, quantity is only one factor to be taken into consideration; comparing drug cases only by reference to weights risks a fundamental departure from principle.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.4 – Current sentencing practice > 28.1.4.2 – Quantity as a comparator

refs.q: For the purpose of determining the relative seriousness of one trafficking offence against another, it is useful to convert the weight of the drug into multiples of a large commercial quantity or a commercial quantity, and the parties should present their plea submissions accordingly.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.4 – Trafficking

refs.q: Nor will describing the amount as being “more than 120 times the minimum marketable quantity”, or referring to the estimated wholesale or retail value, provide any meaningful guidance as to the seriousness of the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.4 – Current sentencing practice > 28.1.4.2 – Quantity as a comparator

refs.q: Assessments are commonly offered in respect of the value of drugs and can be a valuable indicator of the scale of the offending and may provide some basis for comparison with other cases.

title: Statutorily mitigated forms (onus on offender, balance of probabilities); possession v trafficking (De Simoni)
statement: The DPCS Act provides lower maxima where statutory mitigating factors are proved by the offender on the balance of probabilities: cultivation not for trafficking; possession of a small quantity of cannabis; possession unrelated to trafficking (cannabis or any drug); using cannabis. The mitigated possession forms that raise whether the possession was related to trafficking must be approached with care: a person convicted of possession cannot be sentenced as if for trafficking — “possession for sale” is not a valid basis for aggravation (De Simoni), but “possession for a purpose relating to trafficking” may aggravate if proved beyond reasonable doubt, unless that purpose amounted to trafficking (this arises most where the s 73(1)(c) “any other case” band applies). (Commonwealth: the Criminal Code creates scaled offences but no offence provable in a mitigated form — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

limbs.text: Possession for sale v possession for a purpose relating to trafficking (De Simoni)

refs.q: The mitigated forms of the possession offence which raise the issue of whether the possession was related to trafficking must be approached with care.

refs.q: An offender who is convicted of possession cannot be sentenced as though they had been convicted of the more serious offence of trafficking. Courts have drawn a distinction for the purposes of sentencing between “possession for sale” and “possession for a purpose relating to trafficking”. While the former is not a valid basis for aggravation (as it would contravene the rule from De Simoni), the latter is a permissible basis for aggravation if it is proved beyond reasonable doubt, unless that purpose amounted to trafficking.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.1 – Mitigating factors

title: Quantity is the primary statutory factor; no judgments of relative drug harm (Pidoto: trafficking and cultivation)
statement: Quantity is the primary statutory factor of seriousness; because Parliament created a quantity hierarchy (a harm-based scheme would look very different), courts must not judge the relative harmfulness of different drugs (Pidoto) — that would need special expertise, detailed investigation and extensive information. Schedule 11 sets large commercial, commercial, traffickable and small quantities. The drug’s identity is not a primary basis for distinction (except for cannabis, it is relevant only to whether an aggravated or mitigated form was committed). The harm of drugs generally to users and the community remains legitimate, and quantity is not the only factor. Pidoto is limited to trafficking and cultivation: possession, use, trafficking to a child and supply to a child are excluded — but 28.3.1 also states the no-hierarchy proposition for “possessing, or using” (flag.pidoto_scope_possession_use).

refs.q: In R v Pidoto the Court of Appeal said that since Parliament has created a statutory hierarchy based on quantity, it is not proper for the courts to make judgments about the relative harmfulness of a drug.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.2 – Quantity

refs.q: Drugs of dependence are principally defined by the lists in Parts 1-3 of Schedule 11 of the DPCS Act. The tables in these Parts list the quantity required to constitute a large commercial, commercial, traffickable or small quantity of each drug of dependence.

refs.q: The type of drug is not a primary basis for distinction in either the Commonwealth or Victorian statutory schemes.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.3 – Identity of drug

The legislation only precludes a court from considering the purported harm of a given drug relative to the purported harm of another drug, not to the harm drugs in general do to the user and to the community. Those are legitimate considerations.

title: Measuring quantity: purity, plants, continuing (Giretti) trafficking, co-offenders, aggregation
statement: It appears that the “small” and “traffickable” quantities refer to pure substance. A drug may be treated as pure if it meets the prevailing purity standard (British Pharmacopeia judicially noticed). Plant weight is measured as at the offence (a green crop’s actual weight), though usable yield matters to gravity; a cutting becomes a plant when it develops a root (even if it dies). A continuing business of trafficking can be one Giretti offence with accumulated quantities (mixed drugs permitted). Quantities are not divided among co-offenders. Mixture components may be aggregated by adding proportions of the relevant threshold (exceeding one qualifies), but not across separate counts; the drugs in a concoction do not create as many offences as there are drugs, and that the substances are mixed may be taken into account.

refs.q: Despite these distinctions, a drug may be treated as “pure” even if it contains minor contaminants if its purity matches the prevailing standard for a pure drug of that kind.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.2 – Quantity > 28.2.2.1 – Substance to be measured

refs.q: Australian courts take judicial notice of the standards for the purity of pharmaceutical drugs set by the British Pharmacopeia.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.2 – Quantity > 28.2.2.1 – Substance to be measured

refs.q: When determining the weight of the plant, it should be measured in light of conditions existing at the time the offence is committed. So, if the crop is “green” it’s weight is whatever it is in that condition, not that which it would be when dried and so become usable. However, the extent to which the crop would produce usable material is relevant when assessing the gravity of the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.2 – Quantity > 28.2.2.1 – Substance to be measured

refs.q: Effectively, a cutting becomes a plant when it develops a root. Not a root system, a root. Nor does it need to be viable - it continues to be a plant even if it dies.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.2 – Quantity > 28.2.2.1 – Substance to be measured

refs.q: In R v Giretti (‘Giretti’) the Court of Appeal found that “trafficking” can encompass not just discrete acts, but also continuous offending, where that offending is properly characterised as a single act of trafficking. One basis for that characterisation is where the separate acts could be seen to be part of the unified conduct of a business of trafficking. When considering a continuous offence of this nature, it is permissible to accumulate the individual quantities proven. A Giretti charge does not have to be confined to one particular type of drug, and can involve a mixed drug dealing business, providing it was an ongoing activity.

title: Traffickable quantity (evidentiary presumption only); small quantities (cannabis fine); s 76 adjourned bond
statement: A traffickable quantity does not affect the maximum (in either scheme); possession of it is prima facie evidence of trafficking. Small quantities affect the maximum only for cannabis possession (fine of five penalty units instead of one or five years’ imprisonment if established). Apart from this, the only relevance of the small quantity is s 76: under it, a person charged with possession or use (or the inchoate forms) should presumptively be released on an adjourned bond without conviction “if other strict criteria are met” — and the table says cultivation unrelated to trafficking (s 72B(a)) “may qualify” too. The criteria are not set out in the Manual (flag.s76_scope_cultivation): s 76 is possibly available — ask the user; never pass or fail a sentence on s 76 alone.

refs.q: In the State scheme, the DPCS Act provides that a person’s possession of a traffickable quantity of a drug is prima facie evidence of trafficking by that person in that drug.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.2 – Statutory factors > 28.2.2 – Quantity > 28.2.2.4 – Significance of traffickable quantities

refs.q: Parts 2 and 3 of Schedule 11 of the DPCS Act specify small quantities for most drugs of dependence and narcotic plants. However the only instance where this is relevant to the maximum penalty is where the drug is cannabis, and the offence is possession. title: Drug offences: information the court needs; common gravity features
statement: Drug offences are a substantial social evil. Common features found relevant to gravity and culpability: quantity (actual or attempted); role in the hierarchy; financial gain or motive; knowledge or belief; size and sophistication; duration; assistance to authorities; criminal history; prospects of rehabilitation. Criminal history appears in that list, but prior convictions cannot be used to increase a sentence (flag.priors_as_aggravation_30_3). title: Quantity, purity, plants, value and yield as indicators of gravity
statement: Maxima range from 10 years to life at the upper end; generally, the higher the quantity, the more serious, reflecting Parliament’s ascending order of seriousness — but giving quantity chief importance without other factors is error. The standard sentence’s middle-range notion is harder to apply where quantity is central. No mathematical adjustment between several offences by quantity. Large seizures support inferences (not for personal use; large-scale business; expected profit). Purity matters (higher purity increases gravity; where the purity of a mixture is known, comparing the pure proportion with the pure threshold is not error). Commercial by number of plants but not weight may indicate lower seriousness (e.g. Belbruno, charged among other things with trafficking a commercial quantity of cannabis: 168 plants, potential weight a little over 10 kg, described as a low to mid-range commercial quantity). Value can indicate scale and may give some basis for comparison, and is regularly accepted as a guide to gravity where it reveals the offender’s actual or anticipated benefit — but the legislation emphasises quantity (flag.drug_value_comparator). Potential yield and value matter for cultivation, though hard to estimate; much may depend on the plants’ stage of development and the care needed.

refs.q: Drug offences are extremely serious crimes as indicated by the maximum penalties which range from 10 years’ to life imprisonment for offences at the upper end of the range. And because the sentencing regime is quantity-based, the amount of the drug involved is a significant factor. Generally, the higher the quantity, the more serious the offence will be.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.1 – Quantity

refs.q: However, it is an error to attribute chief importance to quantity, without considering other relevant factors. While weight may be a significant factor in assessing an offender’s criminality or the gravity of the crime, it is not the sole variable affecting sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.1 – Quantity

refs.q: The Court has also noted that while the standard sentence is for a notional offence in the middle range of objective seriousness, giving content to that difficult notion is made more difficult in cases where the offending has a quantitative threshold and the quantity trafficked is central to assessing the gravity of the offence.

title: Role in a drug enterprise (labels are not the focus; Olbrich)
statement: Role is significant: principals are typically more culpable than couriers or middlemen, who are more culpable than street dealers and users — but the terms used vary widely, labels are not the focus, there is no rigid benchmark, there is no reason to think enterprises are formally structured, and courts sentence on the known facts. Olbrich: identifying the precise role is not essential (nor required in every case; its utility depends on what is known); “courier” and “principal” may be a useful shorthand, but cannot obscure what the offender did, and the label should not distract from the tasks performed, relationships and the trust and responsibility given (e.g. living at the crop premises; many communications about quantity and price can show a principal role). In serious drug offences couriers and other low-level participants are important, if not essential, and deserve suitable punishment, and a sole proprietor of a “one man” cultivation is not a mere crop sitter: normally, offending even at that level calls for immediate imprisonment (limbs below: the commercial offences; for non-commercial trafficking and cultivation the scope of “serious drug offences” is unresolved, a caution: flag.serious_drug_offences_low_level_custody). Steps such as possession, movement and storage can show an executive function; a precise equivalence between co-offenders is not required (an evaluative judgment). What others in the hierarchy stood to gain is irrelevant. (Commonwealth importation and possession: the R v Nguyen principles — e.g. a rebuttable inference of profit; good character of less weight; attempted possession no less serious than importation — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

limbs.text: Low-level participants in commercial trafficking and cultivation: normally immediate imprisonment

refs.q: In this respect it is important to remember that couriers and other low level participants are important, if not essential, to serious drug offences and deserve suitable punishment because the narcotics trade would collapse without their participation.

Normally, drug offending even at this level calls for immediate imprisonment.

refs.q: • The criminality of the offender is assessed by considering their involvement in the steps taken to effect the offence. refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: A sentence will generally reflect the level of the offender in the hierarchy. Principals typically have a higher degree of moral culpability than couriers or middlemen, who in turn have a higher degree of culpability than street level dealers and persons possessing drugs for personal use. But this does not mean there is a particular benchmark or tariff rigidly applied in formulating sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: A court can only sentence on the basis of the facts known, and a full picture of relative roles and responsibilities is unlikely to be known with any precision.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: In Olbrich v The Queen, the High Court held that identifying the precise nature of an accused’s involvement is not essential to the sentencing process.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: The Court further said that distinguishing between a “courier” and a “principal” may be a useful shorthand description of different kinds of participation in the enterprise, and that in a given case different levels of culpability may attach to those roles. But it always necessary to remember the crime that the offender is being sentenced for and characterising them as a “courier” or “principal” cannot obscure the assessment of what they did.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: Moreover, in certain circumstances, such as “one man” cultivation operations where the offender is the sole proprietor, they cannot also be classified as a mere “crop sitter” and their moral culpability will be high. Normally, drug offending even at this level calls for immediate imprisonment.

refs.q: Even though it was not possible to precisely identify the role played by each offender, the steps taken by each (individual and joint possession, movement, and storage) displayed an ‘executive function’ beyond that of a functionary.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: Lastly, whether others in the hierarchy stood to gain from an offender’s conduct does not affect their sentence; the question is what the offender did and who they are, not what others might have hoped to gain.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: But the terms used for roles vary widely and as discussed below such labels are not the focus of a court’s consideration.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: It is not a task that must be undertaken in every case and its utility is limited by the extent to which the material facts about the person’s involvement in the offending are known.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: In this respect it is important to remember that couriers and other low level participants are important, if not essential, to serious drug offences and deserve suitable punishment because the narcotics trade would collapse without their participation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: The label attached to the offender should not distract from the various factors relevant to assessing the gravity of the offence, including tasks the offender might have performed, the nature of their relationship with others in the enterprise, or the degree of trust and responsibility given to them. For example, in Nguyen v The Queen, the Court found that the offender moving into the premises where the crop was grown and cultivated put them in a position of significant trust within the enterprise. And in that context, a large number of communications between a “principal” and the offender further permitted the inference that their role was not confined to that of a “crop sitter”. So too did the content of such communications where quantity and price were discussed; content like that was sufficient to conclude the offender had an interest in the revenue that extended beyond idle curiosity and that they were a principal in the syndicate.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: It said the sentencing judge had been entitled to find the role played by each involved foresight, planning, and was motivated by the promise of financial gain.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: Although the two might have played different roles, it was open to regard them as on par with each other. A precise degree of equivalence was not required, assessing the relative criminality involved is an evaluative judgment. The degree of culpability for each was not to be measured merely by comparing the period of time when each was in possession of the drugs.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: The offender’s role in the hierarchy of any drug enterprise is also significant in determining gravity and culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: Traditionally, courts have distinguished between street dealers, couriers, middlemen, wholesalers and principals at the apex of the organisation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.4 – Offender’s role

refs.q: ‘There is no reason to think large scale drug offences are undertaken by organisations that are structured by rank or roles distributed according to some formal job description’.

refs.q: Similarly, in Awad v The Queen, which involved two offenders, the Court noted that despite having apparently different roles and being in possession of the drugs for differing periods of time, both offenders still went to a warehouse with repackaging equipment and that given the large quantity of the drugs involved, it was open to conclude they would be involved in the further movement of the drugs.
