title: Financial gain or motive
statement: Greed is more culpable than funding one’s own addiction; willingness to harm the community for reward increases culpability, and in these circumstances general and specific deterrence “loom large”. Larger expected reward means more serious offending; the offender may prove on the balance of probabilities little or no benefit, or a lower value of the drug (consistently lower sentences for GHB reflect its reward differential). Pidoto bars harm differentiation, not consideration of reward. Giving proceeds to family is not significantly mitigating; failing to obtain a reward or complete a sale is generally not mitigating; providing armed support to a sale may be as culpable as organising it. (fns 4370 and 4418 cite [2021] VSCA 26 as “Mourkakos”, which the Manual elsewhere names “Navaratnam”: flag.vsca_2021_26_two_names.)

refs.q: Thus, an offender who is motivated by greed will be considered more culpable than one whose only motivation was to fund their own drug addiction or use. An offender is also more morally culpable because of their willingness to engage in criminal conduct that is harmful to the community in expectation of reward.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: The amount of the reward received or anticipated is also relevant to the gravity of the offence: offending expected to bring a large financial reward is more serious than one where the reward is small or non-existent. An offender may seek to mitigate their culpability by establishing on the balance of probabilities that they stood to derive little or no financial benefit.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: Pidoto and Adams established that under quantity-based sentencing regimes, there is no scope to differentiate between drugs based on ‘perceived differences in harmfulness’. Neither case said that anticipated financial reward is irrelevant.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: However, the fact that an offender gave much of the money gained to their family or others is not a significant mitigating factor, the important fact is that a substantial financial reward was gained from the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: Failing to obtain a reward or complete a sale is generally not mitigating,
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: In these circumstances, the principles of general and specific deterrence ‘loom large’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: Similarly, they may also attempt to mitigate the offending by proving that a quantity of the particular drug had a lower wholesale or retail value of another drug. This is why consistently lower sentences for GHB are reasonably justified by the enormous reward differential for offending involving that drug compared with others. The offender’s culpability is materially reduced because their likely financial reward is relatively small.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: and an accused who did not organise the sale or profit from it, may nonetheless be as culpable as the person who did if they accompany them to the sale ‘knowing that the transaction would take place and for the purpose of providing armed support…in successfully carrying out the transaction.’
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

refs.q: An offender’s culpability may be affected by their motivation for the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.5 – Financial gain or motive

title: Knowledge or belief; sophistication and scale
statement: Absent contrary evidence, the court may sentence on the basis the offender knew the quantity (no speculation about a lesser belief); recklessness as to the substance is no different from knowledge; knowingly returning to selling the same drug may make a later offence comparable to a more serious one. Sophistication and scale elevate seriousness (quantity primarily, price also); lack of sophistication or impossibility matters little where quantity is serious; specialised equipment supports inferences of scale; the strain on community resources from extensive police involvement and investigation may also indicate scale; a sophisticated, large cultivation may permit an inference of a principal role (its fn 4390 authority is uncertain: flag.fn4390_nguyen_2017). (Commonwealth importation: ignorance of the pure quantity is not unusual, and expected reward may then be a better guide — outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

refs.q: However, a later offence may be ‘comparable’ to an earlier offence that was objectively more serious if it involves the offender knowingly returning to selling the same drug.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.6 – Knowledge or belief

refs.q: Unless there is evidence to the contrary, a court may sentence on the basis that the accused knew the quantity of drug he or she was dealing with, and it is not necessary or appropriate to speculate that the accused may have thought he or she was dealing with a lesser quantity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.6 – Knowledge or belief

refs.q: Similarly, when assessing an offender’s culpability, there should be no difference between offenders who are reckless as to the nature of the substance and those who know what it is.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.6 – Knowledge or belief

refs.q: The sophistication and scale of the drug enterprise will elevate the objective seriousness of the offending. The primary indicator of scale will generally be the quantity of drug involved, but price may also be indicative. The lack of sophistication and impossibility of an operation’s success may not be of great significance in the face of serious offending (as measured by the quantity of the drug involved).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.7 – Sophistication and scale

refs.q: A court may infer that an operation of some scale and sophistication would be possible given the possession of a significant quantity of specialised equipment, even when there is no evidence of the precise quantity of drugs that might be manufactured from that equipment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.7 – Sophistication and scale

refs.q: Lastly, the sophisticated nature and large scope of a drug cultivation operation may permit an inference that the offender played a principal role in caring for the crop and so occupied an important position in the enterprise.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.7 – Sophistication and scale

refs.q: In an importation case, an offender’s knowledge or belief as to the identity or quantity of the drug imported is relevant to sentencing, but it is not unusual for an offender not to know how much ‘pure’ drug they are importing and so where there is ignorance of quantity a court may be better guided by other considerations such as expected reward.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.6 – Knowledge or belief

refs.q: The strain on community resources as a result of extensive police involvement and investigation may also be an indicator of the scale of a drug operation and is useful in the assessment of the gravity of the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.2 – Common features going to gravity and culpability > 28.3.2.7 – Sophistication and scale

title: Importation: reckless and intentional importers treated alike (Commonwealth scheme)
statement: Under the (Commonwealth) importation scheme, recklessness as to the substance is treated the same as intention (otherwise lower maxima would have been provided for reckless offenders) — outside this app’s Victorian scope.

refs.q: The legislative scheme makes clear that offenders who are reckless as to the substance imported are to treated the same way as those who intentionally import a given substance.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.3 – Importation

refs.q: If there had been a plan to treat the two differently, this would have been reflected in separate provisions imposing lower maximum terms on reckless offenders than the maximum sentence for intentional offenders.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.3 – Importation

title: Trafficking: attempts, potential harm, fake drugs
statement: Trafficking includes attempts, but attempts are not necessarily sentenced as completed offences; the 16-year standard sentence for LCQ trafficking does not apply to attempted trafficking (sso.scope). Trafficking is no less serious because the drugs did not reach consumers: seriousness may be assessed by potential consequences and intentions; potential harm is as serious as actual harm; absence of actual harm gets little weight where distribution is thwarted by arrest, covert police or ineptitude. Supplying a substance purporting to be a drug is objectively serious, though the criminality may be less than a genuine plan to supply drugs (fn 4394, a NSW case).

refs.q: Trafficking covers both doing the act that constitutes trafficking and attempting to do such an act; there is no difference between trafficking and attempted trafficking.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.4 – Trafficking

refs.q: Trafficking is no less serious simply because the drugs do not make their way to the ultimate consumer. But this does not mean that all acts that constitute trafficking or attempts to traffick should be treated the same or that the same sentence should be imposed for an attempt as for a completed offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.4 – Trafficking

refs.q: A court may assess the seriousness of a trafficking offence by its potential consequences and the offender’s intentions, regardless of what they were actually able to achieve. Potential harm is as serious as actual harm when considering acts of trafficking, and the offender’s moral culpability is not lessened because there is no prospect of drugs actually reaching the streets. The absence of actual harm may be given little weight where distribution is thwarted by the offender’s arrest, covert police intervention, or the offender’s own ineptitude.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.4 – Trafficking

refs.q: Standard sentence – 16 years (other than for attempted trafficking)
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.1 – Victorian penalties > 28.1.1.1 – Trafficking and supply

refs.q: In a similar vein, fraudulent transactions, where an offender supplies a substance purporting to be a drug when it is not, are objectively serious offences, although the criminality in such cases may be less than where there is a genuine plan to supply drugs: R v Kijurina [2017] NSWCCA 117, [99]–[103].
The actual or potential harm of particular conduct is potentially relevant depending on the circumstances of each individual case.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.4 – Trafficking

title: Cultivation: custody; overlap with trafficking; theft of electricity
statement: The Court of Appeal has said that, save perhaps in exceptional circumstances, commercial-quantity cultivation requires custody (“possibly wholly suspended, if still available”) — but for offending on or after 20 March 2017 by an adult, CQ cultivation is a Category 2 offence and LCQ cultivation Category 1 (the register; cat2.custodial_unless, cat1.custodial_required), and suspended sentences have been progressively abolished from 1 May 2011 (the dates by court and offence class: suspended.abolished). Where possession for sale is the basis of a trafficking charge, cultivation and trafficking overlap, with the same maxima at commercial and large commercial levels: examine the common factual elements as a matter of common sense, not semantics — only the elements not in common are separately punished. Cultivation is often charged with theft of electricity (crop farmers commonly bypass meters to power grow lights): sentencing judges should consider what impact this might have on orders for cumulation; though the theft may be an integral part of the hydroponics system, it is a discrete offence, and a measure of cumulation may be appropriate.

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has stated that, save perhaps in exceptional circumstances, cultivation of a commercial quantity requires the imposition of a custodial sentence, though it may be possible to wholly suspend the sentence, if that sanction is still available in the circumstances of the particular case.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.5 – Cultivation

refs.q: This may raise question of double punishment or double jeopardy, and a sentencing court must look closely at the factual elements of the offending to determine if there are any in common. Those which are not in common must be the subject of separate punishment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.5 – Cultivation

refs.q: ‘[i]t should be approached as a matter of common-sense, not as a matter of semantics’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.5 – Cultivation

refs.q: ** Category 2 offence if the offender was 18 or older at the time of offending.
* Category 1 offence if the offender is 18 years or older at the time of offending.

There is overlap between cultivation and trafficking offences, where possession for sale is the basis of the trafficking charge, and when a commercial or large commercial quantity is involved the two offences carry the same maximum penalty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.5 – Cultivation

refs.q: This can be a difficult exercise, but as the High Court explained in Pearce v The Queen ‘[i]t should be approached as a matter of common-sense, not as a matter of semantics’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.5 – Cultivation

refs.q: Cultivation offences are often charged alongside the theft of electricity. It is common for crop farmers to bypass electricity meters in order to power grow lights. Sentencing judges should consider what impact this might have on orders for cumulation. While the theft may be an integral part of the hydroponics system, the act itself is a discrete offence and it may be appropriate to impose a measure of cumulation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.5 – Cultivation

refs.q: Victoria progressively abolished suspended sentences from 1 May 2011.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.8 – Suspended sentence

title: Sale to children; police involvement; violence in trafficking
statement: The DPCS Act creates separate offences for trafficking or supplying drugs to children, and “supply or trafficking to children within 500 metres of a school is a statutory factor leading to qualification for a higher maximum penalty”; the child’s age and the circumstances also bear on gravity. Which offences carry the 20-year “within 500 metres of a school” maximum is stated inconsistently (the table prints it for s 71AC and s 71B; 28.3.6 and fn 4409 point to sale to children, ss 71B(1A) and 71AB(2)): apply it only when the user confirms the statutory condition (flag.school_500m_condition). Police involvement may affect culpability (a spectrum; the primary focus is how it bears on the offender’s culpability), but little where police merely facilitate offending the offender was ready to commit; factors listed below. Trafficking that relies on violence and intimidation is more serious and warrants a heavier sentence (using violence to complete a transaction is more culpable).

refs.q: Factors that affect the impact of police involvement on culpability include: • the way their involvement ‘contributed to the offending, including the nature and degree of any pressure or coercion applied, or encouragement or inducement offered….’ • the extent to which their involvement contributed to the offending • whether they dealt directly with the offender or through an intermediary • the more remote the police involvement, the less weight it will generally have on sentencing • how readily did the offender respond to a police request for drugs • it will carry great weight if their will was overborne and less if they regarded the request as a welcome expansion to their trafficking • it also carries less weight if the trafficking was instigated by the offender rather than the police • was the offender already trafficking when the police became involved and if so, what was the scale of the offender’s operation at that time and after the police involvement • if the police request was accommodated through the offender’s existing supply lines it will carry less weight, than where it could only be accommodated by a material change to the scale of the offender’s operation and supply lines.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.7 – Police involvement

refs.q: The DPCS Act creates separate offences for trafficking or supplying drugs to children, and supply or trafficking to children within 500 metres of a school is a statutory factor leading to qualification for a higher maximum penalty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.6 – Sale to children

refs.q: Further, the age of the “child” and the circumstances of the offending are also relevant in determining gravity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.6 – Sale to children

refs.q: The involvement of a police operative may affect the gravity of the offending or the offender’s culpability, but this is limited where police simply facilitate an offence the accused was ready and willing to commit.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.7 – Police involvement

refs.q: Police involvement does not have a predetermined impact on culpability - there is a spectrum along which that impact is assessed, ranging from very little to substantial.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.7 – Police involvement

refs.q: Drug trafficking that depends on violence and intimidation for its operational effectiveness is more serious than trafficking, which does not.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.8 – Violence

refs.q: The violence is intrinsic to the criminal activity and warrants a heavier sentence than would otherwise be called for.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.8 – Violence

refs.q: DPCS Act ss 71B(1A), 71AB(2).
Trafficking s 71AC Level 4 – 15 years Level 3 – 20 years if within 500 metres of a school 1 January 2002
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 28.1.1 – Victorian penalties > 28.1.1.1 – Trafficking and supply

refs.q: The primary focus should be on how the circumstances of their involvement bear on the culpability of the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.7 – Police involvement

refs.q: An offender who engages in drug trafficking for profit is undertaking transactions of sale and purchase, and by using violence to complete a transaction they are more culpable than an offender who is not so brutal.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.3 – Gravity and culpability > 28.3.8 – Violence

title: Drug offences: offender circumstances (character, age, addiction, status, cooperation)
statement: Age is relevant but carries less weight in drug cases because competing considerations (gravity, deterrence, denunciation) “may assume greater significance” (for young offenders see audit.youth_principles). Addiction is not usually mitigating (less likely above street level; a sufficient link is needed) but may bear on rehabilitation, specific deterrence and protection. Professional status or breach of an employer’s trust may aggravate. Cooperation is important given detection difficulty, and informers risk their safety in and out of prison. (Commonwealth importation: good character ordinarily gets less weight in serious importation cases — limb below; for Victorian offences see factor.good_character.)

limbs.text: Good character in serious importation (Commonwealth)

refs.q: An offender’s personal circumstances, including good character, will ordinarily be given less weight in serious importation cases than might otherwise be so.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: This is because people involved in serious drug importation activities are often approached because of their good character.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: An offender’s personal circumstances, including good character, will ordinarily be given less weight in serious importation cases than might otherwise be so.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: Similarly, while the age of the offender is relevant, it does not carry as much weight in drug cases because competing considerations, such as gravity, deterrence, and denunciation may assume greater significance.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: Nor will an offender’s own addiction usually be a mitigating factor. However, it may sometimes be relevant to their prospects of rehabilitation, or the needs for specific deterrence and to protect the community. Whether addiction is mitigating will depend on the circumstances, and it is less likely to operate for activities that are above street-level. Further, there must a sufficient link between the addiction and the offending to mitigate sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: In some circumstances an offender’s professional status, or their breach of an employer’s trust – by using an official position to facilitate a drug offence – may be an aggravating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: An offender’s cooperation with authorities is important in drug offences because of the difficulties involved in their detection. Moreover, offenders who provide information about drug offending frequently jeopardise their own safety both within and outside the prison environment and this is also an important consideration.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.4 – Circumstances of the offender

title: Drug offences: purposes
statement: General and specific deterrence, just punishment, denunciation and community protection; sentences must reflect serious community harm and high maxima and signal that financial reward is neutralised by the risk of severe punishment.

refs.q: Given how serious drug offences are, it is not surprising courts have emphasised the sentencing purposes of general and specific deterrence, just punishment, denunciation, and protection of the community. Sentencing for drug offences must reflect the serious harm they cause within the community and the high maximum penalties set by Australian parliaments. They must signal that the potential financial reward is neutralised by the risk of severe punishment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.5 – Sentencing purposes

title: Drug offences: concurrency within a single transaction; Giretti charges and commonality (Dang)
statement: Drug sentencing commonly requires decisions about concurrency and cumulation. Offences in a single transaction should generally be concurrent (e.g. possession that was a consequence of manufacture was consumed by the plea to trafficking, and cumulating part of the sentences was error; punishment on a count may even be unlawful). A Giretti charge is not duplicitous because trafficking is a continuing activity. Separate Giretti charges may share commonality: conduct indistinguishable in time or behaviour, no differentiation by victim or result, no separate obligations, part of one ongoing course relied on as a Giretti charge, or a single business selling different drugs. Counterweights: that different drugs are trafficked deserves separate recognition (subject to totality), and some cumulation is appropriate where a hydroponic operation involves theft of electricity (fn 4430).

refs.q: Generally, where two or more offences are committed in the course of a single transaction, all sentences should be concurrent rather than cumulative.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Similar circumstances may lead not just to a conclusion that cumulation is inappropriate, but to a determination that any punishment on a count is unlawful.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: But issues of double punishment may arise in such offending where there are separate Giretti charges; ‘it is a matter of determining whether, in the commission of the offences,…there is any commonality….’ In Dang v The Queen the Court held that two Giretti charges of trafficking in methylamphetamine and heroin resulting from a single business of selling drugs had commonalities that were not distinguished by the different narcotics being trafficked. The Court said there may be commonality between charges where: • the conduct relied on was indistinguishable in time • the conduct was indistinguishable in behaviour • there was no differentiation by victim • there was no differentiation by result • there were no separate obligations owed to specific or contemplated individuals • the conduct occurred as part of a general on-going course of conduct and was relied on precisely for that reason as a Giretti charge • the facts establish there was a single business involved in the sale and supply of different drugs.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: As a result, sentencing commonly requires decisions about concurrency and cumulation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: The Court of Appeal held as the possession was a consequence of the manufacture, the plea to trafficking consumed the count of possession, and it had been an error to cumulate part of the sentences on the two counts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: A Giretti charge is not duplicitous because “trafficking” is a continuing activity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: See also Nguyen 2019 [62] (the fact that different drugs are trafficked deserves separate recognition in sentencing, with due regard being had for the overall offending and the principle of totality) and R v Draper [2002] VSCA 63, [10]–[12] (some cumulation is appropriate where a hydroponic operation involves the theft of electricity).
Drug offences are commonly committed either in association with other offences, or as part of a substantial series of offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: For example, in R v Glaister, the offender was convicted of trafficking by manufacture and of possession.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.6 – Formulation of sentence

title: Drug offences: no indefinite sentences; serious offender offences; forfeiture and CCE; serious drug offender
statement: No drug offence is a “serious offence”, so indefinite sentences are unavailable. Serious offender offences: trafficking LCQ or CQ, cultivation LCQ or CQ, and conspiracy, incitement, aiding/abetting or preparatory acts for them (certain Commonwealth convictions can qualify an offender; the serious offender consequences do not apply to Commonwealth offences). Forfeiture and CCE offences: any indictable Victorian drug offence or Schedule 2 offence (including producing, selling or supplying, and advertising a psychoactive substance); the Manual does not say whether, or how, the $50,000 test of 9.4 applies to a drug offence (flag.cce_drug_offences_value). Automatic and civil forfeiture: trafficking LCQ, CQ, to a child, trafficking; cultivation LCQ, CQ; and conspiracy, incitement, aiding/abetting of those. A serious drug offender declaration (s 89DI; a person sentenced for repeat offending of the same kind) makes community protection the principal purpose (disproportionate sentence permitted), presumes cumulation and must be recorded. Each list applies only to the offences of its limb. (The footnotes cite these DPCS provisions as “The Act”: flag.fn4438_4468_the_act_dpcs.)

limbs.text: Serious offender drug offences (plus conspiracy, incitement, aiding/abetting and preparatory acts for them)

refs.q: However, some State drug offences may be included in the following statutory categories. Serious offender offences • Trafficking large commercial quantity. • Trafficking commercial quantity. • Cultivation in large commercial quantity. • Cultivation in commercial quantity. • Conspiracy where the purpose of the conspiracy is commission of one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences. • Inciting where the offence incited is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences. • Aiding or abetting where the offence assisted is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences. • Doing a preparatory act where the offence prepared for is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.7 – Statutory schemes

limbs.text: Automatic and civil forfeiture offences

refs.q: In addition, the following are automatic forfeiture offences and civil forfeiture offences: • trafficking large commercial quantity • trafficking commercial quantity • trafficking to a child • trafficking • cultivation in large commercial quantity • cultivation in commercial quantity • conspiracy where the purpose of the conspiracy is commission of one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences • inciting where the offence incited is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences • aiding or abetting where the offence assisted is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.7 – Statutory schemes

refs.q: Indefinite sentences are not available in relation to drug offences, as there are no drug offences that are “serious offences” under the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.7 – Statutory schemes

refs.q: However, some State drug offences may be included in the following statutory categories. Serious offender offences • Trafficking large commercial quantity. • Trafficking commercial quantity. • Cultivation in large commercial quantity. • Cultivation in commercial quantity. • Conspiracy where the purpose of the conspiracy is commission of one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences. • Inciting where the offence incited is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences. • Aiding or abetting where the offence assisted is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences. • Doing a preparatory act where the offence prepared for is one of the above trafficking or cultivation offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 28 – Drug offences > 28.7 – Statutory schemes

refs.q: However, convictions for certain Commonwealth offences can operate to qualify an offender found guilty of a Victorian Schedule 1 drug offence to be sentenced as a serious offender. These include: • import/export commercial quantity of a border-controlled drug or plant • import/export marketable quantity of a border-controlled drug or plant • possession of a commercial quantity of an unlawfully imported border-controlled drug or plant • possession of a marketable quantity of an unlawfully imported border-controlled drug or plant • possession of an unlawfully imported border-controlled drug or plant • possession of a commercial quantity of border-controlled drug or plant reasonably suspected of having been unlawfully imported • possession of a marketable quantity of a border-controlled drug or plant reasonably suspected of having been unlawfully imported.

title: Commonwealth drug quantity scheme (Criminal Code): commercial, marketable and trafficable quantities; pure quantities; comparisons
statement: The Criminal Code identifies commercial, marketable and trafficable quantities (Criminal Code Regulations 2019 schedules); the thresholds for the same drug may differ as a controlled and a border-controlled drug (e.g. heroin). Criminal Code quantities are of the pure substance, and combined quantities may be calculated where an organised criminal activity is proved; the trafficable quantity creates a rebuttable presumption whose nature depends on the offence. For comparisons, DPP (Cth) v KMD converts quantities to percentages of a CQ; a high-end marketable quantity offence may be more serious than a low-end CQ offence, so some CQ cases may be comparators; a Commonwealth CQ is generally equal to or higher than a Victorian LCQ, and expressing an importation as a multiple of the CQ shows its scale and allows comparison across drugs. Outside the app’s Victorian scope; for Victorian offences see guide.drugs.quantity_as_comparator and guide.drugs.measuring_quantity.

refs.q: The Criminal Code identifies three quantities: commercial, marketable, and trafficable. Schedules 1 and 2 of the Criminal Code Regulations 2019 (Cth) contain two tables which identify controlled and border-controlled drugs, plants, and precursors and states their marketable, commercial and trafficable quantities.

title: Perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice: gravity
statement: It strikes at the heart of the justice system; an attempt is an equally serious substantive offence (not inchoate). Gravity depends on the circumstances (factors below, with the Manual’s footnote qualifications). The likelihood of success has substantially reduced significance; potential consequences may weigh more. “Justice” includes the proceedings of judicial tribunals, and the attempt can be committed before curial proceedings have begun (e.g. intentionally frustrating or deflecting police from prosecuting), including action to prevent the institution of proceedings.

refs.q: But since the offences are broadly defined, and can arise in a variety of circumstances, the gravity of the offending will depend on the particular circumstances of the case. Some factors going to gravity and culpability include: • the consequences the offending was calculated to avoid; • the duration of the deception and whether it was actively repeated or persisted in, or passively allowed to continue; • whether it involved threats or violence, noting however, that the absence of threats of physical violence does not necessarily ameliorate the overall seriousness of the conduct; • whether it was spontaneous or premeditated; • did the deception result in deceiving a court or tribunal or creating false public records, and if so, what were the consequences of the deception; • the gravity of the criminal conduct the offender was attempting to pervert; • was someone else recruited or coerced, especially an official or vulnerable person, into participating in the corruption, or was there an attempt at recruitment or coercion; • did the offender prey on a pre-existing fear; • was the offending committed in a curial setting, particularly to gain a sentencing advantage; and, • motive.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice

factors.text: duration: a momentary, quickly corrected lapse is at the bottom of the scale; maintaining a fabrication is more serious

refs.q: A momentary lapse of judgment, as when an offender gives police false identification but quickly corrects themself, is at the bottom of the scale. More serious is where the offender maintains the fabrication, despite police attempts to uncover the truth.

factors.text: premeditation: offending that evolved may reduce culpability; substantial planning raises seriousness

refs.q: Where offending is said to ‘[evolve], rather than being a premeditated course of behaviour’, the offender’s culpability may be reduced:
Conversely, offences which involve a substantial degree of planning and premeditation will raise the seriousness of the offending:

factors.text: threats: persistent and cynical control and exploitation of a victim’s known vulnerabilities can be as serious as explicit threats or violence

refs.q: Persistent and cynical control and exploitation of a victim’s known vulnerabilities can make this offending just a serious as if there were explicit threats or actual violence.

factors.text: motive: an imagined conflict of loyalties may reduce culpability; a profit motive aggravates

refs.q: For example: an imagined conflict of loyalties may reduce the offender’s culpability as the offending is done out of concern for another but being motivated by possible profit is an aggravating factor:

Perverting the course of justice is a serious offence because it strikes at the heart of the justice system. An attempt to pervert the course of justice is an equally serious substantive offence. It is not inchoate despite the term “attempt”, and any conduct that meets this description is serious.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice

refs.q: While the likelihood of success is usually relevant in determining the seriousness of an attempted offence, its significance is substantially reduced for attempts to pervert the course of justice. Instead, the potential consequences may assume greater weight than any concern about whether the attempt succeeded or was likely to succeed.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice

refs.q: The scope of this offence is wide and is designed to cover any act which tends to and is intended to pervert the course of justice. For this purpose, “justice” is not confined to that administered by the courts but includes the proceedings of judicial tribunals. While the “course of justice” typically begins when process issues that invokes the jurisdiction of a court or when a step is taken that marks the beginning of criminal proceedings, the offence of attempting to pervert the course of justice can be committed before curial proceedings have begun. For example, while police investigations are not an ordinary part of the course of justice, an accused who intentionally acts in a way that has a tendency to frustrate or deflect police from prosecuting a criminal offence thereby frustrates the course of an anticipated future curial proceeding and may be guilty of the offence. And action taken to prevent the institution of a proceeding is as much an interference with the course of justice as one taken to obstruct a proceeding after it has already commenced.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice

refs.q: In DPP (Vic) v Oksuz the Court of Appeal said the attempt was serious because it involved an offender trying to deter a witness from giving evidence in a criminal proceeding and so attempted to undermine the prosecution’s ability to bring an accused person to justice.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice

refs.q: This obviously results in serious harm to public safety and the rule of law.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice

title: Perpetrators and targets within the legal system
statement: Gravity and culpability may be highest where the offender is embedded in the legal system (police, judicial officers, lawyers, other trusted personnel). Police abuse of power can undermine public confidence in the police (abusing criminals may be considered more serious; culpability is not reduced because victims are offenders; an experienced officer who tries to corrupt a more junior one may be more culpable). The public is entitled to expect that only people of good character are appointed to judicial office, so a judicial officer’s good character gets far less weight. Offences against justice by a lawyer, or by someone who intends to enter the profession, are treated especially seriously; where a lawyer attempts bribery or uses other means to pervert the course of justice, the status as a lawyer automatically increases seriousness. Offending may also be aggravated where the offender holds another trusted position in the legal system (e.g. a rehabilitation provider giving false evidence). Targeting police (bribery — refusal of the bribe does not meaningfully reduce seriousness; entrapment may reduce sentence; less serious without threats) or judges (treated very seriously: the public must not be left with the perception that judges do not treat bribery seriously) is serious; as with police, actions against lawyers may also be serious (e.g. threats to a prosecutor to secure the withdrawal of charges).

refs.q: When the offending is committed by a person who is ‘embedded in the legal system’, the gravity of the offending and the culpability of the offender may be at their highest. People who are ‘embedded in the legal system’ include: • police • judicial officers • lawyers • other support personnel.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.1 – Perpetrators in the legal system

refs.q: Police officers can exercise considerable power over others and the abuse of that power is serious as it has significant social consequences. It can undermine public confidence in the police, erode the morale of honest officers, and encourage other police to turn a blind eye. Police may be especially tempted to extort money or abuse their power when dealing with criminal offenders, who are unlikely to complain because it would reveal that they too have offended. For this reason, police abusing criminals in this way may be considered more serious than when they deal with honest members of the public who are more likely to report attempts at extortion. Equally, a police officer’s moral culpability is not reduced because the victims of their corruption are themselves criminal offenders. Attempts by an experienced police officer to corrupt a more junior officer or acquiescing to a junior officer’s corruption may make the senior officer more culpable than the junior officer.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.1 – Perpetrators in the legal system > 29.2.1.1.1 – Police officers

refs.q: Where the offender was a judicial officer at the time of the offending, their previous good character cannot be given anything like the weight it would for different offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.1 – Perpetrators in the legal system > 29.2.1.1.2 – Judicial officers

refs.q: Where the offender is a member of the legal profession or someone who intends to enter the profession, offences against justice will be treated especially seriously. Given the frequent contact between lawyers and police officers, opportunities abound for lawyers to attempt bribery or to use other means to pervert the course of justice. When this occurs the status of the accused as a member of the legal profession automatically increases the seriousness of the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.1 – Perpetrators in the legal system > 29.2.1.1.3 – Lawyers

refs.q: Offending may also be aggravated where the offender is in another trusted position in the legal system. For example, in Dieni v The Queen, the offender was a coordinator and counsellor at a drug rehabilitation centre. His offending involved giving false evidence about his intention to supervise and support offenders in rehabilitation programs, and about their compliance with the conditions of bail or sentencing orders. This offending was objectively serious because it undermined the trust courts placed in the evidence from rehabilitation providers and undermined the efforts of other offenders to rehabilitate.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.1 – Perpetrators in the legal system > 29.2.1.1.4 – Other trusted personnel

refs.q: The gravity of the offence of perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice may also be affected by who the offender has attempted to influence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.2 – Targets in the legal system

refs.q: Acting against the police is serious, such as in attempting to bribe a police officer. The fact that the bribe was not accepted does not meaningfully reduce the seriousness of the offence, though an element of entrapment may entitle the offender to a reduced sentence. Attempting to influence through bribery will also usually be less serious where no threats are involved.

refs.q: Attempts to compromise the judiciary are treated very seriously.

refs.q: As with police officers, actions against lawyers may also be serious. For example, where attempts to secure the withdrawal of charges are made by subjecting the prosecutor to threats of either physical violence or vexatious legal proceedings.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.2 – Targets in the legal system > 29.2.1.2.3 – Lawyers

refs.q: The public is entitled to expect that only people of good character will be appointed to judicial office.

refs.q: The public has an interest in seeing that the courts will not tolerate such attempts and cannot be left with the perception that judges do not treat bribery seriously, as that may itself promote a belief that judges can be bribed.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.1 – Perverting and attempting to pervert the course of justice > 29.2.1.2 – Targets in the legal system > 29.2.1.2.2 – Judicial officers

title: Contempt: gravity (wilful v inadvertent; jurors and witnesses; disobedience; refusal to give evidence)
statement: Contempt is serious in any form (threat to the rule of law); wilful (deliberate or contumacious) contempt is more serious than inadvertent or technical. Interfering with jurors (naming, threatening, abusing) is very serious, and so is interfering with witnesses (who may not give evidence at all, or may shade it); prejudicial publication needs no intent, but absence of intent is an important mitigating factor. Orders must be strictly obeyed until discharged, even if their validity is doubted (the Manual notes the limits of this principle for orders of an inferior court without jurisdiction: fn 4518, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6); public defiance may increase gravity; continuing disobedience despite notice of the order and of the contempt proceedings aggravates; contempt by a large representative body (like a union) is more serious than by an individual; and a public disturbance requiring considerable resources to maintain order is more serious; distinguish the tendency to frustrate the order (gravity) from the contemnor’s intentions, which 29.2.2.2 says are only relevant to culpability — though it ends by saying that the consequences of publication are relevant to culpability (flag.contempt_gravity_culpability_29_2_2_2). For refusal to give evidence, consider the gravity of the underlying offence and, where possible, the likely weight of the evidence withheld (often not possible, and unreliable); refusal is generally more serious than a false claim of inability (perjury).

refs.q: Contempt comes in different forms, but it is a serious offence regardless of the form since at the core of each is a threat to the rule of law and administration of justice.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt

refs.q: However, the degree of seriousness may depend on the form and circumstances, with wilful instances (e.g., those that are ‘deliberate or contumacious’) of each type being considered more serious than those that were inadvertent or technical.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Contempt that interferes with the function of the jury is very serious. Calling a juror by name or threatening them or using offensive language are aggravating factors.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.1 – Interfering with jurors or witnesses

refs.q: It is also contempt of court to publish something that, ‘as a matter of practical reality,’ has a tendency to interfere with the course of justice in a particular case or that has a ‘real and definite tendency to prejudice or embarrass pending proceedings’. Proof of an intent to interfere is unnecessary, but the absence of intent is an important mitigating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.1 – Interfering with jurors or witnesses

refs.q: When an order is made it is the duty of those bound by it to strictly obey its terms. This is vital to the administration of justice. This duty exists until the order is discharged and applies even if there is doubt as to its validity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.2 – Disobedience of court orders or rules

refs.q: Defiance of the order does not have to be public, but public defiance may increase the gravity of the offending. Continuing disobedience of a court order, in the face of notice of its making and the bringing of contempt proceedings, is also an aggravating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.2 – Disobedience of court orders or rules

refs.q: In assessing gravity, the extent to which the conduct tends to frustrate the order should be distinguished from the contemnor’s intentions, which are only relevant to the related assessment of their culpability. For example, a real and substantial risk that the terms of a suppression order might be breached by media publication of certain facts demonstrates the tendency to frustrate the purpose of the order. This is relevant to assessing the gravity of the contempt. It is the consequences of publication that are relevant to assessing the contemnor’s culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.2 – Disobedience of court orders or rules

refs.q: But the gravity of the underlying offence for which the witness refuses to give evidence should be taken into account in assessing the seriousness of the refusal.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.3 – Refusal to give evidence

refs.q: If a witness falsely states that they are unable to answer a question, that will usually constitute perjury and may constitute contempt. Of the two, contempt is generally considered more serious because deliberate falsehoods do not obstruct the administration of justice to the same extent as refusals to answer questions.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.3 – Refusal to give evidence

refs.q: But see Pelechowski v Registrar, Court of Appeal (NSW) (1999) 198 CLR 435, [55], [71] on the limits of this principle for orders made by an inferior court without jurisdiction.

Contempt is also committed where an offender interferes or attempts to interfere with a witness, because if a witness cannot freely and voluntarily give evidence without fear of threats or violence, they may not do so at all or may shade their evidence. Any conduct calculated to interfere with this freedom is ‘a most serious and fundamental interference with the administration of justice’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.1 – Interfering with jurors or witnesses

refs.q: And contempt involving a public disturbance that requires the deployment of considerable resources to maintain public order is more serious than one that does not.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.2 – Disobedience of court orders or rules

refs.q: Consideration should also be given, where possible, to the likely weight of the evidence withheld.

refs.q: This will not always be possible and any assessment of the weight of unknown evidence may be unreliable.

refs.q: This is because an intentional contempt contains an attitude of defiance towards a court or a court’s order that undercuts both the court’s authority and respect for the law.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt

refs.q: This is a direct and serious interference with the independence, security, and function of the jury, and is likely to have a serious impact on the juror.
