refs.q: Similarly, where the contempt is committed by a large representative body (like a union), it is more serious than contempt committed by an individual.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.2 – Disobedience of court orders or rules

refs.q: A witness’ refusal to give evidence is another type of contempt.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.3 – Refusal to give evidence

refs.q: It is important that witnesses answer questions, especially when directed to by the court, tribunal or other authority.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.2 – Contempt > 29.2.2.3 – Refusal to give evidence

title: Contempt: considerations in punishment; endorsement rule; aggravation proved beyond reasonable doubt
statement: Consider whether disobedience was wilful or based on an honest though unreasonable belief. Protect jurors; consider the type of threat and capacity to carry it out and the objective effect on the trial. Where an order lacks the indorsement the Supreme Court rules require (a warning that non-compliance exposes the offender to imprisonment for contempt), hesitate to imprison — though a fine for wilful contempt is not precluded; waiver should not be done lightly and requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of awareness of obligations and consequences. Non-exhaustive considerations are listed below (the weight of having sought legal advice depends on what the evidence discloses of it; an offender who maintains privilege cannot complain if it gets little weight; an organisational system for preventing contempt is an important mitigating factor, undercut by failing to comply with it). Bankruptcy does not preclude a fine nor justify imprisonment, and financial difficulty does not discount a fine. Aggravating factors must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

refs.q: • the nature and circumstances of the contempt; • its effect on the administration of justice; • the contemnor’s culpability; • the need for general and specific deterrence; • the existence of any prior convictions for contempt; • the contemnor’s financial means; • whether they have exhibited contrition and made a full apology; • the contemnor’s intent, and specifically whether the contempt was contumacious; • the seriousness of the offence; • whether any harm was actually caused; • the existence or otherwise of any organisational system for the prevention of contempt; • whether legal advice was sought;
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: • but the weight to be given to this factor depends upon the extent to which the evidence discloses the nature of the advice, and the circumstances in which it occurred. An offender who asks for lenience based on this factor while maintaining legal professional privilege cannot complain if a court does not give it significant weight; and, • the nature and purpose of any publication.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: A court should consider whether the conduct amounted to a wilful disobedience of an order or whether the accused held an honest, though unreasonable, belief that the order did not apply or have the purported effect.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Where the contempt involves a threat to the jury, the court will take account of the principle that jury service is a cornerstone of the criminal justice system and those participating in it need to be protected. However, it is also relevant to consider the type of threat made to them and the offender’s capacity to carry it out, as well as the objective effect of the conduct on the trial (but not the personal feelings of any judge or juror who experienced the contempt).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Where the rule has not been complied with, a court should hesitate to impose a sentence of imprisonment. Waiver of the indorsement rule requires ‘the utmost strictness in procedure and proof’. It must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was aware of their obligations under the order and the consequences of breaching it.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: ‘The list of considerations is not exhaustive and each case will depend on its own facts’. But any factors that are considered aggravating must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: This does not, however, preclude the imposition of a fine for wilful contempt.
A court has discretion to waive compliance with this rule, but the seriousness of contempt means this should not be done lightly.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: In deciding whether to punish for contempt and in determining the appropriate penalty, a court should consider:
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

refs.q: A court is not precluded from considering imposition of a fine because the offender is bankrupt, but neither does this provide a basis for imposing a term of imprisonment where that would not otherwise be appropriate:
Nor does financial difficulty discount the possibility of a fine:
This is an important mitigating factor but failing to comply with it undercuts its weight:
The Supreme Court rules require an order to include a statement noting that the failure to comply with its terms will expose the offender to the possibility of imprisonment for contempt.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.2 – Contempt

title: Perjury: gravity
statement: Perjury is serious whatever the motive (easy to commit, hard to detect; undetected perjury produces injustice and erodes confidence), even for seemingly minor matters such as a false driver nomination to avoid a parking or traffic fine. Curial perjury is more serious than non-curial; curial perjury not producing a false conviction or acquittal may be less serious than perjury exposing another to conviction. Perjury by police and lawyers is more serious; repeated (not spur of the moment) perjury is more serious; foreseeable impact on a third party is relevant.

refs.q: Perjury is a serious offence because justice cannot be administered unless people tell the truth under oath; justice ‘inevitably suffers whatever the motive for the perjury, and in whatever circumstances it is committed’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: It can occur in both curial and non-curial proceedings, and while both instances are serious, curial perjury is regarded as the more serious. However, perjury in a curial context that does not result in a false conviction or acquittal may be considered less serious than perjury that places another person at risk of conviction.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: Similarly, police and lawyers stand in a special relationship in relation to the administration of justice. This makes perjury by them more serious than if it were committed by others.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: Finally, perjury that occurs on more than one occasion, rather than on the spur of the moment, is more serious.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: The impact of perjury on a third party is relevant, particularly if the consequences of the offending on that person could have been foreseen by the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 29.3.3 – Perjury

refs.q: This is so even when the perjury appears to involve only a minor infraction. For example, making a false statement to avoid paying a parking or traffic fine does not seem significant, but it still undermines a system which depends on public honesty in nominating the driver who is in fact responsible. It is a serious offence given its effect on public confidence in the enforcement system and by requiring public money to be spent investigating and prosecuting.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: It is an offence that is easy to commit, yet not easy to detect or prove.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: Where perjury goes undetected, it can produce unjust results and lead to a decline in community confidence in the reliability of the courts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

refs.q: The circumstances in which perjury can be committed are infinite.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.2 – Gravity and culpability > 29.2.3 – Perjury

title: Offences against justice: purposes
statement: Perverting calls for sentences that denounce (even lower-range conduct) and deter. Contempt: courts have more recently held that the civil/criminal distinction is not satisfactory; punishment is punishment; contumacious contempt calls for just punishment and fines that deter and show the court will ensure obedience; punishing wilful disobedience disciplines, vindicates authority and maintains respect for law. Perjury requires general deterrence and community disapproval.

refs.q: Perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice calls for sentences that are sufficient to denounce the conduct, even for conduct falling in the lower range of seriousness, and to deter others.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.4 – Sentencing purposes > 29.4.1 – Perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice

refs.q: ‘Punishment is punishment, whether it is imposed in vindication or for remedial or coercive purposes’. And fines, the usual sanction for contempt, constitute punishment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.4 – Sentencing purposes > 29.4.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Contumacious contempt calls for just punishment. The amount of a fine must reflect the contumacious conduct, be sufficient to deter both the offender and others, and be sufficient to demonstrate the court’s readiness to ensure that its orders are obeyed.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.4 – Sentencing purposes > 29.4.2 – Contempt

refs.q: The difficulties of detection and proof are such as to require both general deterrence and community disapproval to be marked in fixing a sentence for perjury.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.4 – Sentencing purposes > 29.4.23 – Perjury

refs.q: Historically, sentencing for contempt depended on whether the contempt was classified as civil contempt or criminal contempt. The defining feature which brought contempt into the criminal sphere was that it involved deliberate defiance or was contumacious. The distinction between civil and criminal contempt was thought to lie in the different purposes of punishment: civil proceedings were said to be remedial or coercive of an individual’s private interest, where criminal proceedings were taken ‘in the public interest to vindicate judicial authority or maintain the integrity of the judicial process’. More recently, courts have held that this is not a satisfactory distinction. Even where a private person brings a proceeding to enforce an order or undertaking for their benefit, there is also a public interest since that proceeding vindicates the court’s authority. Further, all orders are made in the interests of justice and any non-compliance is necessarily an interference with the administration of justice, even if the position can be remedied between the parties.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.4 – Sentencing purposes > 29.4.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Punishing for a contempt that involves wilful disobedience to a court order serves the substantial purpose of disciplining the contemnor, vindicating the authority of the court, and maintaining respect for the law.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.4 – Sentencing purposes > 29.4.2 – Contempt

title: Offences against justice: formulation (cumulation; contempt penalties and the Sentencing Act; perjury custody)
statement: Perverting offences are indictable, forfeiture and forensic sample offences, not triable summarily; cumulation may suit attempts linked to avoiding detection for other offences. Contempt should be approached, so far as possible, consistently with criminal conduct generally: in the higher courts the penalty is at large, and in all courts common-law principles apply (parsimony, single course of conduct, totality); penalties include imprisonment for a definite or indefinite term, fines, sequestration, and (Supreme Court) a suspended sentence, including on a condition of unpaid community work; coercive punishment of indeterminate length may suit an ongoing refusal to give evidence. There is “some question” how far the Sentencing Act applies — it does not apply in its entirety (sections specifically held to apply include: non-parole periods, order of sentences, concurrency and cumulation, youth detention orders, imprisonment, fines, recording or not recording a conviction, discharge and dismissal), and some community-based options might be inconsistent with the superior court’s power to commit for a fixed term — so the hard order checks treat a contempt sentence as a caution, not an error (flag.contempt_sentencing_act_and_orders). A conviction may be recorded only for criminal contempt, which is more likely to lead to imprisonment. Costs may be awarded, but imprisonment in default of costs is improper; no statutory categories apply. Perjury: full concurrency would be very rare; for curial perjury custodial sentences should be imposed unless there are exceptional circumstances; indictable, forfeiture and forensic sample offence; may be heard summarily.

refs.q: Perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice are indictable and forfeiture offences. They are also offences for which a forensic sample order may be made. They may not be determined summarily. Cumulation may be appropriate where the attempt to pervert justice was related to efforts to avoid detection or prosecution for other offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.1 – Perverting or attempting to pervert the course of justice

refs.q: In the higher courts, the penalty for contempt is at large and, in all courts, common-law sentencing principles apply. This means the principle of parsimony requires selecting the least severe sentence necessary to achieve the purpose of punishment, and that an offender should receive the benefit of the “single course of conduct” and totality principles.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Possible penalties included imprisonment for a definite or indefinite term, fines, and sequestration of assets. The Supreme Court may also impose a suspended sentence, including upon a condition that that the contemnor perform unpaid community work.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: There is some question to what extent the Sentencing Act 1991 applies to contempt proceedings, but it does not apply in its entirety.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Sections that have specifically been held to apply include: • the power to impose a non-parole period; • the order of sentences; • whether sentences apply concurrently or cumulatively; • the power to impose youth justice centre and youth residential centre orders; • the power to imprison; • the power to fine; • the power to record a conviction and discharge the offender; • the power to dismiss the charge without recording a conviction; and, • the discretion to record a conviction.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Costs may also be awarded, in contrast to normal criminal proceedings. Such costs tend to be awarded on the standard basis, though circumstances may persuade the court to award costs on a lower scale. A sentence for contempt that orders an offender to be imprisoned for one month in default of paying costs is improper.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: If the contempt is found in the refusal to give evidence in an ongoing proceeding, it may be appropriate to impose coercive punishment of an indeterminate length.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Contempt of court is a unique offence, and no statutory categories apply.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: While there is no absolute rule that a sentence for perjury should be served cumulatively on any other sentence of imprisonment it would be ‘very rare indeed’ for full concurrency to be ordered.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.3 – Perjury

refs.q: In Victoria, when the perjury is committed in curial proceedings, custodial sentences should be imposed unless there are exceptional circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.3 – Perjury

refs.q: Perjury is an indictable offence and a forfeiture offence. As it is an indictable offence, it is one for which a forensic sample order may be made. It may also be determined summarily, but no other statutory categories apply.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.3 – Perjury

refs.q: A number of the community based sentencing options provided by the Act might be inconsistent with a superior court’s inherent power to summarily punish contempt by committing the offender for a fixed term.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: However, a conviction may only be recorded in a case of criminal contempt, and a finding of criminal contempt is more likely to result in a term of imprisonment:
Zhang [26]–[27], [36], relying on SCV Rules r 75.11(4).
However, because contempt is a serious offence it should be approached, so far as possible, consistently with the approach to dealing with criminal conduct in general.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Regardless of whether the supposed distinction between civil and criminal contempt continues, the types of available punishment for both are broadly the same.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: And because the Act deals with a range of matters important to the imposition and operation of sentences, a court may have regard to them as a matter of common sense when dealing with contempt.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Firstly, it pre-emptively sentences the offender for the future contempt of failing to pay costs; an offence which has not been committed, and of which the offender has not been convicted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Secondly, if the offender fails to pay costs and is then imprisoned, they will not need to pay costs on release and this effectively deprives a successful plaintiff of their costs.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: This is important because although costs have a punitive element, they are still primarily orders made for the benefit of the plaintiff.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.2 – Contempt

refs.q: Cumulation is important when formulating a sentence for perjury (a comparison with contempt may also be appropriate).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 29 – Offences against justice > 29.5 – Formulation of sentence > 29.5.3 – Perjury

title: Riot, violent disorder and affray: offences and current practice
statement: Common law riot, rout and affray were abolished in 2017 (replaced by violent disorder and statutory affray). Riot prosecutions are rare and practice cannot be discerned (most 2016–2021 sentences relate to one serious prison riot, which cannot indicate practice for riot in general); violent disorder is too new. Affray practice varies widely: short custodial sentences are common where serious injury or death occurs; CCOs, fines or good behaviour bonds are within range for less serious cases with compelling mitigation.

refs.q: The common law offences of riot, rout and affray were abolished in 2017. Riot and rout were replaced with the statutory offence of violent disorder, while affray was replaced with statutory affray.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order

refs.q: Prosecutions for riot in Victoria are rare. In 2016, the County Court stated that it is not possible to discern current sentencing practices.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 30.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 30.1.2.1 – Riot and violent disorder

refs.q: Violent disorder, which is a statutory offence that replaced the common law offences of rout and riot, is a relatively new offence and there have not been enough cases to discern current sentencing practices.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 30.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 30.1.2.1 – Riot and violent disorder

refs.q: Sentencing practices for affray under both common law and statute can differ widely since affray may occur in wide-ranging circumstances and involve numerous sentencing considerations, such as the seriousness of the offence, whether there were significant aggravating or mitigating factors, whether there was a plea of guilty or not, or whether there were significant priors. Short custodial sentences are common where serious injury or death occurs. But Community Correction Orders, fines or good behaviour bonds are all within range for less serious instances of the offence and where there are compelling mitigating circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 30.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 30.1.2.2 – Affray

refs.q: Most sentences imposed in Victoria between 2016 and 2021 relate to one prison riot event. As this was a serious example of riot, most offenders had a custodial sentence imposed. However, this cannot indicate sentencing practices for riot in general.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 30.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 30.1.2.1 – Riot and violent disorder

refs.q: This chapter covers offences that involve violence and public alarm.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order

refs.q: Riot, rout and unlawful assembly were common law offences that described an escalating chain of offending by a collective to commit unlawful acts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order

refs.q: Please refer to the Sentencing Advisory Council statistics database for more information on current sentencing practices for riot and affray.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 30.1.2 – Current sentencing practice > 30.1.2.2 – Affray

title: Riot (by analogy, rout) and violent disorder: gravity and individual culpability
statement: Riot derives gravity from numbers (crowd psychology, sudden escalation); principal factors are size (numbers, duration, alarm), actual violence and harm. Participants bear some responsibility for collective harm, adjusted for their part and blame; an individual’s culpability is not assessed in isolation. Culpability factors: leadership/encouragement (aggravating); no planning or premeditation (mitigating); attacks on police or prison officers (aggravating; generally custody); disguises (relevant to whether the participant intended violence); harm to persons or property; knowledge or foresight of danger or injury. The Manual states this reasoning for riot; apply it to rout by analogy. Violent disorder does not replicate riot but is intended to capture much of its conduct (a violent mob mentality); maximum 10 years, or 15 years for the aggravated form (face covering) — where aggravated violent disorder is charged, the face covering is an element and must not also be counted as aggravating (limb below).

limbs.text: Violent disorder: maximum 10 years; aggravated form (face covering) 15 years — the face covering is then an element

refs.q: As with riot, the gravity of violent disorder is reflected in its maximum penalty of 10-years’ imprisonment. The statute also creates an aggravated form of violent disorder, where the offender wears a face covering to disguise their identity or protect themselves from a crowd-controlling substance. The maximum penalty for the aggravated form is 15-years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.2 – Violent disorder

refs.q: In categorising facts as aggravating or mitigating, a court cannot count a factor that is an element of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances

refs.q: Riot is a very serious offence which derives its gravity from persons acting in numbers and using those numbers to achieve their purpose. A riot usually involves an inherent danger of injury to persons, property or both. There is a danger that participants will respond to “the psychology of the crowd” and that mob violence may suddenly erupt at a high level and quickly move in new directions.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: The principal factors to consider in assessing the gravity of riot are the size of the riot, the actual level of violence used and the harm caused to people or property. Considerations for the size of the riot include the number of people involved, the duration of the riot, and the level of alarm generated.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: A person who participates in a riot bears some responsibility for the collective damage and harm caused. However, a sentencing judge should take into account the part an individual played in the offence and the extent to which they were to blame for the riot as a whole.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: Identity of the victim – attacks on police or prison officers in the execution of their duties are an aggravating factor and generally call for a custodial sentence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: Planning – an individual who was not involved in the planning of a riot and whose participation was not premeditated is a factor going to mitigation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: As with riot, the gravity of violent disorder is reflected in its maximum penalty of 10-years’ imprisonment. The statute also creates an aggravated form of violent disorder, where the offender wears a face covering to disguise their identity or protect themselves from a crowd-controlling substance. The maximum penalty for the aggravated form is 15-years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.2 – Violent disorder

refs.q: • Disguises – attempting to obscure one’s identity to achieve anonymity is relevant to determining whether the perpetrator intended to behave violently or commit unlawful acts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: The culpability of an individual participant should not be assessed in isolation, as the acts are not committed in isolation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: Violent disorder does not replicate the abolished common law riot offence, but it is intended to capture much of the conduct that would have been captured by common law riot. Violent disorder is a serious offence because it creates a violent mob mentality.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.2 – Violent disorder

refs.q: Matters that affect an individual’s culpability in a riot include:
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: • Leadership and encouragement – assuming a leadership role and actively encouraging others to join in or commit acts throughout a riot are aggravating factors as they underscore the essence of the offence: weight in numbers.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: • Harm to persons or property – a person’s active involvement in damaging property or injuring others is considered more serious than others who are mere followers.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

refs.q: Likewise, if a person knew that a riot was dangerous or foresaw or intended a particular injury or a type of injury, that may be treated as an aggravating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.1 – Riot

title: Affray: gravity and individual culpability
statement: Affray requires unlawful violence or threats that would terrify a reasonably firm person; seriousness varies with duration, numbers, weapons and injuries. It is a collective offence: individual acts are not taken in isolation, as any participation promotes the totality of the affray. Statutory affray (s 195H): maximum 5 years, or 7 years for the aggravated form (face covering — then an element, not separately aggravating); common-law affray had a 5-year maximum and no aggravated form (register). Factors: extent of injury (but do not sentence for more serious offending the offender is not responsible for); location (public and moving; private with witnesses or children); planning (pre-arranged armed meetings are serious); weapons (aggravating even if unused); role (leadership, capacity to stop it, recruiting, enthusiastic participation).

limbs.text: Statutory affray (s 195H): 5 years; aggravated form (face covering) 7 years — the face covering is then an element

refs.q: The Crimes Act 1958 creates an aggravated form of affray which applies where the offender wore a face covering to disguise their identity or protect themselves from a crowd-controlling substance. The maximum penalty for this aggravated form is 7-years’ imprisonment, compared to the maximum penalty for the basic offence being 5-years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.3 – Affray

refs.q: In categorising facts as aggravating or mitigating, a court cannot count a factor that is an element of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances

refs.q: For an affray to be made out at common law and in statute, there must be a degree of unlawful violence or a threat of violence which would terrify a reasonably firm person present at the scene.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.3 – Affray

refs.q: Broadly speaking, the gravity of an affray is informed by its duration, the number of participants involved, whether weapons were used, and any injuries sustained.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.2 – Gravity and culpability > 30.2.3 – Affray

refs.q: The Crimes Act 1958 creates an aggravated form of affray which applies where the offender wore a face covering to disguise their identity or protect themselves from a crowd-controlling substance. The maximum penalty for this aggravated form is 7-years’ imprisonment, compared to the maximum penalty for the basic offence being 5-years’ imprisonment.

title: Public order offences: purposes, parity and double punishment
statement: Riot: general deterrence is key (especially prison riots). Affray: general and specific deterrence, denunciation and community protection (courts frequently condemn groups of men who go out drinking and “throw their weight around”; where the motive is revenge, general deterrence and denunciation are important). Rehabilitation may get more weight for youthful offenders. Parity across many offenders: pragmatic approach from the first sentence, explaining disparities without mathematical precision. Where affray and offences arising from or contributing to it are sentenced together, take care to avoid double punishment: the affray sentence cannot be increased for shared elements (e.g. causing injury), and cumulation should be limited consistently with totality.

cautions.text: The Manual says similar priors “may be an aggravating factor when compared with other co-offenders”; prior convictions cannot be used to increase a sentence — they bear on culpability, propensity and mitigation (see factor.prior_and_subsequent_convictions; flag.priors_as_aggravation_30_3).

refs.q: Where a riot or affray participant has previous convictions for similar offences, it will be part of the context for sentencing and may be an aggravating factor when compared with other co-offenders.

refs.q: but it cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish an offender.

refs.q: General deterrence is the key sentencing purpose in riot to make it less likely that others will join a riot in the future. For riots that occur in a prison setting, deterrence assumes a particular importance to prevent “the law of the jungle” from taking hold.

refs.q: For affray, courts have emphasised general and specific deterrence, denunciation and community protection as key sentencing purposes.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.3 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: For youthful offenders in riot or affray offences, rehabilitation may be given more significance over deterrence and community protection.

refs.q: Parity As riots frequently involve a large number of offenders, parity is potentially complex to apply where there is great variation in individual roles and personal circumstances. This is especially apparent where only a small number of offenders have been sentenced out of a large cohort, and where there may have been different sentencing judges. In these cases, a sentencing judge should adopt a pragmatic approach by looking at the first sentence imposed on a participant to discern any real and substantial differences between offenders. Any disparity between offenders should be explained, but precise mathematical evaluations of differences are unnecessary.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 30 – Offences against public order > 30.4 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Where affray shares specific legal elements with other offences (such as causing injury offences), the court cannot increase the sentence for affray simply because of those factors. While some cumulation may be ordered, it should be limited so as to not offend totality or double punishment.

title: OHS offences: scope; summary jurisdiction; forfeiture
statement: Most OHS offences are under the OHSA (other safety statutes and the harmonised WHS laws are outside the chapter). Almost all indictable OHSA offences are triable summarily and are forfeiture offences (Confiscation Act Schedule 1) — but not civil or automatic forfeiture offences — and are not forensic sample offences; workplace manslaughter cannot be heard summarily.

refs.q: The majority of occupational health and safety (‘OHS’) offences in Victoria are governed by the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic) (‘the OHSA’).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences

refs.q: Almost all indictable offences under the OHSA are triable summarily and are forfeiture offences, but are not forensic sample offences. The sole exceptions are the workplace manslaughter offences, which cannot be heard and determined summarily.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices

refs.q: Confiscation Act 1997 (Vic) sch 1. They however are not civil or automatic forfeiture offences under that Act.

While there are many ancillary statutes dealing with safety in specific contexts, and other states and territories (except WA) are also governed, with minor variations, by the harmonised Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Cth), these are outside the scope of this chapter.

title: Offences before 1 July 2005: OHSA 1985 general penalties and the s 53 additional penalty for prior convictions
statement: Most of the OHSA commenced on 1 July 2005; earlier offending fell under the OHSA 1985, s 47 general penalties: indictable 500 penalty units (individual) / 2500 (company); summary 100 / 400. All OHSA 1985 breaches were indictable; breaches of regulations could be summary. With a prior OHSA 1985 conviction, s 53 allowed an additional penalty: indictable — individual 10–500 penalty units and up to 5 years’ imprisonment, company 50–2500 penalty units; summary — individual 10–200 penalty units and up to 2 years’ imprisonment, company 50–400 penalty units. Where s 53 is invoked the court identifies the further penalty and omits prior convictions from the base penalty (no double counting), without a two-step process (this statutory additional penalty is not a breach of the rule against using priors in aggravation: audit.priors_and_remorse_not_aggravating). Factors: nature and number of priors, proximity, relevance, character, and whether the priors and present convictions show a systemic, general or flagrant failure to comply. The current OHSA has no additional-penalty provision. The intake must capture the offence date.

refs.q: Most sections of the OHSA commenced on 1 July 2005. Before then the relevant legislation was the Occupational Health and Safety Act 1985 (Vic) (‘OHSA 1985’).

title: OHS: comparable cases compare the seriousness of the breach, not the harm
statement: Comparable cases help only if relevantly comparable or instructively different, related to the relevant offence, and with sufficient information; for OHS offences the point of comparison is the seriousness of the breach of duty, not the death or harm caused (flag.ohs_outcome_relevance).

refs.q: As with other offences, the use of comparable cases is of limited assistance. They are helpful only where they are relevant comparators — whether because they are materially the same, or because they are instructively different — and sufficient information must be provided to enable meaningful comparisons.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 31.1.3 – Current sentencing practice

refs.q: For OH&S offences, it is the seriousness of the breach of duty, not the causing of a death or harm, which is the relevant point of comparison between cases.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 31.1.3 – Current sentencing practice

refs.q: The cases must also be related to the relevant offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 31.1.3 – Current sentencing practice

title: OHS: gravity is the breach and the risk (“measure of evidenced disregard”); the outcome illuminates the risk
statement: OHS offences are not merely quasi-criminal (heavy maxima). Company and individual (even a sole director) are assessed separately. Punish the gravity of the breach, not its consequences: the scheme is generally risk-based (death or injury is not an element of most OHS offences, though s 32 requires serious injury), and death or injury is relevant to gravity only so far as it shows the seriousness of the risk; harm proved beyond reasonable doubt to have resulted directly is also taken into account as victim impact (31.3.2.4, 31.6.1) — the Manual states both positions (flag.ohs_outcome_relevance). Gravity = seriousness of the departure from duty + extent of risk (likelihood of an endangering event and potential gravity of the consequence): the “measure of evidenced disregard”. High consequences from an unforeseeable, low-end breach remain low-end; the next level is a failure, through inadvertence or negligence, to appreciate a risk the offender should have dealt with; the gravest is wilful disregard of a known risk; where a risk is self-evident or identified, having no system for it (especially at no cost) increases moral culpability. Employers cannot let employees improvise or rely on their skills, and must ensure the person responsible for safety is appropriate; directing dangerous work significantly aggravates; wilful disregard by the responsible person aggravates; employees’ foolish risks do not lessen seriousness.

refs.q: Occupational health and safety offences are different to most other criminal offences but are not merely quasi-criminal. The heavy maximum penalties available indicate how seriously they are regarded by the legislature.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: In such a case, the liability and culpability of both are considered separately, especially where each is charged with different offences. An offender must be punished according to the gravity of the breach of the duty owed and not for the result or consequences of the breach.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Generally, the legislative scheme is risk-based and not outcome-based, and the fact that the victim died or suffered injury will only be relevant in so far as it demonstrates the degree of seriousness of the relevant threat to health or safety resulting from the breach.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: • the seriousness of the breach itself (the extent of departure from the statutory duty); and • the extent of the risk of death or serious injury which might result. This is assessed by: • the likelihood of the occurrence of an event as a result of the breach endangering the safety of employees or others; and • the potential gravity of the consequence of such an event, demonstrated by the actual consequences of the event.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: The seriousness of the offending in other words is the ‘measure of evidenced disregard’ concerning the safety of employees in the circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Therefore, where the seriousness of the consequences of the breach is high but the breach is at the lower end of the scale (for example, as a result of its unforeseeability), the gravity of the breach will be taken to be at the lower end of the scale.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Finally, the gravest offending is where the employer may have wilfully disregarded employee safety by ignoring a known risk. Similarly, where the risk is self-evident or previously identified, a failure to have any systems in place to prevent or mitigate the risk, especially for no expenditure, increases moral culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Where a company directs employees to carry out their work in a dangerous manner, this will significantly aggravate the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Wilful disregard of occupational health and safety by the person responsible for the issue aggravates the employer’s offence, and the seriousness of the offence is not lessened due to an employee’s foolish risks to their own safety.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: This is because the occurrence of death or injury is not an element for most OH&S offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: But note that OHSA s 32 requires serious injury for that offence.

The next level of seriousness is where there is a lack of appreciation of the risk – risks that the offender should have been aware of and taken appropriate steps to deal with but failed to do so either through inadvertence or negligence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: An employer cannot allow employees to ‘improvise’ their own methods of work or rely solely on the experience and skills of its employees - it must take relevant steps to avoid risk.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: The employer must also ensure that the person responsible for workplace safety is appropriate for that job.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Offences under the OHSA may be charged against both a company and an individual, even where the individual is the sole director of the company.

refs.q: The gravity of the breach is measured by:

title: OHS: foreseeability of risk; notice; special or obvious risks
statement: Foreseeability concerns the risk, not the precise accident (an accident may be evidence of whether the risk was reasonably foreseeable). No prior incidents or complaints does not reduce gravity (the employer must ensure safe systems), but ignoring explicit notice (inspector warnings, prior incidents or checks) aggravates (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 4681, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Employers must be alert to special or unexpected industry risks; failure to foresee them is not exculpatory unless nothing more could reasonably be done; exotic or unforeseen risks (e.g. activity outside training) may mitigate. Failures regarding self-evident or inherent risks, or obvious equipment defects, are serious departures.

refs.q: The question of foreseeability of risk is not dependent on whether a precise accident was foreseeable.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.1 – Foreseeability of risk

refs.q: The lack of previous incidents or reports about the current systems do not decrease the offence gravity, as it is the employer’s responsibility to ensure safe systems and not the responsibility of employees to design the system or bring complaints about it. However, where an offender was explicitly put on notice about a potential risk such as through warnings by workplace inspectors, a previous workplace incident, or a previous safety check, disregarding that notice will aggravate the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.1 – Foreseeability of risk

refs.q: The failure to foresee such risks will not be exculpatory unless no further steps could reasonably have been taken. The exotic, unusual or unforeseen nature of the risk may be a factor in mitigation, especially activity that was outside the parameters of training, supervision and instruction received.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.1 – Foreseeability of risk

refs.q: Alternatively, some risks may be self-evident, obvious or inherent in the work that the company undertakes, and therefore any failures to provide a safe working environment may be taken to be a significant departure and a serious breach. Obvious defects in equipment can also constitute a very high departure from the statutory duty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.1 – Foreseeability of risk

refs.q: Cf New Sector Engineering [58].

Rather, an accident may provide evidence that informs whether the risk was reasonably foreseeable – the obligation to eliminate or reduce risk does not depend on the particular way in which the risk ultimately materialises.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.1 – Foreseeability of risk

refs.q: Employers must be alert to special or unexpected risks which exist in their industry.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.1 – Foreseeability of risk

title: Workplace manslaughter: negligent manslaughter principles apply
statement: Principles for negligent manslaughter are useful (the Manual cross-refers to 22.2.2); the degree of negligence and its duration matter: continued or repeated negligence despite obvious risks, or blatant disregard, is more culpable than an aberration or temporary lapse; seriousness is assessed substantially by the measure of evidenced disregard for safety.

refs.q: Because this is a relatively new offence, the Court of Appeal has said that given the similarities between it and the offence of negligent manslaughter at common law, the principles guiding the imposition of sentence for that offence are useful in sentencing for workplace manslaughter.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.2 – Workplace Manslaughter

refs.q: All other things being equal, negligent conduct that is continued or repeated over an extended period in the face of obvious risks to health and safety, or which represents a blatant disregard for health and safety of those in the workplace, will generally be considered more culpable than aberrant conduct or that which is a temporary lapse in an offender’s otherwise satisfactory conduct.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.2 – Workplace Manslaughter

refs.q: And like all OH&S offences, the seriousness of a particular instance of workplace manslaughter must be assessed to a substantial extent ‘by reference to the measure of evidenced disregard for the safety of employees in the particular circumstances’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.2 – Workplace Manslaughter

refs.q: See also 22.2.2 – Negligent manslaughter.

In particular, the Court noted that both the degree of negligence and the period of time over which the negligent conduct continued will be relevant in determining the gravity of workplace manslaughter.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.2 – Gravity and culpability > 31.2.2 – Workplace Manslaughter

title: OHS: responsible actor, safety systems, worker non-compliance, harm and causation
statement: Most OHSA offences are absolute liability; the origin of the failure matters to culpability. Each duty-holder’s duties are unaffected by others’ failures; sentence depends on control and involvement; senior employees with safety responsibility generally receive higher sentences. The OHSA requires reasonably practicable steps: the key is the failure to do what was reasonably practicable, not the incident — failure to follow management’s systems v failure to establish them. Employers need not prevent all accidents but must take reasonably practicable measures; high-risk environments require strict, rigorous, religiously maintained standards; systems are judged in context (industry practice is relevant). Worker contraventions do not excuse the employer (being “let down” is not mitigating; the employer cannot claim incapacity to control employees, especially when a known disregard of procedures continues); systems must be actively implemented (31.3.2.3). Exposure of anyone present is relevant; the actual result is of very limited relevance to gravity, though direct injury or death may be considered as an impact of the offence — but causation is not part of the offence, may be difficult to determine after conviction and must be proved beyond reasonable doubt before it is used, and a court using injuries to assess risk must ensure a causal relationship (31.3.2.4; flag.ohs_outcome_relevance). Long or ongoing breaches and vulnerable exposed persons are serious.

refs.q: The circumstances of the offence are a relevant factor in determining the extent of a failure to ensure that employees are not exposed to risk to their health and safety, and thus to determining gravity and culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.3 – Circumstances of the offence

refs.q: Most offences under the OHSA are absolute liability offences, so liability is direct and does not rely on attributing an employee’s conduct to the employer. However, while the origin of the failure is not relevant to liability, it is relevant in assessing the company’s culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 31.3.1 – Responsible actor

refs.q: For an incident where multiple offenders are involved (i.e. through a shared operation or sub-contracting), the OHS duties of each are unaffected by the failures of others. The appropriate sentence, however, will depend on the individual circumstances and how much control or involvement each offender had.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 31.3.1 – Responsible actor

refs.q: Employees with greater responsibility for the safety of their fellow workers are likely to receive higher sentences than other employees, whose conduct is more peripheral, but the court will consider the context and control of the individual’s role and responsibilities.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 31.3.1 – Responsible actor

refs.q: For example, it is relevant whether the breach was the result of a failure to adhere to systems put in place by management or was a failure by management to establish adequate safety systems and procedures in the first place.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 31.3.2 – Duty and breach > 31.3.2.1 – Generally

refs.q: While the OHSA does not require employers to ensure that accidents never happen, they must take reasonably practicable measures to eliminate or reduce the risk.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 31.3.2 – Duty and breach > 31.3.2.2 – Failure of employers to establish and maintain adequate safety systems

refs.q: In environments where the risk of catastrophic injury or death is high, constant, and readily foreseeable, the legislative obligation of "so far as is reasonably practicable" must involve the creation of strict, rigorous and comprehensive standards which are then religiously maintained.

title: OHS: offender circumstances (remorse, plea, priors, size, community involvement)
statement: Objective seriousness takes precedence; offender circumstances matter less. Post-incident rectification may show remorse and rehabilitation, but less so after considerable prior disdain (and may show risks were easily avoidable); examples: independent audits, training and maintenance, going above and beyond WorkSafe requirements. Pleas retain utilitarian value (less if late). No adverse finding from declining an interview; trial conduct may bear on remorse. Evading responsibility (qualifications, liquidation or phoenixing, litigating against employees) may show an absence of genuine remorse; supporting employees and paying debts, and executives attending, count in favour; remorse is judged through authorised representatives (the Manual notes contrary authority on phoenixing and corporate remorse: fns 4723, 4728, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Prior convictions are viewed in context (the company as a whole; historical convictions of previous entities of limited relevance; scale of operations and exposure to risk; directors of new companies); a good safety record mitigates. Size does not affect the standard of care or culpability but is relevant to means (fine), context and exposure, criminal history, and the offender’s position (e.g. statutory bodies); charitable and community activity indicates good corporate citizenship (directors’ to a limited extent).

refs.q: For OHS offences, the objective seriousness of the offence takes precedence in the sentencing synthesis. Therefore, while it is still appropriate to consider the circumstances of the offender, these are of lesser significance than for other criminal offences.

title: OHS: purposes (general deterrence; specific deterrence for corporations)
statement: General deterrence is significant: Parliament’s high maxima require a penalty sufficient to compel attention to safety and prevent future risks; hopelessly inadequate systems or a cavalier attitude increase the need for punishment and denunciation; rarely, a widely publicised incident may itself deter. Retribution and rehabilitation have very little role for corporations (authority drawn from antitrust cases: fn 4747); specific deterrence is the means (previous OHS convictions may bear on its importance, though isolated priors may not show persistent disregard; remorse and cooperation reduce it; failing to remediate or comply with notices increases it). Liquidation does not automatically reduce specific deterrence (those behind the company; but 31.7.2 says that for a company in liquidation specific deterrence has little or no part: flag.ohs_liquidation_specific_deterrence).

refs.q: General deterrence is a significant sentencing factor for OHS offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Where a system of work is ‘hopelessly inadequate and vague’, or where there is a cavalier attitude to safety, the need for strong punishment and denunciation will be increased.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Retribution and rehabilitation have very little role to play in sentencing a corporation. Specific deterrence is the means by which a corporation is to be hindered from engaging in contravening conduct.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Alternatively, where the post-offence conduct indicates remorse and cooperation, specific deterrence will be mitigated. But where the offending company failed to take remedial steps after a breach of duty, or where it failed to comply with improvement notices or reverted charges, the need for specific deterrence will be increased.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Liquidation does not automatically reduce the weight to be given to specific deterrence, given that a company is controlled by its directors who may operate in the industry in future.

refs.q: See, eg, ACCC v ABB Transmission and Distribution [2002] FCA 559, [17]; ACMA v TPG Internet Pty Ltd [2014] FCA 382, [63] (although in terms of antitrust laws).

As Parliament views breaches of the OHSA seriously by virtue of the high maximum penalties, the court must ensure a level of penalty for a breach that is sufficient to compel attention to occupational health and safety issues to ensure prevention of future risks to health and safety.

refs.q: The offender’s previous convictions for OHS offences may be relevant to determining the importance of specific deterrence, though isolated previous convictions may not indicate a persistent disregard for worker safety.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 31 – Occupational health and safety offences > 31.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: In very rare situations, where an incident occurs that is already widely publicised in that small field, the event itself may act as a significant deterrent to potential further breaches.

title: OHS: rolled-up charges, VIS, conviction, fines, aggregate fines, and OHSA orders
statement: Breaches of one provision in ss 21–32 from the same facts may be rolled up (single penalty; same maximum). Although OHS offences are generally risk-based, the court must take into account injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offence, including through victim impact statements. Usual sanction is a fine (adjourned undertakings possible). Not recording a conviction against a company is significant leniency; serious offending should still be convicted (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 4760); a conviction may be recorded against the company but not the director. Fines: not a valuation of a life; the court must consider the offender’s financial circumstances as far as practicable, but they cannot immunise a company — the fine must be commensurate with objective seriousness and general deterrence, and its symbolic importance must not be overlooked; inability to pay does not prevent a fine; fines may be ordered against insolvent companies (general deterrence); for a company in liquidation, the judge must ignore the fact that it is in liquidation and that the fine will never be paid, and consider its assets and prospects at the time of trading (31.7.2: specific deterrence then has little or no part — but 31.5 says liquidation does not automatically reduce it: flag.ohs_liquidation_specific_deterrence); post-incident safety spending is not deducted; stays or instalments must not let the fine become a cost of doing business. Directors may be made jointly and severally liable where the company cannot pay and insolvency was foreseeable, unless they reasonably believed solvency and took reasonable steps. For separate penalties on company and director (especially a sole director and shareholder), consider the aggregate, who bears the penalty, each one’s capacity to pay, and whether the company will meet the fines (e.g. phoenixing); a sole director affects quantum, not the penalty itself. Aggregate fines (including for rolled-up or representative charges; not exceeding the sum of maxima) may reflect totality; different duties to different classes of persons may warrant individual penalties (but see fn 4784: flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). OHSA orders: reinstatement or damages for discrimination; adverse publicity orders (protective; on the court’s initiative or the prosecutor’s application; costs not exceeding the maximum; notice of the offence, consequences, penalty and related matters, with evidence to WorkCover); improvement projects (conditions; costs not exceeding the maximum); release on a health and safety undertaking for up to two years — equivalent to a release on adjournment and available in addition to other penalties — with three mandatory conditions and special conditions.

refs.q: Where two or more breaches of a single provision in sections 21-32 of the OHSA arise out of the same factual circumstances, these may be rolled-up into a single charge, attracting a single penalty. This does not affect the maximum penalty for a single offence, though it will likely be relevant in fixing the appropriate penalty.

title: Inchoate maxima: the register row for the charge; general rows yield to specific ones; life is not a “prescribed maximum”; attempt 60% rule
statement: Use the register row for the charge. Many inchoate maxima are “the maximum penalty which applies to the primary offence” (for multiple offences, the accumulated maxima). The general Crimes Act rows for a mandatory penalty and a penalty “at large” apply only “unless otherwise covered by another item in this table” (fns 4804–4807). Conspiracy or incitement where the penalty is at large (s 321C(1)(b), s 321I(1)(b)): Level 4 – 15 years. Because life imprisonment is not “a prescribed maximum penalty”, the operative maximum for a Crimes Act conspiracy (or incitement) to commit an offence punishable by life is 15 years (Dimozantos; fn 4805, repeated in fn 4807) — but not for conspiracy or incitement to murder or treason (s 321C(1)(ba), s 321I(1)(ba): Level 1 – life; the footnotes’ carve-out is worded inconsistently: flag.inchoate_life_maximum_footnotes), and not where another row covers the charge: DPCS s 79 conspiracy and s 80 incitement to certain drug offences carry the primary offence’s maximum (guide.drugs.extended_liability). Summary-only offences: Level 6 – 5 years or the primary maximum, whichever is greater. Attempts: s 321P(1)(a) “as set out in the table” (not reproduced: flag.attempt_table_not_reproduced; it applies with necessary changes to interstate penalties); where the penalty is not specified by a Level in that table, 60% of the maximum for the offence (s 321P(1)(b)); at large, Level 6 – 5 years; attempted murder or treason, Level 2 – 25 years; a lower penalty in another enactment prevails (s 321P(2)); an attempt outside Victoria carries the maximum in that place (a penalty above life is read as life); attempts within DPCS ss 71–71AC, 72–72B and 73 carry the primary offence’s maximum, and s 191(1) (attempting to fraudulently induce investment) is Level 4 – 15 years. The Commonwealth rows (32.1.2) are outside the app’s scope.

title: Inchoate offences: current practice (conspiracy, incitement, attempts)
statement: Conspiracy does not inevitably attract less than the completed offence. Incitement convictions are relatively rare (most commonly incitement to murder, which may merit more than some murders; upper-range incitement to murder indistinguishable from conspiracy to murder should align with conspiracy sentences). Attempts ordinarily attract less than completed offences even without a lower maximum — an approach that accords with the Crimes Act penalty scheme (s 321P(1)(a)) — because an attempt usually causes less harm (treating attempted murder as seriously as murder is “an affront to common sense”; an attempted aggravated sexual assault is not as serious as the completed offence) and to preserve the incentive to desist. The significant exceptions are attempted drug offences (many DPCS offences include attempted conduct without differentiation in penalty) and attempting to pervert the course of justice; where a benign substance was substituted by authorities there is little difference between attempt and completion.

title: Inchoate offences: gravity (content and probability of success; plotting is dangerous)
statement: Inchoate offences vary widely; seriousness is coloured by the substantive offence, and an attempt at a serious offence is serious. Equal maxima for some conspiracies show Parliament’s view; attempts are not ordinarily commensurate with conspiracy (different elements; a lower maximum). Conspiracy’s essence is joint plotting, which is inherently dangerous (likelihood, capability, further plans, difficulty of detection). Gravity of conspiracies and attempts turns on the content (the offence contemplated or attempted and the consequences if completed) and the probability of success (distance travelled, real prospects, performance, duration and reality; sophisticated or naïve, serious or half-hearted, competent or mismanaged). The improbability or impossibility of success is relevant to the criminality of most conspiracies and attempts (commonly little weight for incomplete drug offending); lack of equipment, means or intelligence may reduce criminality; withdrawal or failure to proceed from a very early stage may be less serious (each case on its merits); a sophisticated near-success weighs more than a naïve attempt. Thwarting by police, prevention measures, luck or bungling does not reduce criminality. Content and probability are weighed in all the circumstances: a hopeless attempt at a serious offence is not necessarily less serious than a near-complete attempt at a lesser one, though the difference between well- and poorly planned attempts diminishes as the substantive offence’s seriousness decreases. Harm caused or avoided is relevant, but attempted violent thefts that terrify are not much less serious. For incitement the key is the offence incited.
