refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: However, offences such as attempts to commit a violent theft which instill terror in a victim will not be significantly less serious merely because the offender did not succeed in making off with any property or money.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: In relation to incitement, the most important consideration the nature of the substantive offence incited.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: Inchoate offences vary widely in seriousness and in criminality. It is difficult to make definitive statements about seriousness, given that the nature of an inchoate offence will be coloured by the type of substantive offence it embraces.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: Parliament’s view of the objective gravity of certain conspiracies can be seen where the maximum penalty fixed by statute is the same as that for the substantive offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: The essence of the crime of conspiracy is that a number of individuals plot together to achieve their unlawful purpose as a group. This element of joint effort distinguishes conspiracy from incitement and attempts. For the following reasons plotting is considered inherently dangerous, and more serious than if an individual were acting alone to plan and commit the offence:
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability

refs.q: The content of the conspiracy looks at the nature of the substantive criminal offence contemplated or attempted and the seriousness of the consequences that would follow if the substantive offence were completed.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: The probability of success factor is described in various ways, including the distance which the conspirators have travelled towards their goal of achieving the illegal objective, the “real prospects” of achieving the objective, the “performance” or the “duration and reality” of the offence, which reveals the ‘quality, the magnitude and the effectiveness’ of the conspiracy itself.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: In evaluating the probability of success, the court will also consider whether the offending was sophisticated or naïve, undertaken seriously or half-heartedly, competently executed or hopelessly mismanaged, as well as all other surrounding circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: An inability to carry out the agreed plan because the conspirators lack the equipment, the means of obtaining it, or the intelligence to obtain it may reduce the criminality of the scheme. A withdrawal or a failure to carry the matter through from a very early stage may also constitute an offence of lesser seriousness, although each case must be assessed on its merits.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: The evaluation of the impact of the content of the conspiracy and the probability of success must be weighed in each case in the light of all of the circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: However, the difference between a well-planned and a poorly planned attempt diminishes as the seriousness of the substantive offence decreases.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

refs.q: In this respect, harm caused or avoided is relevant. Certain inchoate offences may be less serious offences than their completed analogue, as a completed offence will frequently cause loss and harm that does not occur in the case of an incomplete offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.1 – Relationship between criminal objective and progress made

title: Conspiracy: individual culpability
statement: Besides the content of the conspiracy and its probability of success, culpability depends on role, benefit and participation (instigators and greater beneficiaries more culpable; the sentence reflects the organisational nature of the conspiracy and the offender’s role, not only acts performed; involvement may vary between co-conspirators, and comparative financial gain may guide), duration, planning and sophistication (deliberately hard to detect), and persistence despite detection or desistance before it.

refs.q: The role, benefit and level of participation: an offender who is the instigator of the conspiracy, or who stands to derive greater benefit than the other co-conspirators will bear greater culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.2 – Factors going to culpability in conspiracy cases

refs.q: The individual’s acts and declarations will inform but not determine the degree of criminality, as the sentence must reflect the organisational nature of the conspiracy and offender’s role in it and should not be confined to examining the acts actually performed by offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.2 – Factors going to culpability in conspiracy cases

refs.q: • The duration of the conspiracy. • The degree of planning and sophistication - particularly where the offending is complicated and deliberately difficult to detect. • Whether the offender persisted in the face of detection or police intervention, or ultimately desisted from offending prior to detection.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.2 – Factors going to culpability in conspiracy cases

refs.q: In addition to the general factors of the content of the conspiracy and the probability of success, the following matters affect an individual’s culpability in a conspiracy.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.2 – Factors going to culpability in conspiracy cases

refs.q: The level of involvement may vary between co-conspirators. For some conspiracies, the comparative financial betterment between co-conspirators is a reasonable guide to the relative degrees of participation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.2 – Gravity and culpability > 32.2.2 – Factors going to culpability in conspiracy cases

title: Inchoate offences: victims, remorse, purposes and overt acts
statement: Intended victims (or those who would have been present) are victims once relevantly affected by learning of the plan. Remorse takes the form of contrition for the prospective damage. General deterrence is normally primary for conspiracy; general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are important for incitement and attempts, coloured by the substantive offence. Where overt acts are one transaction with the conspiracy, no separate sentence may be appropriate; overt acts are not aggravated merely because part of a conspiracy; where separate sentences are imposed, avoid double punishment by limiting the sentence on the conspiracy or the overt acts, or by identifying their separate criminality.

refs.q: The intended victim of an incomplete offence – or any person who would have been present had the intended offence been committed – will be victims for sentencing purposes upon learning of it, if they are relevantly affected by their subsequent knowledge of the planned crime.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.3 – Circumstances of the offence > 32.3.1 – Meaning of ‘victim’

refs.q: Remorse on the part of an offender who commits an inchoate offence takes the form of ‘contrition for the prospective damage’ that may have flowed from the actual commission of the substantive offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.4 – Circumstances of the offender > 32.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: Normally, general deterrence is a primary sentencing purpose for conspiracy offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: General deterrence, denunciation and just punishment are important sentencing considerations for incitement and attempt offences, although the weight to be given to these purposes will commonly be coloured by the substantive offence incited or attempted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.5 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: If the overt acts of the conspiracy offence are so closely related to the acts of the substantive offence as to make the offences one act or transaction, it may be appropriate to impose no sentence for the substantive offences. If the court does impose a separate sentence for substantive offences committed as overt acts of a conspiracy, those offences should not be treated as aggravated merely because they were committed as part of a conspiracy.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Alternatively, the court should identify the separate criminality of the conspiracy and the overt acts to avoid double punishment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.6 – Formulation of sentence

refs.q: Where separate sentences are imposed, the need to avoid double punishment may limit the sentence imposed on either the conspiracy or the overt acts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 32 – Inchoate offences > 32.6 – Formulation of sentence

title: Firearms offences: scope of the chapter; prohibited persons
statement: The Firearms Act 1996 contains a spectrum of summary and indictable offences (possess/use/carry for prohibited and non-prohibited persons; acquire/dispose; discharge; firearm prohibition orders; manufacture; safety, alteration, administration, storage). The chapter focuses on prohibited person possess firearm, discharge offences and contravening a firearm prohibition order, plus imitation firearms (Control of Weapons Act) and (Commonwealth) importation. A person may be a prohibited person in several circumstances, including having served (in the past 15 years) or serving a term of imprisonment for an indictable offence or some drug and weapons offences, or being subject to a final family violence or personal safety intervention order or a community-based order (Firearms Act s 3). A “prohibited weapon” includes an imitation firearm.

refs.q: This chapter focuses on sentencing for prohibited person possess, use, or carry firearms (‘prohibited person possess firearms’) offences, discharge firearm offences, and contravening a firearm prohibition order offences due to their prevalence in recent years.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences

refs.q: The Firearms Act 1996 (Vic) (‘Firearms Act’) contains a spectrum of summary and indictable firearm offences in Victoria.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences

refs.q: This chapter also considers sentencing for firearm offences in other legislation, such as imitation firearm offences in the Control of Weapons Act 1990 (Vic) and importing firearm offences in the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) and Customs Act 1901 (Cth).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences

refs.q: These offences can be broadly categorised as possess, use, or carry offences, which distinguish between “prohibited person” and “non-prohibited person” offences; acquire/dispose offences; discharge offences; firearm prohibition order offences; manufacture offences; and other offences relating to safety, alteration, administration, and storage.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences

refs.q: There are a number of circumstances in which a person may be treated as a prohibited person, they include: a person who is serving, or in the past 15 years has served, a term of imprisonment for an indictable offence or some drug and weapons offences, or served a term of imprisonment in another State or Territory, or a person who is subject to a final family violence intervention order, a personal safety intervention order, or a community-based order.

Non-prohibited persons offences further distinguish between registered and unregistered firearms, as well as between longarms (separated into five subcategories) and handguns (separated into two subcategories).
A “prohibited weapon” is an imitation firearm or an article listed in Schedule 2 of the Control of Weapons Regulations 2021 (Vic)

title: Prohibited person possess firearm: current practice (Berichon categories)
statement: Practice generally follows Berichon: (1) possession not associated with ongoing criminal activity — usually a low order of imprisonment unless criminal history warrants more (normally under two years); (2) possession for a criminal activity or purpose (security, enforcement) — more severe. The categories do not fetter discretion: each sentence turns on the particular circumstances of the offending and the offender. Imprisonment is most common; avoid double punishment with sentences for offending related to the same firearm (fn 4875 cross-refers to “1.4.1 – Double punishment below”; the chapter’s double punishment discussion is 33.4.1); a combination of imprisonment and a lengthy CCO may suit compelling mitigation, but may be out of range alongside other serious offences. On the use of criminal history see flag.firearm_status_priors_aggravation.
note: Practice figures in this item are descriptive (a Manual practice statement): never a default, tariff or range check (audit.statistics_and_medians; audit.comparable_cases_use).

refs.q: The first category is where the firearm possession is not associated with ongoing criminal activity. Sentences of a low order of imprisonment are usually appropriate for these unless the criminal history of the offender warrants a more substantial sentence. The second category is where the firearm possession is for a criminal activity or purpose, such as to provide security for a criminal activity or as a means of enforcement. This category will attract a more severe sentence. However, the categories are not a prescriptive framework that fetters sentencing discretion.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.1 – Prohibited person possess firearm

refs.q: The most common sentencing disposition is a term of imprisonment. Cases which fall into the less serious category normally attract sentences lower than two years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.1 – Prohibited person possess firearm

refs.q: In some cases where there are compelling mitigating circumstances, a combination sentence of imprisonment and a lengthy community corrections order may be appropriate. But where a possess firearm offence is charged with other serious offences, a combination sentence may not be in range.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.1 – Prohibited person possess firearm

refs.q: Current sentencing practice for prohibited person possess firearm offence generally follows the two categories of seriousness articulated in Berichon v The Queen.

refs.q: The sentence to be imposed in each case must turn on particular circumstances of the offending and the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.1 – Prohibited person possess firearm

refs.q: Cases in the more serious category generally attract a higher sentence, but care must be taken to avoid double punishment if there are other sentences imposed for offending related to the same firearm.

title: Other firearm offences: no clear trends
statement: Firearm offences arise in wide-ranging circumstances and are often charged with other serious offences (drug trafficking, armed robbery, property and person offences); offending and offenders (criminal history, prohibited or FPO status, mitigation) vary greatly, so there are no clear trends for firearm offences other than prohibited person possession; offences introduced in 2018 (contravening a firearm prohibition order; discharging at premises or vehicles) have limited cases.

refs.q: Because of this, there are too many variables to discern clear trends in sentencing for firearm offences other than prohibited person possess firearms.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.2 – Other firearm offences

refs.q: There are limited cases to establish current sentencing practices for these firearm offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.2 – Other firearm offences

refs.q: Firearm offences can be committed in wide-ranging circumstances and are often charged alongside other serious offences, such as drug trafficking, armed robbery, property offences and offences against the person.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.2 – Other firearm offences

refs.q: The circumstances and seriousness of offending can vary significantly.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.2 – Other firearm offences

refs.q: There is also great variability in the circumstances of an offender, such as their criminal history, whether they are a prohibited person or subject to a firearm prohibition order or mitigating factors.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.1 – Penalties and current sentencing practices > 33.1.3 – Current sentencing practices > 33.1.3.2 – Other firearm offences

title: Firearm possession offences: gravity
statement: Possession offences are very serious: obvious risk of serious injury or death, heightened by association with criminal enterprise even without use. Objective gravity is primarily influenced by the Berichon categories (possession without a criminal purpose is generally less morally culpable), but they are not fixed sub-categories. Factors that may elevate seriousness even without a criminal purpose: criminal history (especially firearms priors); circumstantial evidence of unlawful purpose (but be cautious — absent direct evidence, a criminal purpose should be inferred only if it is the only reasonable inference; lack of a credible explanation may be insufficient); ammunition; no lawful use; cut-down firearms (little leniency). Factors that may aggravate: number; nature (modified, home-made, high-powered); loaded or with ammunition; insecure and readily accessible; duration (longer may aggravate; short possession by design to avoid detection may not mitigate); prohibited person or FPO status and the nature and extent of prior history; value. Less serious: non-functional firearm (cannot be fired, not merely unloaded) and no ammunition. Each possession offence also has its own policy considerations (guide.firearms.specific_possession_offences). Criminal history and status: they must not lift the sentence beyond what the offence warrants, and where the status is an element it is not counted again (flag.firearm_status_priors_aggravation).

limbs.text: Maximum of 10 years: prohibited person possess firearm or imitation firearm, possess traffickable quantity, and contravening a firearm prohibition order (s 5(1), s 7C(1), s 112B, s 5AB(2), s 5AB(3)); the register gives the other possession offences lower maxima (e.g. s 5(2), s 5AB(1))

refs.q: Prohibited person possess firearm/imitation firearm, possess traffickable quantity of firearms, and contravening a firearm prohibition order all carry a maximum penalty of 10 years imprisonment, representing the inherent seriousness with which Parliament views these offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: Firearm possession offences are very serious. Prohibited person possess firearm/imitation firearm, possess traffickable quantity of firearms, and contravening a firearm prohibition order all carry a maximum penalty of 10 years imprisonment, representing the inherent seriousness with which Parliament views these offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: Possession creates an obvious risk of causing serious injury or death and this risk is heightened when the possession is associated with an ongoing criminal enterprise or other criminal conduct, even if there is no evidence of its use or threatened use.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: But courts needs to be mindful that the two Berichon categories are not fixed sub-categories which prescribe the manner in which a court must assess the gravity of the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: but in the absence of direct evidence that an offender had used firearms for a criminal purpose, courts should be cautious in drawing a conclusion that the possession was for a criminal purpose, unless the conclusion was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the circumstances. The fact that an offender fails to offer a credible explanation for possessing the firearm may not be sufficient to support an inference that they were possessed for a criminal purpose
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: courts have remarked that cut down firearms have only one realistic use – committing violent crimes – and even if its possession is not connected with a criminal purpose, an offender cannot expect much lenience.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: the number of firearms involved – the larger the number of firearms possessed, the greater the seriousness of the offending
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: the duration of possession – possession for a longer period may aggravate offending, but possession for a short period may not mitigate offending it if was by design to reduce the risk of being caught
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: Factors which are considered to be markers of less serious offending include where the firearm is not functional (i.e., where the firearm cannot be fired, not merely that it was unloaded) and where the offender did not possess ammunition.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: The objective gravity of possession offences is primarily influenced by the Berichon categories of seriousness. Generally, a person who does not possess a firearm for a criminal purpose is considered less morally culpable.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: There are many factors which may elevate the seriousness of a possess firearm offence, even if it is not associated with an ongoing criminal purpose. Some of these factors include:
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • an offender’s criminal history, especially any prior firearms convictions
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • any circumstantial evidence that enables the conclusion that the firearm possession is for an unlawful activity
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • where the offender also possessed ammunition
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • possessing a firearm with no lawful use will be viewed more seriously than possessing a firearm which can be used lawfully
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: The various possession offences share factors that are relevant to assessing gravity. Aside from the Berichon categories of seriousness, factors that may aggravate a firearm possession offence include:
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • the nature of the firearms – modified firearms for ease of concealment and firing, home-made weapons and high-powered firearms that are capable of great lethality are considered more serious • whether the weapon is loaded and/or the presence of ammunition
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • where the firearm and ammunition are not kept in a secure location, are readily accessible and capable of being retrieved and discharged quickly
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • the status of the offender either as a prohibited person or the subject of a firearm prohibition order, and the nature and extent of their prior criminal history
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: • the monetary value of the firearms may also be relevant.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences

refs.q: There are also policy considerations relevant to assessing the gravity of each of the possession offences as discussed below.

title: Prohibited persons, traffickable quantities, imitation firearms and firearm prohibition orders
statement: Prohibited person possession reflects the Act’s purpose of public safety and peace by keeping firearms from those who cannot meet community standards (e.g. prior criminal history, intervention orders, criminal enterprises); criminal history and criminal associations are particularly relevant; possession may be less serious where the prohibition stems from unrelated minor matters (e.g. a previous intervention order) with no firearm or violence history. Traffickable quantity (prohibited and non-prohibited persons alike) targets the prevalence and harm of illegal firearms, their commercial movement, the risks of accumulation and the difficulty of detection; the threshold was reduced from 10 to three to two; the number above the threshold corresponds to seriousness. Imitation firearms: seriousness varies with prohibited status; for prohibited persons the same maximum “suggests” equal severity, but sentences treat them as less serious than real firearms (flag.imitation_weapon_competing_authority); victims may believe they could be shot, so incapacity to fire may be of limited relevance; possession unconnected with a criminal purpose may be less serious. Firearm prohibition orders (introduced 2018; made in the public interest by the Chief Commissioner where a firearm may be used to endanger public peace and safety): contravention is particularly aggravated if soon after service; deliberate defiance significantly increases culpability.

limbs.text: Prohibited person possess firearm: criminal history and criminal associations; the reason for the prohibition

refs.q: The criminal history of an offender and whether they are known to operate in criminal circles is particularly relevant to assessing the gravity of prohibited person possess firearm offence. Where an offender has no prior firearm convictions or history of violence and is a prohibited person for unrelated, minor offending (e.g., a previous intervention order), the firearm possession may be viewed less seriously.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences > 33.2.1.1 – Prohibited person possess firearm

refs.q: Its seriousness is underscored by Parliament reducing the quantity of traffickable firearms from 10 in 2003 to three in 2015 and then two in 2018. The number of firearms possessed over the threshold quantity corresponds to the seriousness of the offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences > 33.2.1.2 – Possess traffickable quantity of firearms

refs.q: However, the sentences imposed in cases where both offences are charged suggest that courts treat the possession of an imitation firearm as less serious than possession of a firearm, despite the offences carrying the same maximum penalty.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences > 33.2.1.3 – Possess imitation firearm

refs.q: Therefore, the fact that the firearm is incapable of being discharged may be of limited relevance in certain circumstances. On the other hand, if the possession was not connected to a criminal purpose or other offending, courts may view it less seriously.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences > 33.2.1.3 – Possess imitation firearm

refs.q: The offence is particularly aggravated if an offender was served with the firearm prohibition order shortly before the offending. Deliberate defiance of an order put in place for public peace significantly increases an offender’s culpability.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 33 – Firearms offences > 33.2 – Gravity and culpability > 33.2.1 – Possession offences > 33.2.1.4 – Contravening a firearm prohibition order

title: Discharging a firearm with reckless disregard (at premises or vehicles)
statement: Maximum 15 years (s 131A(1)); 20 years if while carrying out a serious indictable offence (s 131A(2): the table and the register say “serious indictable offence”; the 33.2.3 text says “an indictable offence”). The high penalties reflect potentially lethal consequences; the offence was introduced in 2018 in response to a perceived increase in drive-by shootings (before then it would likely have been charged as reckless conduct endangering life or serious injury, 10 and 5 years). Key aggravating feature: discharge at a person, or at premises or vehicles where people may be present (e.g. the bullet strikes the victim; residential premises when occupants are likely present; a vehicle known or inferred to be occupied). Other indicia: premeditation and planning (stolen or hired vehicles, sourcing a weapon, stealth); nature of firearm (semi- or fully automatic, high-powered); motivation; aim and penetration; role; whether anyone was injured. Discharge with no one nearby may be less serious; the indicia measure the risk and the offender’s culpability. The 33.2.3 discussion is of s 131A; for Crimes Act s 31C(2) (discharge reckless to the safety of police or protective services officers, 15 years) the Manual gives no offence-specific gravity guidance (limb).

title: Firearms offences: double punishment with related charges; the s 7C(2) bar
statement: Firearm possession is often charged with other offences whose elements overlap (e.g. armed robbery) or which it aggravates (e.g. threat to kill). Where the firearm aggravates another charge and a prohibited person possession charge is also laid, the possession charge must not be elevated to the criminal-purpose category because of that other offending, nor include penalty for that use; it may be elevated only on evidence of a distinct criminal purpose (then modest cumulation is not double punishment). If possession is sentenced in the serious category, it cannot also aggravate the other charge, though totality may justify a higher individual sentence and cumulation where possession materially adds to overall criminality. Multiple charges about the same firearm (possession and discharge; possession and disposal; FPO contraventions) risk double punishment — do not treat possession more seriously because the firearm was discharged in other criminal activity that is separately punished — but distinct criminality (especially FPO contraventions) may warrant higher sentences and some cumulation; aggregate sentences may avoid double punishment. The Manual cross-refers to 3.4.7 (double punishment, weapons offences).

limbs.text: Statutory bar (Firearms Act s 7C(2)): a person convicted or found guilty of possessing a traffickable quantity of firearms is not liable for an offence under ss 5(1), 6(1)–(6), 6A(1)–(3), 7(1)–(6), 7B(1)–(2) — caution where s 7C(1) and one of those offences are both charged

refs.q: If a person is convicted or found guilty of this offence, they are not liable for an offence under ss 5(1), 6(1)–(6), 6A(1)–(3), 7(1)–(6), 7B(1)–(2): Firearms Act s 7C(2).

Where an offender is charged with offending that is aggravated by using a firearm and for being a prohibited person in possession of a firearm, the possession charge should not be elevated to the more serious category (possession for a criminal purpose) because the firearm was used in the course of the other offending. To avoid double punishment, the sentence imposed for the possession charge should not include any penalty for the use or possession of the firearm in the other offending. The possession charge may only be elevated in seriousness if there is evidence to conclude that the possession was for some criminal purpose distinct from the other offending charged. Where there is distinct criminality, a modest cumulation imposed on the firearms charge would not be double punishment.

refs.q: Alternatively, if a firearm possession charge is sentenced in the more serious category, the firearm possession cannot then be considered an aggravating factor of another charge.

refs.q: However, where separate firearms offences involve distinct criminality, and especially where the offender contravenes a firearm prohibition order, there is no double punishment in imposing a higher sentence for each of the firearms charges and ordering a degree of cumulation between the charges. In some cases, courts have sought to avoid double punishment by imposing an aggregate sentence on multiple firearm charges.

title: Terrorism: general gravity considerations; victims; conspiracy; impossibility
statement: Terrorism offences are inherently serious. Considerations: planning, research, complexity, sophistication and commitment; duration; depth of radicalisation (extremist material, communications); indoctrination of others and their vulnerability; the maximum. Prolonged planning to massacre civilians is of extremely high gravity (particularly where the offender appreciates the wrongfulness); targeting police, public events on national holidays and willingness to kill civilians suggest very high moral culpability. Continued adherence to a violent ideology is not ordinarily aggravating, but its abandonment (proved by the offender) mitigates; relatively superficial conviction may attenuate gravity. Victims’ circumstances and harm (including witnesses) must be considered (the Manual’s source is Commonwealth: Cth Crimes Act s 16A(2)(d)–(e), fn 4958; for the Victorian s 4B(1) offence see factor.statutory_victim_and_harm); harm includes harm to the public and polity, not mathematically related to victim numbers. Terrorist conspiracies are more serious than individual offending (agreement more advanced, joint effort more likely to succeed, harder to detect and shut down, more enduring zeal). Incompetence or impracticability does not diminish a serious offence.

refs.q: The courts have been clear and unequivocal: terrorism offences are an inherently serious category of offending.

statement: Relevant considerations: length and detail of the document; whether intended to result in violent attacks and incite others; clandestine distribution (dark web, rallies); recruiting others to review drafts; time spent.
