title: Terrorism: offender circumstances (renunciation, plea, mental condition, youth)
statement: Mitigating personal factors get substantially less weight. Respectful, co-operative conduct at trial may be disregarded as mitigation, and disruption need not be treated as aggravating. Renunciation of extremist beliefs is crucial to rehabilitation (adherence at the time of the offence and at sentencing is a crucial question; if the views are no longer held, the court must make an allowance); the offender must prove it on the balance of probabilities (public renunciation especially compelling; transformation without contrition, or in sheltered custody, is viewed sceptically; conversion to another religion is unnecessary). The plea’s utilitarian value has no special weight; it may cautiously indicate relenting; late pleas, or prior explicit contempt (remorse then credible perhaps only if given in oral evidence and tested), weaken remorse; boasting admissions earn only a modest discount. Mental condition may make the offender an inappropriate vehicle for general deterrence, reduce specific deterrence or make custody more onerous, and a causal relationship with extremist beliefs has sometimes been taken into account. Young offenders can plan carefully: youth is relevant but its weight may diminish measurably for planned extreme violence (general deterrence and denunciation may take primacy; rehabilitation moderated); radicalisation at 17 did not of itself reduce culpability (Alou), though immaturity rather than fanaticism may earn significant consideration (Bayda).

limbs.text: Commonwealth offenders: the Cth Crimes Act s 16A circumstances (contrition, rehabilitation, plea, age and mental condition)

refs.q: The Cth Crimes Act requires the court to take into account various circumstances of a Commonwealth offender, including: • the degree to which the offender has shown contrition for the offence • the offender’s prospects of rehabilitation • any plea of guilty, and • the offender’s age and mental condition.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender

limbs.text: Commonwealth post-sentence regimes: the prospect of a control order (div 104) or continuing detention order (div 105A) is at most a marginal concern; it is no insurance against future risk; no hardship is inferred from it without specific evidence; the Manual presumes the same for extended supervision orders

refs.q: That the offender might, at the conclusion of their sentence, be subject to a control order under div 104, or a continuing detention order under div 105A, is, at most, a marginal concern in sentencing. The potential for such orders does not operate as insurance against future risk to diminish the role of community protection or any other sentencing consideration.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: Furthermore, a court should not infer hardship to the offender from the prospect that they might at the end of their term of imprisonment become the subject of a continuing detention order, absent specific evidence to that effect. The offender’s awareness of the statutory regime in div 105A may equally provide them a beneficial incentive to pursue rehabilitation. Presumably, these principles apply to the prospect of an extended supervision order.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: As a general proposition, mitigating personal factors will be given substantially less weight in sentencing for terrorism offences than for other forms of offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: As with any factual matter in mitigation, the offender bears the onus of establishing on the balance of probabilities that extremist beliefs have been abandoned.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.1 – Renunciation of extremist beliefs

refs.q: However, the ostensible transformation of an offender in the absence of contrition should be met with skepticism.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.1 – Renunciation of extremist beliefs

refs.q: The utilitarian benefit of a guilty plea has no special mitigatory weight in the case of terrorist offences and falls to be assessed according to individual circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.2 – Plea of guilty

refs.q: • render the offender an inappropriate vehicle for general deterrence • reduce the need for specific deterrence, and/or • make more onerous the offender’s conditions in custody.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.3 – Mental condition

refs.q: So while youth is always a relevant consideration in mitigation, its weight can be diminished ‘quite measurably’ in sentencing for young terrorist offenders who have participated in, planned, and/or carried out actions of extreme violence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.4 – Youth

refs.q: It is open to a sentencing court to disregard an offender’s respectful and co-operative conduct during the trial as a factor in mitigation. Conversely, the court is not obliged to consider any disruption caused by an offender as an aggravating factor.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: A crucial question in establishing prospects of rehabilitation is the extent to which the offender adheres to any extremist views at the time of the offence and at sentencing.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.1 – Renunciation of extremist beliefs

refs.q: Successful rehabilitation is dependent, at least in part, on the renunciation of extremist beliefs. If those views are no longer held prospects of rehabilitation are stronger, and so it follows, a matter for which the court must make an allowance.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.1 – Renunciation of extremist beliefs

refs.q: In Mohamed, an offender who gave evidence at their plea hearing repudiating Islamic State and violent jihad was found to be ‘genuinely on the path to de-radicalisation’ with reasonable prospects of rehabilitation. A renunciation that is made publicly is especially compelling.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.1 – Renunciation of extremist beliefs

refs.q: In particular, courts are wary of reform that occurs in an environment in which the offender is sheltered from the influences that impelled them to offend. Of course, it is not necessary for the offender to convert to another religion to renounce any fanaticism inherent in an offence for which they are convicted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.1 – Renunciation of extremist beliefs

refs.q: The plea itself may be taken as a cautious indicator that a terrorist offender is in the course of relenting from their extremist beliefs. However, the closer a guilty plea is entered to trial, the more reluctant the court may be to infer an acknowledgement of wrongdoing or an expression of remorse. Moreover, where an offender has held ‘explicit contempt’ for Australian laws and people, a show of remorse might only be credible if it is given in oral evidence and tested in cross-examination.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.2 – Plea of guilty

refs.q: Any sentencing discount for an offender who, in making admissions to police, boasts about their plans to commit terrorist acts, should be only modest.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.2 – Plea of guilty

refs.q: A terrorist offender’s mental condition is relevant on sentence insofar as it may:
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.3 – Mental condition

refs.q: Sentencing courts have sometimes taken into account a causal relationship between the offender’s mental condition and their subscription to extremist beliefs. This relationship may be evident where a mental condition has ‘materially contributed’ to the offender’s susceptibility to, and engagement with, militant ideas.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.3 – Mental condition

refs.q: Young offenders are capable of carefully planning terrorist attacks with foresight as to the consequences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.4 – Youth

refs.q: Put succinctly, in some cases, ‘[t]he protection of our society, and the upholding of its most fundamental values, necessitate that … general deterrence and denunciation must be given primacy above the ameliorating effect of youth’. This may call for moderation of the principle that rehabilitation is not only in the interests of the offender, but also the community. In Alou, the fact that an offender was radicalised at 17 years of age did not establish a causal link between the offence and youth to reduce moral culpability. This may be contrasted with Bayda, where offending regarded as the manifestation of demonstrable immaturity, rather than deep fanaticism, entitled the offenders to ‘significant consideration’ for their youth.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.3 – Circumstances of the offender > 34.3.4 – Youth

title: Terrorism: purposes
statement: Purposes: prevent circumstances increasing the likelihood of terrorist acts, punish and denounce, incapacitate and protect the community — substantial weight to denunciation, general deterrence, community protection and just punishment; personal mitigation gets substantially less weight. Intending to die does not reduce deterrence (the Manual notes contrary remarks: fn 5071, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6). Preparatory offending is denounced in the strongest terms even where no harm results. Community protection looms large where views are retained (the concern is the perfection of the very crime); for lone wolf attacks community protection, punishment and general and specific deterrence are the focal points. Rejection of extremist views and rehabilitation may reduce specific deterrence and protection (lower head sentence and NPP), reflecting the community’s interest in minimising reoffending.

refs.q: The broad purpose of sentencing in terrorism offences is to prevent circumstances which increase the likelihood of terrorist acts occurring, to punish and denounce those who contemplate such acts, and to incapacitate those who prepare for or plan them so as to protect the community from the consequent danger. Accordingly, the sentence will usually reflect and give substantial weight to the purposes of denunciation, general deterrence, community protection, and just punishment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: The fact that the offender intended to die during a terrorist attack will not reduce the weight to be given to specific or general deterrence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Conversely, the need for specific deterrence and community protection may be reduced where the offender has rejected extremist views and demonstrated some rehabilitation. In such cases, sentencing objectives might be achieved with a lower head sentence and non-parole period, given the ‘vital public interest’ in promoting the rehabilitation of would-be terrorists.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: The nature of terrorism offences dictates that personal mitigating factors are given substantially less weight than for other forms of offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Besim [112]; MHK 288 [53]. But see remarks in Lodhi II 490 [87]: ‘[D]eterrence in both respects may, in many cases, be entitled to less weight whenever it appears, as the example of suicide bombers suggests, that the force of an ideological or religious motivation is such that deterrence is unlikely to work’.
Courts will denounce in the strongest terms preparatory terrorism offending and should signal that such crimes will be met with significant punishment, even where no harm comes of it.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Community protection looms large, especially where the offender has not resiled from their extremist views, because the court is not only concerned with future conduct of a recidivist nature, but with the perfection of the very crime for which the offender has been convicted. Because of the difficulty in detecting and preventing lone wolf terrorism attacks, community protection, along with punishment and both general and specific deterrence, are the focal points in sentencing for that variety of offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: Far from giving priority to the private interests of the offender, this reflects the court’s concern with the community’s interest in minimising the risk of re-offending, having regard to the objective seriousness of terrorism offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.4 – Sentencing purposes

title: Commonwealth terrorist act and advocacy offences: gravity
statement: Engaging in a terrorist act spans mass murder to lesser property damage; look at all the circumstances. Religious and ideological motivation and intent to intimidate government distinguish it from private crimes, so comparison with (e.g.) attempted murder is wrong — though the public/private division is not binary (an unseen attack intended to advance an extremist cause and intimidate the public is no less serious, Shoma); spontaneity does not diminish gravity where the act grew from longstanding extremist views. An adult who equips and encourages a child to commit a terrorist act may be as culpable as the principal. Advocating terrorism is serious (it heightens the probability of an act in Australia) but, with a 5-year maximum, one of the least serious terrorist offences; relevant matters include the number and duration of acts of advocacy, social media, graphic imagery, enthusiasm, audience, original or reposted material and reference to Australia. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: The offence of engaging in a terrorist act covers a broad spectrum of potential offending; from crimes of mass murder at one end to far lesser crimes of property damage at the other.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: It is vital to look at all the circumstances of the individual offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: The terrorist act offender’s religious and ideological motivation, and intention to intimidate the government, distinguishes their acts from those committed in the pursuit of private ends, which come within established offences against the person. It is wrong therefore to sentence such an offender on the basis of a comparison drawn between a terrorist act offence and, for instance, the offence of attempted murder.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: However, the division between the public and private spheres is not binary.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: While the knife attack carried out by the offender in Shoma was neither seen, nor intended to be seen, it was nevertheless done with the intent to advance an extremist cause and to intimidate the public. The absence of witnesses did not make the offending any less serious than a ‘lone wolf’ knife attack in public.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: Moreover, the fact that a terrorist act was spontaneous or dreamed up only hours before its commission will not diminish its gravity where it was the product of longstanding, extremist views harboured by the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: It is an offence to aid, abet, counsel, or procure the commission of a terrorist act. The moral culpability of an adult aider and abettor who equips, and further encourages, a child to commit a terrorist act may be close to, if not at the same level as, that of the principal offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: Alou [190]. Alou was 18 years and 2 months of age at the time of the offence. The court concluded that the 15–year-old principal offender could not have committed the terrorist act unless equipped with the loaded firearm provided by Alou.
Advocating a terrorist act is a serious offence because it heightens the probability of a terrorist act being committed on Australian soil.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: However, in carrying a maximum penalty of 5 years’ imprisonment, it is one of the least serious terrorist offences prescribed by the Criminal Code.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

refs.q: In assessing gravity, the following matters may be relevant: • the number of acts of advocacy • the length of time over which the advocacy took place • the use of social media to accelerate the spread of the message • the circulation of graphic violent imagery and messages • the offender’s level of enthusiasm and encouragement in promoting terrorist acts • the number of persons who subscribed to, and viewed, the offender’s material • whether the material was created by others or reposted by the offender, and • specific reference to Australia in the advocacy.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.2 – Terrorist act offences

title: Commonwealth terrorist organisation offences: gravity and culpability
statement: A terrorist organisation is one directly or indirectly engaged in preparing, planning, assisting or fostering a terrorist act, or a listed organisation. Its history bears on objective seriousness and culpability; seriousness depends on whether it advocates or engages in indiscriminate killing of civilians, is well organised and resourced with intention and capacity, is geographically confined, directly threatens Australia, and recruits children, engages in sexual violence or uses landmines. The court does not evaluate the merits of its ideology (a matter for the legislature) though it may take into account proved dangerousness; claimed commitments to international humanitarian law or to targeting only government forces may not reduce culpability; participation in a non-international armed conflict is irrelevant. Joining an established organisation “eyes wide open” may be more culpable than joining a “rag-tag collection of malcontents” after indoctrination, but membership is always very serious. Membership spans leadership to informal participation; knowledge of objectives and methods and duration matter; a passive, sympathetic chronicler is towards the lowest order; belief in the cause may not of itself affect culpability; membership connected to personal trauma and intergenerational persecution may reduce culpability, and a primary motive to oppose genocide may mitigate somewhat. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: A ‘terrorist organisation’ is an organisation that: • is directly or indirectly engaged in preparing, planning, assisting in or fostering the doing of a terrorist act, or • has been listed in regulations made pursuant to the Criminal Code (‘listed terrorist organisations’).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: The history of the terrorist organisation of which the offender was a member is relevant to the objective seriousness of the offence and the culpability of the offender.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: The objective seriousness of the offence depends on whether the organisation: • advocates or engages in the indiscriminate killing of civilians • is well-organised and resourced at the time of the offence with an intention and capacity to carry out terrorist acts • is geographically confined • through its activities, presents a direct threat to Australia, and • recruits children, engages in sexual violence or uses landmines.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: In assessing objective seriousness, it is not appropriate for the court to evaluate the merits of the organisation’s ideology. While the court can take into account the proved dangerousness of the organisation, the ideology of the organisation is a matter for the legislature in deciding whether to declare the organisation as a terrorist organisation.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: Similarly, the court does not need to take into account any claimed commitment by the organisation to international humanitarian law but may instead look at what the organisation has done or is proposing to do. Even a claimed commitment to targeting only governmental or security forces may not meaningfully reduce the culpability of the organisation if it treats civilian bystanders as acceptable collateral.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: It is not relevant that the organisation participates in a ‘non-international’ armed conflict within the meaning of the Geneva Conventions.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: The history of the organisation is relevant to moral culpability because it is probative of its members’ state of mind. For example, it is likely that an offender joins an established organisation such as Al Qaeda with ‘eyes wide open’; that is, already committed to the organisation’s terrorist philosophy and objectives. In contrast, an offender generally joins a ‘rag-tag collection of malcontents’ in a state of uncertainty or confusion after being seduced by a process of indoctrination. An offender of the latter kind may be less morally culpable than the former.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: But the criminal culpability involved in the membership of a terrorist organisation is always very serious, even where its activities go no further than acts preparatory to a terrorist act.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: The membership of a terrorist organisation comprehends a broad range of conduct, spanning charismatic leadership to informal participation. It is relevant what level of knowledge an offender had of the organisation’s objectives and methods, and the length of time that they remained a member. An offender whose involvement was that of a passive, sympathetic observer seeking to chronicle the struggle of the organisation has been characterised as towards the lowest order of seriousness.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: Lelikan No 5 [56]. While this principle survived appeal, the New South Wales Court of Criminal Appeal found that the offender’s writings and activities in travelling with guerrillas over an extended period of time revealed him to be more than a ‘sympathetic chronicler’ of events: Lelikan 520–521 [140].

Belief in the rightness of the organisation’s cause may not, of itself, affect moral culpability. However, where an offender's informal membership of a terrorist organisation is innately connected to personal trauma and intergenerational persecution, their moral culpability can be reduced. There may also be some mitigation where an offender’s primary motivation in joining a terrorist organisation is to oppose and prevent a genocide.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

refs.q: Listed terrorist organisations can be viewed here on the Australian National Security website.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.3 – Terrorist organisation offences

title: Commonwealth preparatory terrorist offences: the two axes of seriousness
statement: Preparing for or planning a terrorist act is an offence even if no act occurs, without a specific target, or for more than one act; the provisions bite early; the life maximum is a salient indicator of seriousness. Because plots are often detected early and preparatory acts are indefinite, culpability is measured not only by the steps taken but by the nature and extent of the act contemplated — two axes: “actions in contemplation” (the criminal objective) and “acts actually done”; the most serious examples are far advanced on both. On the first axis (of fundamental importance) killing is more serious than property damage, deliberate killing than risk of death, many deaths than few; the absence of a finally selected target carries little weight; planning an attack on police or prison officers is very grave; the offender’s state of mind may be assessed from actions and plea. The second axis is assessed by the general considerations (34.2.1); considerable premeditation and methodical planning elevate dangerousness, and an intention still held at arrest, thwarted only by interception, is much more serious. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: A person commits an offence if they do any act in preparation for or planning, a terrorist act, even if the terrorist act does not occur, and if the preparation or planning is done without a specific target, or for more than one terrorist act.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: These provisions are intended to bite early, long before preparatory acts mature into circumstances of deadly consequence for the community.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: The maximum penalty of life imprisonment is a salient indicator of the objective seriousness with which preparatory terrorist offences are to be regarded.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: As terrorist plots are often detected at their inception, it can be difficult to identify a particular victim who has suffered harm in a recognised sense. And the indefinite nature of preparatory acts means that the offence embraces a wide range of possible physical elements. That being so, an offender’s culpability should not be measured purely by the steps and actions they have taken, but, additionally, by a proper understanding of the nature and extent of the terrorist act contemplated.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: These twin features can be seen as tracking two ‘axes of seriousness’ along which the gravity of preparatory offences may be assessed, as follows: • 'Actions in contemplation', focussing on the offender’s criminal objective, including both threats and other activities targeted at property, electronic systems, public health or safety and the physical well-being and lives of other persons, and • 'Acts actually done', which may include conversations, research, acquisition of equipment, strategic planning, recruitment of offenders and everything done in preparation or planning short of the terrorist act itself.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: Ali 473 [70]–[72]. The axes were applied in R v Halis [2021] VCC 1277.
Logically, the most serious example of the offence will be far advanced along both axes.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: Identifying the seriousness of the terrorist act contemplated (first axis) is a sentencing consideration of fundamental importance, and other things being equal, the offending will be more serious if the planned terrorist act involved: • the killing of persons, rather than causing of property damage • deliberate killing, rather than the risk or possibility of people being killed, and • the killing of many people, rather than one or a few.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: As to culpability, little reductive weight will be given to the absence of a finally selected target. Preparing for, or planning, a terrorist attack on police or prison officers is a very grave offence, whether or not random members of the public are also targeted. In considering what would have happened, had the intended terrorist attack occurred, courts have been prepared to assess the offender’s state of mind, so far as it can be ascertained, by reference to their actions and plea.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: The preparatory acts (second axis) themselves should be assessed by reference to the general considerations (see 34.2.1 – Generally).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

refs.q: Conduct reflecting ‘considerable premeditation, determination and commitment’ and ‘diligent and methodical’ planning over a period of time elevates dangerousness. And a preparatory offence is much more serious if, as at the date of arrest, the offender still intended to carry out the terrorist act, and would have done so but for being intercepted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.4 – Preparatory terrorist offences

title: Commonwealth financing terrorism offences: gravity
statement: Relevant factors: the amount, the identity of the organisation, and the offender’s surrounding conduct. Even a relatively small amount ($5,000 enabling travel to assist Islamic State, Atai) may be a serious example, and elaborate steps over a long period magnify criminality (a significant organisational role). Where an undercover operation meant the funds could never reach the organisation, the offence may still be substantially serious (a broad analogy with drug supply that does not reach the public): that the funds did not arrive is relevant, but the intention to provide them and the failure to stop the transaction remain primary. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: In considering the objective gravity of financing terrorism offences, the following factors may be relevant: • the amount of money involved • the identity of the terrorist organisation, and • the conduct of the offender surrounding the commission of the offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.5 – Financing terrorism offences

refs.q: In Atai, facilitating the movement of $5,000 thus enabling a person to travel to Syria to provide direct assistance to Islamic State was a serious example of making funds available to a terrorist organisation. Engaging in elaborate steps, over a lengthy period of time, magnifies criminality. Despite the ‘relatively small’ amount of money involved, the offender was regarded as playing a ‘significant organisational role’ where they used their contact in the Middle East to facilitate the person’s travel, advised them on their journey, and followed up to ensure their safe arrival.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.5 – Financing terrorism offences

refs.q: Where the activities of an undercover operation mean that there was no prospect of the funds reaching a terrorist organisation, the offence may still be one of substantial seriousness. A broad analogy is drawn with drug supply offences where the drugs do not reach the public. Although it is a relevant factor that the funds did not reach their destination, it remains a primary consideration that the offender intended to provide the funds and took no action to stop the transaction.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.5 – Financing terrorism offences

title: Commonwealth foreign incursion and recruitment offences: gravity; not a “species of terrorism”
statement: Since 1 December 2014 these offences are in Part 5.5 of the Criminal Code (CFIRA repealed); the life maximum for most plainly reflects increased gravity. CFIRA principles remain relevant and vice versa, bearing in mind the different penalty regimes (CFIRA’s “services” language does not exist for the Criminal Code offences). Gravity factors (Alqudsi): the nature and extent of the services, their intention and intended effect; others include duration, planning, commitment, range of conduct (reconnaissance, weapons, armed guard), personal involvement in overthrowing a government, awareness, allegiance, contact with organisations, indoctrination of others, whether an undercover operation was needed for the offence, extremist religious thinking, rank, and the risk of return with enhanced capabilities. Poor planning (a plot foredoomed, success extremely remote) may reduce gravity. Though now within the Cth Crimes Act definition of a terrorism offence, they should not be regarded as a “species of terrorism” (the Manual notes contrary authority: fn 5027, flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6) and must not be sentenced as terrorist act offences (their fault element lacks the ideological or coercive intent). The Manual says it is uncertain how far the designation has affected their inherent gravity: depth of radicalisation may be considered for Criminal Code offences, but extremist ideology may matter less for CFIRA offending, and statements of extremist belief, though synthesised, do not elevate CFIRA objective seriousness. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: On 1 December 2014, the Crimes (Foreign Incursion and Recruitment) Act 1978 (Cth) (‘CFIRA’) was repealed, and foreign incursion and recruitment offences were relocated, with increased maximum penalties, into Part 5.5 of the Criminal Code. The new maximum penalty of life imprisonment for most of these offences plainly reflects increased gravity.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: The purpose of the provisions is ‘to ensure that Australia discharge[s] its international obligation to make criminal the activities of …. [those] who propose to engage in hostile activities in a foreign state and/or assist foreign fighters to do so’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: Some statements of principle derived from CFIRA cases remain relevant in sentencing for offences under the Criminal Code – and vice versa, although the different penalty regimes must be borne in mind.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: For example, the following significant factors relevant to offence gravity were originally described in the CFIRA case of Alqudsi: • the nature and extent of the services performed • the intention with which they were performed, and • their intended effect.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: Note, the form of the offence under the CFIRA referred to performing ‘services’ for people intending to enter a foreign country with intent to engage in hostile activities; that language does not exist for the Criminal Code offences.

Other considerations held to be relevant in assessing objective seriousness and culpability include: • the duration of the offending • the extent of the planning and/or research involved • the offender’s level of commitment and enthusiasm • the range of the offending conduct – whether it included activities such as reconnaissance, maintaining weapons, or performing armed guard duty • whether the offender is personally involved in, or merely provides encouragement to others involved in, the overthrow of a government by force or violence • the offender’s level of awareness of the events going on around them • whether the offender has pledged allegiance to a terrorist organisation or foreign fighting force • whether the offender had direct (or indirect) contact with a terrorist or insurgency organisation • any attempt/s to persuade or indoctrinate others • whether the offence would have been committed if not for the involvement of an undercover police operation • adherence to extremist religious thinking • the offender’s position/rank within a group of co-offenders, and • the risk that the offender might return ‘with enhanced capabilities which may be employed to facilitate terrorist or other acts’ in Australia.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: Gravity may be reduced where the offending is characterised by poor planning, especially if a plot is foredoomed to failure, or the likelihood of success extremely remote.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: In light of their repositioning into the Criminal Code, foreign incursion offences are also included within the definition of a terrorism offence under the Cth Crimes Act s 3. However, they should not be regarded as a ‘species of terrorism’.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: Elmir 281–282 [34]–[39]. Cf DPP (Cth) v El Sabsabi [2017] VSCA 160, [48] (‘El Sabsabi’); Brookman [61].

Moreover, a foreign incursion offender must not be sentenced as if they were convicted of a terrorist act offence; the fault element of these offences does not include any of the features required to prove a terrorist act (i.e., an intention to advance an ideological cause or to coerce or intimidate government).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

refs.q: It is uncertain to what extent designation as a terrorism offence has impacted the inherent gravity of foreign incursion offences. Clearly, the court may take into account the ‘depth and extent’ of an offender’s radicalisation in assessing the gravity of offences under the Criminal Code. However, it may be of relatively lesser significance that an offender subscribes to extremist ideology when offending against the CFIRA. As such, while an offender’s statements about their ‘beliefs in relation to killing in the name of Allah’ or the ‘creation of an Islamic caliphate’ are to be properly synthesised in the sentencing discretion, they are not matters that elevate the objective seriousness of CFIRA offending.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.2 – Gravity and culpability > 34.2.6 – Foreign incursion and recruitment offences

title: Commonwealth terrorist organisation offences: leadership excluded from membership sentencing; concurrency
statement: To avoid double punishment or a breach of De Simoni, leadership of a terrorist organisation is excluded when sentencing for membership (directing activities is a separate offence, Criminal Code s 102.2); totality may warrant substantial concurrency for overlapping membership and advocacy offences. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: To avoid either double punishment or a breach of the De Simoni principle, an offender’s leadership of an terrorist organisation must be excluded from consideration when sentencing for the offence of being a member of the organisation, as there is a separate offence of directing the activities of a terrorist organisation in Criminal Code s 102.2.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence

refs.q: Having regard to the principle of totality, and the circumstances of the offending, a substantial degree of concurrency may be warranted for overlap between a membership offence and a terrorism advocacy offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence

title: Commonwealth terrorism regimes (three-quarters NPP rule; warnings; post-sentence orders)
statement: For Commonwealth terrorism offences: a single NPP of at least three-quarters of the head sentence (Cth Crimes Act s 19AG); warnings about continuing detention or extended supervision orders; post-sentence orders under Criminal Code div 105A (maximum three years, successive orders possible). Outside this app’s Victorian scope; the detail is in guide.terrorism.npp_three_quarters_cth, guide.terrorism.warnings_cth and guide.terrorism.post_sentence_orders_cth.

refs.q: When sentencing for a terrorism offence, the court must fix a single non-parole period of at least three-quarters of the head sentence pursuant to the Cth Crimes Act s 19AG (‘three-quarters rule’).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences

refs.q: When sentencing terrorism offenders, the court must give the offender a warning that an application may be made for a continuing detention order or an extended supervision order
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.2 – Warning requirements

refs.q: The maximum length of PSOs is 3 years, although successive orders may be made.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

title: Commonwealth terrorism offences: the s 19AG three-quarters non-parole rule
statement: For a Commonwealth terrorism offence (and attempt, incitement or conspiracy to commit one; other minimum non-parole period offences include Division 80 and espionage offences) the court must fix a single NPP of at least three-quarters of the head sentence, for all federal sentences the person is to serve, whether or not imposed at the same sitting; it supersedes a recognizance release order; for a federal offence that is not a minimum NPP offence sentenced with one, the rule is calculated by reference only to the minimum NPP offence(s). Life is taken to be 30 years (so a minimum NPP of 22 years 6 months). The court need not find what NPP would otherwise apply; it must not fix the NPP and work back, but impose a proportionate head sentence and then apply the rule, without ameliorating the head sentence to offset s 19AG. The rule applies only to imprisonment and does not affect other options. For an offender under 18, the rule applies unless exceptional circumstances justify a shorter NPP, treating community protection as paramount and the person’s best interests as primary. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: When sentencing for a terrorism offence, the court must fix a single non-parole period of at least three-quarters of the head sentence pursuant to the Cth Crimes Act s 19AG (‘three-quarters rule’).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences

refs.q: This requirement also applies to attempt, incitement, or conspiracy to commit a terrorism offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences

refs.q: This provision applies notwithstanding that a court may otherwise have had the discretion to make or confirm an RRO, confirm a pre-existing non-parole period, or decline to fix a non-parole period: Cth Crimes Act s 19AG(5). Other ‘minimum non-parole period offences’ to which s 19A applies are offences against Division 80 (treason, urging violence and advocating terrorism) and ss 91.1(1), 91.2(1) (espionage) of the Criminal Code.

A single non-parole period must be fixed in respect of all federal sentences the person is to serve or complete, regardless of whether the sentences are imposed at the same sitting. If the offender was subject to a recognizance release order (‘RRO’), the non-parole period supersedes that order. When sentencing for a federal offence which is not a minimum non-parole period offence together with one (or more) minimum non-parole period offences, the three-quarters rule also applies to the first offence, but it is calculated by reference only to the minimum non-parole period offence or, if more than one, the aggregate of them.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences

refs.q: The TES is 9 years, but in applying the three-quarters rule, the forged document sentence is disregarded. The aggregate of the terrorism sentences is 8 years, so the statutory minimum NPP is 6 years.
A sentence of life imprisonment is taken to be a sentence of 30 years’ imprisonment.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences

refs.q: Cth Crimes Act s 19AG(3)(a). The minimum non-parole period for a sentence of life imprisonment is therefore 22 years and 6 months per the three-quarters rule.

A court is not required to determine the period or minimum period which would have been required to be served but for the requirements of s 19AG before fixing the non-parole period. The court is not permitted to fix a non-parole period and work backwards to the corresponding head sentence. Rather, it must impose what it considers to be the proportionate head sentence and then fix the non-parole period in accordance with the three-quarters rule. An appropriate head sentence must not be ameliorated to compensate for or offset the effect of s 19AG. The three-quarters rule applies only if the offender is sentenced to imprisonment and does not affect the availability of other sentencing options.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences

refs.q: When sentencing an offender who is under 18 years of age in relation to a minimum non-parole period offence, the court must apply the three-quarters rule unless it is satisfied that ‘exceptional circumstances’ exist to justify fixing a shorter single non-parole period. In determining whether exceptional circumstances exist, the court must treat: • the protection of the community as the paramount consideration, and • the best interests of the person as a primary consideration.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.1 – Minimum non-parole period offences > 34.5.1.1 – Child offender

title: Commonwealth terrorism offenders: warning about post-sentence orders
statement: When sentencing for a specified terrorism offence, contravention of an extended or interim supervision order, or (if the DPP informs the court a warning must be given) contravention of a control order, the court must warn that an application may be made under div 105A for a continuing detention order or an extended supervision order, and that contravention of a continuing detention order is an offence; it must state when the AFP Minister may apply (before the end of that sentence, or any later sentence while continuously detained; for control order contraventions, before the end of that sentence), and may note that whether orders are made is for a court at the time. Failure to warn does not affect the sentence’s validity or prevent an application. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: When sentencing terrorism offenders, the court must give the offender a warning that an application may be made for a continuing detention order or an extended supervision order (see 34.6 – Post-sentence orders).
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.2 – Warning requirements

refs.q: The warning requirements apply to a court sentencing a person who has been convicted of: • specified terrorism offences • contravention of an extended supervision order / interim supervision order, or • contravention of a control order.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.2 – Warning requirements

refs.q: But only if the DPP informs the court that a warning must be given: Criminal Code s 105A.23(1)(b).

The warning must state that an application may be made under div 105A of the Criminal Code for a continuing detention order, requiring the person to be detained in a prison after the end of their sentence, or an extended supervision order, imposing conditions on the person after the end of their sentence, and that contravention of a continuing detention order is an offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.2 – Warning requirements

refs.q: Where the offender has been convicted of a specified terrorism offence or contravention of an extended supervision order / interim supervision order, the court must state that the AFP Minister may apply for post-sentence orders before the end of the sentence for that offence, or any later sentence if the person is continuously detained in custody in a prison. Where the offender has been convicted of contravening a control order, the court must state that the application may be made before the end of the sentence for that offence. It may be noted in the warning that whether such orders are made would be determined by a court at the time of hearing any such application.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.2 – Warning requirements

refs.q: Failure to give a warning does not affect the validity of the sentence for the offence, nor does it prevent an application from being made for post-sentence orders.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.5 – Formulation of Sentence > 34.5.2 – Warning requirements

title: Commonwealth post-sentence orders (div 105A): continuing detention and extended supervision orders
statement: Terrorist offenders who would pose an unacceptable risk of committing a serious Part 5.3 offence may be subject to post-sentence orders (PSOs): a continuing detention order (CDO: further detention in prison) or an extended supervision order (ESO: conditions after release; contravention is an offence); maximum 3 years each, successive orders possible; interim orders up to 28 days, totalling no more than 3 months per type absent exceptional circumstances. The Supreme Court may make them for an offender at least 18 at sentence end, detained in custody in a prison for a specified terrorism offence (Division 72 Subdivision A; a serious Part 5.3 offence, i.e. maximum 7 years or more; Part 5.5 except recruitment advertising; the repealed CFIRA except recruitment advertising), or already subject to a PSO. Application: by the AFP Minister, no earlier than 12 months before the sentence (or order) ends, after reasonable inquiries for facts that would support no order (no particular risk report is required); the Manual notes a sunset: no PSO may be applied for, affirmed or made after 7 December 2026 (fn 5120). Experts: a preliminary hearing within 28 days; the court may appoint experts; the offender must attend, and what they say is inadmissible against them except in div 104/105A proceedings. CDO: satisfied to a high degree of probability, on admissible evidence, of an unacceptable risk, and that no less restrictive Part 5.3 measure (control order, ESO) would be effective; “unacceptable risk” is flexible, weighing likelihood and seriousness, and need not be linked to a specific offence; the AFP Minister bears the onus; if not satisfied the court must consider an ESO. ESO: satisfied on the balance of probabilities of an unacceptable risk and that each condition and their combined effect is reasonably necessary and reasonably appropriate and adapted to protect the community (the object of div 105A is paramount); contents prescribed; an ESO revokes any CDO in force. Relevant considerations are listed (s 105A.6B). Conditions: broad (exclusion zones, residence, travel documents, non-communication, technology bans, programs), no more than 12 hours a day at specified premises; exemption conditions; variation on application. Review: the AFP Minister must apply within 12 months of commencement or the last review, or the PSO ceases. Commonwealth material: outside the app’s Victorian scope; never applied to the Victorian s 4B(1) offence.

refs.q: Terrorist offenders who, if released into the community, would pose an unacceptable risk of committing a serious Part 5.3 offence, may be subject to the regime of post-sentence orders (‘PSOs’) under Division 105A.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

refs.q: There are two types of PSOs: a continuing detention order (‘CDO’) and an extended supervision order (‘ESO’). CDOs commit the offender to a further period of detention in a prison after the completion of their sentence. ESOs impose certain conditions on an offender after they are released into the community, and any contravention of them is an offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

refs.q: The maximum length of PSOs is 3 years, although successive orders may be made.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

refs.q: The Supreme Court may make PSOs in relation to an offender who will be at least 18 years old when their sentence ends and who is currently detained in custody in a prison serving a sentence for any of the following specified terrorism offences: • an offence against Subdivision A of Division 72 (international terrorist activities using explosive or lethal devices) • a serious Part 5.3 offence • an offence against Part 5.5 (foreign incursions and recruitment), or • an offence against the repealed CFIRA.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

refs.q: A person is ‘detained in custody in a prison’ if they are detained in a jail, lock-up or remand centre, including under a continuing detention order or interim detention order, but not if they are in immigration detention: Criminal Code s 100.2(3B).
That is, an offence against Part 5.3 (terrorism offences) for which the maximum penalty is 7 imprisonment years or more: at s 3.
Excluding an offence against subsection 119.7(2) or (3) (publishing recruitment advertisements).
Excluding an offence against paragraph 9(1)(b) or (c) of CFIRA (publishing recruitment advertisements).
An offender will also satisfy the preconditions for a PSO if they are currently subject to one, whether final or interim.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

refs.q: PSOs can be made on interim basis for a period of no more than 28 days in accordance with the procedures set out in ss 105A.9 and 105A.9A. The total period of interim PSOs in relation to an offender may be no more than 3 months for each type of order unless there are exceptional circumstances.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders

refs.q: The AFP Minister (currently the Minister for Home Affairs) or their legal representative may apply to the court for a CDO or an ESO in relation to a terrorist offender. The application must not be made more than 12 months before the end of a sentence of imprisonment for a specified terrorism offence, or the period in which any PSO (including an interim PSO) or confirmed control order is in force.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.1 – Application

refs.q: Ibid s 105A.5. A sunset provision provides that a PSO cannot be applied for, affirmed, or made, after 7 December 2026: at s 105A.25.

The AFP Minister must ensure that reasonable inquiries are made to ascertain facts known to any Commonwealth law enforcement, intelligence or security officer that would reasonably support a finding that neither type of PSO should be made in relation to the offender. There is no requirement to provide any particular risk assessment report prior to the commencement of proceedings.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.1 – Application

refs.q: The court must hold a preliminary hearing to determine whether to appoint one or more relevant experts within 28 days of the offender receiving the application. The court may appoint one or more experts at either the preliminary hearing or a later time if it considers that doing so is likely to materially assist it in deciding whether to make a CDO or an ESO. The AFP Minister and the offender may each nominate experts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.2 – Appointment of expert

refs.q: The court must tell the offender that: • they must attend the expert’s assessment • any information they give at the assessment is not admissible in evidence against them in any criminal or civil proceedings, except in proceedings under div 104 or div 105A (including appeal proceedings), and • the assessment may be taken into account in proceedings to make, vary or review any PSO relating to them. The expert assesses the offender and provides a report to the court, the AFP Minister, and the offender which addresses the offender’s risk of committing a serious Part 5.3 offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.2 – Appointment of expert

refs.q: The court may make a CDO if: • an application has been made for a CDO in accordance with s 105A.5 • having regard to the relevant considerations (see 34.6.3.1 – Relevant considerations), it is satisfied to a high degree of probability, on the basis of admissible evidence, that the offender poses an unacceptable risk of committing a serious Part 5.3 offence, and • there is no less restrictive measure available under Part 5.3 that would be effective in preventing that unacceptable risk.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: Criminal Code s 105A.7(1), Note 2 makes it clear that an ESO is an example of a less restrictive measure.
The rules of evidence and procedure for civil matters apply when the court has regard to these matters: at s 105A.7(1), Note 1.

While a ‘measure’ is a broad descriptor, the court is restricted to having regard to those measures available under Part 5.3 – that is, to control orders and ESOs. No strict boundary exists between measures relevant to the risk assessment and those that would be effective in preventing unacceptable risk; these analyses overlap. ‘Less restrictive measures’ captures measures which the court can be satisfied realistically could be in place, though the evidence does not necessarily establish will be in place.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: But note, Pender was decided before amendments to the Criminal Code removed the words ‘if the offender is released into the community’ from s 105A.7(1)(b). The court is now required simply to consider whether an offender poses ‘an unacceptable risk of committing a serious Pt 5.3 offence’.

‘Unacceptable risk’ is not defined in the Criminal Code, but it has been construed as a flexible concept calibrated to the nature and degree of the risk and adaptive to the circumstances of each particular case. Whether a risk is unacceptable requires consideration of both the likelihood of the risk eventuating, and the seriousness of the consequences if it does. The risk must carry a threat of harm to members of the community that is sufficiently serious as to make it unacceptable to the court. As the provision does not link unacceptable risk to any specific offence, it is sufficient to identify the risk as that of committing one or more serious Part 5.3 offences.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: The AFP Minister bears the onus of satisfying the court of the relevant matters. If it is not satisfied, the court must turn its mind to whether it is appropriate to make an ESO instead and must seek the following information from the AFP Minister: • the proposed conditions that would be sought for an ESO • an explanation for why each of the conditions should be imposed, and • if the AFP Minister is aware of any reasons why those conditions should not be imposed – a statement of facts.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: For the court to be able to make an ESO, one (or more) of the following conditions must apply: • an application has been made for an ESO in accordance with s 105A.5 • an application has been made for a CDO (as above), but the court is not satisfied to make a CDO, or • the court has reviewed a CDO under s 105A.12 and is not satisfied as mentioned in s 105A.12(4)(a). Then, the court may make the ESO if: • having regard to the relevant considerations (see 34.6.3.1 – Relevant considerations) it is satisfied on the balance of probabilities, on the basis of admissible evidence, that the offender poses an unacceptable risk of committing a serious Part 5.3 offence, and • it is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that each condition (see 34.6.3.2 – Conditions) and the combined effect of all of the conditions, to be imposed upon the offender by the ESO is reasonably necessary and reasonably appropriate and adapted, for the purpose of protecting the community from that unacceptable risk.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: Once again, the AFP Minister bears the onus of proof.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: The object of Division 105A – to protect the community from serious Part 5.3 offences – is a paramount consideration the court must consider when deciding whether each proposed condition is reasonably necessary, appropriate, and adapted.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: An ESO must state: • that the court is satisfied of the above matters • the name of the offender • the conditions, and any exemption conditions, it imposes • the period during which the order is to be in force (no more than 3 years), and • that the offender’s lawyer may request a copy of the order.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: If the court makes an ESO, any CDO that is in force immediately before the ESO begins is automatically revoked.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination

refs.q: In deciding whether to make a PSO, the court must have regard to: • the object of Division 105A – that is, to protect the community from serious Part 5.3 offences • the report/s of any relevant experts appointed by the court and/or the AFP Minister and the offender’s level of participation in the assessment • any other assessment conducted by a relevant expert of the risk of the offender committing a serious Part 5.3 offence • any report relating to the extent to which the offender can reasonably and practicably be managed in the community that has been prepared by State or Territory corrective services or any other competent person or body • any treatment or rehabilitation programs in which the offender has had an opportunity to participate, and the level of the offender’s participation in such programs • the level of the offender’s compliance with any obligations to which they have been subject while on parole, a PSO, an interim PSO, or a control order • any prior convictions and findings of guilt in relation to any specified terrorism offence • the views of the sentencing court at the time of sentencing for any specified terrorism offence • whether the offender is subject to any order under a State or Territory law that is equivalent to PSO, and if so, the conditions of that order, and • any other information about the risk of the offender committing a serious Part 5.3 offence.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination > 34.6.3.1 – Relevant considerations

refs.q: The court has a broad power to impose conditions on an ESO, constrained principally by the fact that it must be satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the combined impact of all conditions is reasonably necessary, and reasonably appropriate and adapted, to protect the community from the unacceptable risk of the offender committing a serious Part 5.3 offence. A condition also must not mandate that an offender remain at specified premises for more than 12 hours within any 24 hour period.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination > 34.6.3.2 – Conditions

refs.q: The general rules contemplate a wide array of conditions; prohibiting, restricting and/or imposing obligations on the offender in respect of certain conduct and/or classes of conduct. Examples include conditions relating to: • exclusion from specified areas, residing (or not being present) at a particular premises • a prohibition on applying for travel documents • non-communication with specified persons • bans on the use of specified forms of technology (including the internet), and • participation in treatment, rehabilitation, or intervention programs.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination > 34.6.3.2 – Conditions

refs.q: See s 105A.7B(3)(b) for examples of conditions relating to monitoring and enforcement. The court may specify that certain conditions included in the ESO are exemption conditions. An exemption condition is a condition for which the offender may apply, in writing, to a specified authority, for a temporary exemption.
refs.path: Part E – Specific offences > 34 – Terrorism offences > 34.6 – Post-sentence orders > 34.6.3 – Determination > 34.6.3.2 – Conditions

refs.q: An ESO or an interim supervision order may be varied by consent, or otherwise, in accordance with the procedures set out in s 105A.9C and 105A.9D. If the AFP Minister is satisfied that a condition of an ESO or interim supervision order is no longer necessary, or reasonably appropriate and adapted for the purpose of protecting the community from the unacceptable risk of the offender committing a serious Part 5.3 offence, they may make an application to the court to remove or vary the condition. The offender may also make an application to vary or remove one or more conditions.

refs.q: The AFP Minister must, within 12 months of a PSO commencing, apply to the court for a review of the PSO. If the PSO has since been reviewed, then the next application must be made within 12 months of the most recent review. If an application is not made within time, the PSO ceases to be in force at the end of the relevant period; that is, either 12 months after it began or 12 months after the most recent review. Via this process, the Criminal Code provides for mandatory yearly reviews to ensure that the conditions on ESOs remain reasonably necessary, and appropriate and adapted.
